Energy labels are strictly regulated under product catalogs; they must include the energy efficiency grade, relevant metrics, and a unique identification code. Falsifying or misusing energy labels, or failing to apply them where required, is punishable under the Energy Conservation Law across China.
5-32.note: These inspections involve regulators selecting a sample of products for testing; their results do not represent the overall market compliance rate, nor can they be used to rank online platforms. There are no studies quantifying exactly how many substandard products can be avoided by conducting such checks, which is why this item is rated B. The verification platform cx.cnca.cn used in this section was inaccessible during our checks; the correct entry point is the homepage at cnca.gov.cn. Inspection reports are updated annually, so always consult the most recent edition when referencing them.

5-33.t: Bracelets, jade, luxury watches, and collectibles should be judged by “how much you spend” rather than “how much you save”
5-33.cost: There’s no upfront cost — just don’t justify buying these items by claiming they’ll appreciate in value later. The real challenge is resisting the urge to allocate extra budget for “preservation of value.”
5-33.human: A portion of the purchase price for such items is already consumption tax: watches priced at 10,000 yuan or more incur a 20% tax; gold, platinum, and diamond jewelry faces a 5% tax; other precious stones and jade incur a 10% tax, plus standard VAT. This tax cannot be reclaimed when you resell the item. If you truly love these items, treat them as a personal expense rather than an investment.
5-33.gain: On the purchase side, tax rates are clearly defined in the Consumption Tax Schedule: “luxury watches” are taxed at 20%. Within “precious jewelry and stones,” gold, platinum, and diamond jewelry incur a 5% tax, while other precious stones and jade incur 10%. “Luxury watches” are defined as any watch with a sales price (excluding VAT) of 10,000 yuan or more. On the resale side, the Pawnbroking Management Regulations apply: Article 36 limits pawn terms to a maximum of six months; Article 37 sets interest rates based on the six-month benchmark rate published by the People’s Bank of China, which cannot be deducted upfront from the loan amount. Article 38 caps monthly comprehensive fees for pawning watches or jade at 42‰ of the loan amount, plus an additional 4.2% monthly fee. For real estate mortgages, this cap is 27‰, and for property rights pledges it is 24‰. Article 40 states that if the pawner fails to redeem or renew the pawn within five days of the term’s end, the item becomes forfeited; Article 43 permits auctioning forfeited items valued at over 30,000 yuan, with proceeds first covering auction fees and loan principal plus interest, leaving any remainder to be returned to the pawner (or recovered from them if insufficient).
5-33.note: When pawning these items, remember that monthly comprehensive fees cap at 42‰ of the loan amount — equating to roughly 50% of the loan value over a year. This figure is a rough estimate derived by multiplying the monthly rate by 12, not an exact annual interest rate. While tax and fee rates are explicitly stated, there are no official statistics confirming long-term appreciation for such items; this guide makes no predictions or endorsements. The key point is to avoid treating personal purchases as investments: buying these items simply because you enjoy wearing them is perfectly fine, but adding budget based on hopes of future resale value is a recipe for financial loss. Gold also warrants separate consideration: investment-grade bullion traded by weight differs from jewelry sold by piece, which includes design and labor costs not recovered upon resale. Listed prices on secondhand platforms are not actual transaction values and should not be treated as market benchmarks.

5-34.t: For jewelry and gemstones, only test reports bearing the CMA mark are acceptable; you must also verify the issuing agency on the regulator’s official website
5-34.cost: No cost at all. Checking an agency’s qualifications takes just a few minutes before placing any order.
5-34.human: Certificates can be forged, so what truly matters is confirming the agency that issued it. Any testing organization allowed to issue reports must hold proper credentials, and its reports must display the CMA mark. The regulatory authority publishes a list of certified agencies on its website, making it easy for consumers to confirm whether a given provider is on that list. In actual enforcement cases, some “national inspection certificates” accompanying goods were found to have been fabricated by unrelated parties.
5-34.gain: The relevant rules are laid out in the *Administrative Measures for Qualification Recognition of Inspection and Testing Agencies*. Article 2 states that qualification recognition is a licensing process for agencies that provide data and results with evidentiary value to the public; it involves a thorough review followed by issuance of certification. Article 15 specifies that the CMA mark comprises both the CMA logo and the corresponding certificate number. Article 21 requires any agency issuing such data to display this mark on all reports. Article 22 mandates that authorities publish all certified agencies and their current status online. Article 34 imposes a fine of up to 30,000 RMB on any agency operating without proper certification. Article 37 similarly penalizes up to 30,000 RMB any act of forging, altering, or misusing such certification marks. Real-world examples illustrate these rules: in June 2026, China’s State Administration for Market Regulation released typical cases of fraud in the traditional crafts market. One involved a livestream in Donghai, Jiangsu, where sellers claimed to offer “natural, unacid-washed, unprocessed Burmese A‑grade gems” and displayed a “national inspection certificate.” Laboratory tests, however, revealed the items to be dyed quartzite, treated jadeite, glass, and plastic; the certificate had been produced by a contact of the seller. Another case in the same county uncovered 469 suspected counterfeit crystal products; 210 proved to be natural crystal while 259 were synthetic. In Zhenping, Henan, a shop displayed a board claiming partnership with a “GIA CMA China Gemstone Testing Center” and sold 181 counterfeit “National Gemstone Quality Supervision Center” certification tags alongside bracelets nationwide.
5-34.note: China has established national standards for naming jewelry and gemstones. Test conclusions are often phrased as “quartzite (dyed)” or “jadeite (treated)”; the words inside the parentheses indicate the price difference. Terms such as “A‑grade,” “old‑mine,” and “unprocessed” are marketing buzzwords, not technical conclusions; the livestream mentioned earlier used exactly these phrases. Other deceptive tactics documented in these cases include faking mining sites, staging “miner” livestreams, deploying online trolls to hype sales, and inventing stories about urgent financial needs or family emergencies. Claims that products can “treat rheumatism, boost immunity, improve sleep, or clear blood vessels” are also deemed false advertising and are prosecuted accordingly. For larger purchases, the general verification method is outlined in Section 32 (checking sampling reports and 3C certification). Information on whom to contact when problems arise in a livestream is provided in Sections 29 and 30 (referring to platform rules and requesting data from the platform).

5-35.t: Random sales such as blind boxes and gacha games are treated as “money that won’t come back”
5-35.cost: There is no direct cost involved. You simply need to set a strict budget before buying. The real challenge is resisting the urge to keep purchasing when you fail to get the item you wanted.
5-35.human: Sellers must display the draw rules, probabilities, and quantities of limited‑edition items in a highly visible manner. They are prohibited from manipulating results behind the scenes or offering empty boxes. While the guidelines encourage setting minimum guarantees and limits on spending and number of draws, they are not mandatory. For blind boxes purchased online, if the seller has clearly explained the terms and you have confirmed them, you cannot exercise the seven‑day right to return after opening the box.
5-35.gain: The basis for these rules is the “Guidelines on the Operation of Blind Box Business (Trial)”. Article 9 mandates that a list of key information be displayed prominently so consumers know it before buying. This information includes the product name, type, design, draw rules, distribution of items, quantity of limited items, draw probabilities, and the range of item values. The same article also forbids three practices: altering draw results or probabilities through backend manipulation, refusing or delaying delivery of items via cashbacks or exchanges, and producing empty boxes. Article 11 merely “encourages” operators to implement safeguards such as limits on draw time, spending, and frequency to promote rational consumption. Article 17 applies to blind boxes sold online; if the seller has fully informed you and you have confirmed the terms, the seven‑day return right does not apply after opening. Operators must not replace your explicit consent with pre‑checked boxes. Article 21 states that blind boxes must not be used as a guise for gambling. Article 23 prohibits sales to children under eight; for those aged eight and older, consent from a legal guardian must be obtained.
5-35.note: These guidelines serve as recommendations for operators and are not themselves a basis for penalties. In case of disputes, laws such as the Product Quality Law, Anti‑Unfair Competition Law, and Consumer Rights Protection Law apply. Specific grounds for complaints include failure to disclose probabilities, discrepancies between advertised and actual probabilities, and receipt of empty boxes. Before filing a complaint, record screenshots of the rules and the unboxing process. The exclusion of the seven‑day return right requires that the seller gave full disclosure and you confirmed it; default selections cannot substitute your consent. Additional rules govern sales to minors: no sales to children under eight, and for older minors proof of guardian consent is mandatory. Information on refunding mobile‑game micro‑transactions made by children can be found in section 9 of this chapter. The 24‑hour cooling‑off period for large non‑essential purchases is described in section 23. The cycle of “initial excitement fading into further purchases” is discussed in section 6, item 23.

5-36.t: If you care about what’s in your food, buy pre-packaged products: loose goods at retail counters aren’t legally required to list ingredients
5-36.cost: No cost at all. Pre-packaged versions of the same items are usually a bit pricier than loose ones. Checking the ingredient list takes just a few seconds.
5-36.human: The law only mandates ingredient lists for pre-packaged foods; loose goods have no such requirement. For loose products, retailers only need to display the product name, production date, shelf life, and manufacturer details. So, the absence of any mention of additives does not mean they were not added — it simply means the law does not require them to be listed. If you care about what’s in your food, opt for pre-packaged versions where both the full ingredient list and additive details are clearly printed.
5-36.gain: Article 67 of China’s Food Safety Law stipulates that all pre-packaged foods must carry a label containing nine mandatory pieces of information. The second item on this list is the “list of ingredients or components,” and the seventh item is “the generic names of any food additives used, as defined in national standards.” Article 68 contains far fewer requirements for loose foods: it only requires retailers to display the product name, production date or batch number, shelf life, and the manufacturer’s name, address, and contact details on the packaging or container. There is no mention of ingredient lists or additives here. This distinction is most evident in frozen seafood products. GB 2760—2024 permits the use of phosphoric acid and phosphates as moisture retention agents — commonly referred to as water-retaining agents — in frozen seafood, with a maximum permitted usage level of 5.0 g/kg calculated as phosphate. Use within this limit is fully legal. The main issues arise from excessive usage and the practice of adding ice to increase product weight. Following a 2025 exposé by China Central Television’s 3·15 Gala, which revealed that some shrimp producers illegally added excessive amounts of water-retaining agents (composite phosphates) and added extra ice to boost weight, regulatory authorities mandated that all such products must clearly list water-retaining agents like phosphates, net weight (excluding ice coating weight), and full ingredient lists on their labels (this requirement applies nationwide, per the third 2025 amendment to China’s Food Safety Law, effective 1 December 2025).
5-36.note: The fact that additives are not listed on a product does not mean they were not added — it simply means the law does not require them to be disclosed. If you want to know exactly what a product contains, always choose pre-packaged versions. For frozen shrimp, fish fillets, and similar items, the net weight listed on pre-packaged packaging already excludes ice coating weight; using this figure to calculate unit price gives a much more accurate cost estimate. For loose products priced by weight, the actual edible weight after thawing may drop significantly. Water-retaining agents are legal and not a safety hazard as long as they are used within permitted limits — do not mistake them for toxic substances. Excessive usage and added ice are purely commercial issues: you end up paying a premium price for mostly water content. Conversely, loose goods counters may also fail to display the four mandatory details required by Article 68: product name, production date, shelf life, and manufacturer contact information. Failure to display any of these constitutes a violation of the law. Consumers can choose not to purchase such products or file a complaint via the 12315 hotline. For business owners looking to sell packaged foods, specific labeling requirements are outlined in Section 12, Article 9 of this guide. This item delivers the highest level of benefit to both you and your family.

5-37.t: Stocks that have lost value should also be sold according to pre‑set rules — don’t try to even out costs by buying more
5-37.cost: No cost at all. The hard part is admitting the loss and actually selling the stock.
5-37.human: Human nature drives us to sell winners and hold losers. In seven years of data from 10,000 U.S. accounts, stocks that rose were sold about 50% more often than those that fell. The same investors also tended to add to positions in losing stocks. Yet over the following year those unloved losers underperformed the sold winners by an average of 3.4 percentage points.
5-37.gain: This study examined every trade made by 10,000 accounts at a U.S. discount broker from 1987 to 1993. The proportion of profitable stocks sold (PGR) was 0.148, while the proportion of losing stocks sold (PLR) was 0.098 — a difference of 0.050 with a t‑value exceeding 35. In other words, rising stocks were sold more than 50% more often than falling ones. Investors also bought losing stocks more frequently: the re‑purchase rate for losers was 0.135 versus 0.094 for winners, again with a strong statistical significance. The data also contradicted the belief that “stuck stocks will eventually bounce back.” Over the next year, the excess returns of sold profitable stocks exceeded those of kept losing stocks by 3.4 percentage points. These excess returns represent performance above the market index. As a concrete illustration, selling $1,000 worth of a losing stock instead of a winning one would yield roughly 4.4% more return in the following year; this figure includes tax savings from the early sale under U.S. tax rules (1987‑1993).
5-37.note: This point addresses the decision “to sell or not to sell”; point 15 (“avoid excessive trading”) deals with how often to trade — the two are not contradictory. Following a pre‑defined rule actually reduces the number of trades. Mathematically, buying more shares does lower the average cost per share, but treating this as a way to recover losses is misguided; it merely increases the amount of capital tied up in a single stock (see point 19, “don’t bet everything on one stock”). The tax calculations apply only to the U.S. system and cannot be directly applied in China; all other conclusions remain valid. The data originate from U.S. accounts in the 1980s‑1990s; trading costs and tax regimes differ for A‑share investors. This information is not intended as investment advice.

5-38.t: Planning to invest in overseas assets such as U.S. stocks? Use QDII funds or the Hong Kong Stock Connect program — don’t open accounts with foreign brokers, and don’t use your annual foreign exchange quota for buying foreign stocks
5-38.cost: There’s no direct cost — you can purchase QDII funds via your own bank or brokerage app in just a few minutes. The trade-off is that the selection of available funds is more limited than at foreign brokers.
5-38.human: Starting May 2026, foreign brokers such as Tiger Brokers, Futu, and LongBridge are no longer allowed to accept new accounts from mainland investors. Existing account holders may only sell their holdings and withdraw funds within two years; no further purchases are permitted. Using your annual foreign exchange quota to buy overseas stocks is also prohibited; violators lose eligibility for that quota for the current year and the following two years. The only legal ways to invest in foreign assets remain QDII funds and the Hong Kong Stock Connect program.
5-38.gain: On May 22, 2026, eight Chinese authorities — including the China Securities Regulatory Commission, Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, Ministry of Public Security, People’s Bank of China, State Administration for Market Regulation, National Financial Regulatory Administration, Cyberspace Administration of China, and State Administration of Foreign Exchange — jointly issued a plan to comprehensively curb illegal cross-border securities, futures, and fund activities. The goal is to fully eliminate such activities within two years. Foreign firms may no longer market or solicit clients in China, nor provide services such as account opening, trade execution, or fund transfers. For current account holders, only one-way sales and withdrawals are permitted; after two years, all related websites, trading apps, and servers must be shut down. On the same day, the CSRC announced it would confiscate all illegal earnings of Tiger Brokers, Futu, and LongBridge and impose severe penalties. Official guidance stresses using legal channels such as the Hong Kong Stock Connect, QDII funds, and Cross‑Border Wealth Management Link for overseas investing. Meanwhile, the State Administration of Foreign Exchange explicitly states that personal foreign exchange may not be used for overseas real estate, securities investment, life insurance, or similar unapproved capital‑account purposes. Violators are placed on a “watch list,” lose their annual foreign‑exchange allowance for three years, face administrative penalties, possible anti‑money‑laundering investigations, and negative entries in their credit records (effective May 2026).
5-38.note: These regulations target foreign brokerage firms rather than individual investors; no penalties are specified for investors themselves. Those already holding accounts abroad need only sell and withdraw funds within two years. Each of the three legal channels has its own eligibility criteria — be sure to check with your bank or broker. Past strong performance of U.S. stocks does not guarantee future returns. When investing via QDII funds, follow the same principles outlined in items 17 (broad‑based index funds) and 19 (don’t concentrate assets in a single stock, platform, or market) — opt for diversified index funds rather than betting on one market. Separate limits apply to overseas cash withdrawals; see item 21.6 for details. This information is not investment advice.

5-39.t: Only buy insurance for losses your savings can’t cover; use an emergency fund for losses you can afford
5-39.cost: No money is required. All you need to do is list the major potential losses your household might face and determine which ones exceed your savings capacity. This takes about half an hour.
5-39.human: The premiums you pay won’t all be returned to you; a portion goes toward the insurer’s operating costs and profit. Therefore, insurance is worthwhile only for rare events that would otherwise overwhelm your finances — such as serious illness, a car accident causing injury to others, or the death of a primary breadwinner. For smaller losses that your savings can handle, an emergency fund is the better choice.
5-39.gain: Only a fraction of the premiums collected by insurers is paid out as claims. The remainder covers sales, administration, and profit. Regulations require insurers selling short-term individual health plans to publish their “overall claims ratio” on their website every six months; this figure roughly indicates what proportion of premiums is paid out in claims. On average, buying insurance for any given loss ends up costing you a little extra over time. The upside is that it spreads a potentially catastrophic expense into a series of manageable annual payments. The smaller the loss and the easier it is for you to pay out of pocket, the less advantageous this trade-off becomes. Following this logic, several types of insurance mentioned earlier in this book are worth purchasing: one-year health insurance is covered in Section 7, Item 20; auto liability insurance for drivers is discussed in Item 26 of this section; overseas medical coverage is detailed in Section 21, Item 4; and term life insurance for households dependent on your income is explained in Item 41 of this section (nationwide, effective 2021).
5-39.note: This recommendation is assigned a Grade C because no official statistics exist to determine precisely which policies offer good value. The guidance provided here is meant to help you make a reasoned choice. For low-cost risks — such as cracked phone screens or minor flight delays — you can easily cover the costs yourself, so these policies are generally unnecessary. Similarly, if your savings can sustain you for a year or two without income, you may opt out of critical illness insurance, which compensates for lost earnings during illness. Basic medical insurance is a mandatory social insurance program; it does not fall under this evaluation framework and must be purchased regardless, as explained in Section 7, Item 9. For smaller unexpected expenses, an emergency fund is the appropriate safeguard, as described in Item 27 of this section. Ultimately, the primary beneficiaries of this advice are you and your family.

5-40.t: If someone at home depends on your income, buy term life insurance for the breadwinner first — not for your kids
5-40.cost: A few hundred to a few thousand yuan per year, depending on age, coverage amount, and policy length (this is a rough estimate by the author; no official figures exist). Be sure to disclose your health status truthfully before applying; the process takes about half an hour.
5-40.human: Term life insurance covers you only for a set number of years. If you pass away during that period, your family receives a payout. This coverage is meant to protect dependents who rely on your earnings — for instance, if your mortgage is still unpaid or your children are still young. If no one depends on you financially, this insurance isn’t necessary. Since kids don’t earn income, laws also limit how much death benefit can be paid for them.
5-40.gain: Regulatory definitions classify life insurance as personal insurance where human lifespan serves as the insured event; it includes term life, whole life, and endowment policies. Term life insurance pays out only upon the insured’s death within a fixed timeframe. Whole life insurance remains valid for the entire lifetime. Accident insurance only compensates for death or disability caused by accidents; it doesn’t cover deaths from illness and thus cannot replace life insurance. Contracts requiring death payouts must be approved and agreed upon by the insured; otherwise they’re invalid. Parents may purchase death coverage for minor children without such consent, but total payouts for a child’s death cannot exceed statutory limits. Typical coverage amounts reach 100,000 yuan, and another 100,000 yuan as well, hence the “high benefit” rating. No official recommendation exists for ideal coverage levels; the author’s calculation method adds remaining mortgage debt, projected expenses until children reach adulthood, and several years’ worth of household costs (based on national data revised in 2015).
5-40.note: This C rating stems from the lack of official guidance beyond basic definitions and payout limits; the “prioritize adults” recommendation follows logically from “whoever loses income would jeopardize household stability.” A child’s death doesn’t reduce household income, whereas losing the primary earner leaves mortgage payments and child expenses unpaid. When funds are limited, prioritize term life and one-year medical coverage for adults before considering similar coverage for kids. For details on truthful disclosures and guaranteed renewability, see Section 7, Article 20 (one-year medical insurance). The designated beneficiaries here fall under Category ②: your spouse and children.

5-41.t: Regretting a personal insurance policy signed for over a year? You can cancel it during the cooling-off period and get most of your premium back
5-41.cost: There’s no cost involved. A quick call to the insurer’s customer service line or a short visit to a branch takes just a few minutes. The real challenge is staying calm after signing and taking the time to read through the contract within 15 days.
5-41.human: All personal insurance policies with a term longer than one year include a cooling-off period. For policies bought through banks, this period starts 15 days after you receive the policy document, and cancelling during this time incurs a maximum administrative fee of 10 yuan. After this window closes, you’ll only receive the portion of your premium that the policy allows you to reclaim, which is usually far less than what you originally paid. Insurers often make follow-up calls to check if you fully understand the terms — be honest if you’re still unclear.
5-41.gain: Regulations require all personal insurance policies with a term over a year to clearly state the start date and length of the cooling-off period, as well as the rights policyholders have during this time. The cooling-off period for long-term health insurance must be at least 15 days. For all such policies sold via banks, the contract explicitly sets this period to 15 days, calculated from the natural calendar days after you receive and sign for the policy document. The policy cover must also carry this notice: “You have the right to cancel this policy in full (minus a maximum administrative fee of 10 yuan) within 15 days of receiving it. Cancelling after this period will result in financial losses.” Even after the cooling-off period ends, you can still terminate the contract at any time, and the insurer must refund the policy’s cash value — the portion of your premium that can be reclaimed — within 30 days as per contract terms. Financial regulators note that cancelling long-term personal insurance after the cooling-off period typically results in cash value payouts that are lower than the total premiums paid. Insurers must also reach out to new policyholders of such plans during the cooling-off period to confirm they’re aware of the potential financial losses from cancellation and their rights under this period (applicable nationwide since 2010 and 2019).
5-41.note: The cooling-off period is a mandatory provision for all personal insurance policies with a term longer than one year. There’s no such requirement for one-year medical or accident insurance policies, so you’ll need to check the specific contract terms for these. For policies not bought via banks, the exact duration is defined in the contract — be sure to look up the “cooling-off period” clause as soon as you get the policy. Savings and dividend-paying insurance plans require higher premium payments, so making use of this period is especially worthwhile for these policies; see item 25 in this section for more details on non-savings plans. We rate the benefit as “moderate” because the savings you can achieve are the difference between your total premiums paid and the cash value you receive, which typically ranges from a few hundred to a few thousand yuan — no official statistics exist on this figure. You are the sole beneficiary of this provision.

5-42.t: Before signing at the bank counter, check whether it’s a deposit or insurance
5-42.cost: No cost at all. Just spend a couple of extra minutes reading the contract cover.
5-42.human: Banks may sell insurance on behalf of insurers, but they must not present it as a deposit. The contract cover must clearly state “Insurance Contract” and the insurer’s name in large print; terms like “deposit” or “savings” are strictly prohibited. If the insurer’s name appears on the cover, the money is not a deposit, and cancelling after the cooling-off period will result in losses. In principle, people aged 65 and older can only purchase insurance with guaranteed returns when buying at banks.
5-42.gain: Regulations explicitly forbid banks from bundling insurance with savings deposits, mutual funds, or other bank wealth products. They may not directly compare insurance returns to deposit yields, nor claim uncertain returns as guaranteed. Insurance documents and promotional materials must not use the bank’s name or logo, nor contain phrases such as “deposit,” “savings,” or “jointly offered by the bank.” The contract cover must display “Insurance Contract” in font size no smaller than 72 points and the insurer’s name in font size no smaller than 2 points. For three specific groups of customers, only insurance products with guaranteed benefits may be sold: applicants aged over 65; applicants aged over 60 purchasing installment-payment plans; and applicants whose annual income is below the local per capita disposable income. Policies for these groups must be manually underwritten by insurers rather than issued automatically at bank branches. Insurance agents are prohibited from selling insurance inside bank premises. For any insurance policy sold by a bank with a term longer than one year, a 15-day cooling-off period applies; cancelling after this period incurs financial losses. (Nationwide, effective October 2019)
5-42.note: This item is rated B because the regulations are very clear, yet no official statistics exist on how much money misled consumers have lost. Elderly family members are especially vulnerable to this issue when making deposits at banks; be sure to check the contract cover for them. If you’ve already signed such a contract, you may cancel it within 15 days per Section 42 (Cooling-off Period). For complaints regarding potential misrepresentation, refer to Section 44 (Assistance with Policy Cancellation). The primary beneficiaries of this guidance are you and your elderly relatives.

5-43.t: To cancel your insurance policy, contact the insurer directly — don’t use “policy cancellation agents.” If you feel misled, call 12378 for free assistance
5-43.cost: There’s no cost involved. Simply call the insurer’s customer service line or visit a branch; this may require a bit more effort than using an intermediary.
5-43.human: Online ads promising “full policy refunds with no fees if unsuccessful” usually come from illegal cancellation agents. They typically take 30–50% of any refund amount and demand your ID, bank details, and verification codes. Once the policy is cancelled, coverage ends. If you feel misled, first contact the insurer’s customer service; if that fails, call 12378 — this service is completely free.
5-43.gain: In February 2026, China’s National Financial Regulatory Administration, the Cyberspace Administration, the Ministry of Public Security, the People’s Bank of China, and the China Securities Regulatory Commission jointly issued a warning. It stated that claims of “full policy refunds” are false and contrary to insurance laws. “Policy cancellation agents” charge hefty fees; if you try to withdraw from their services, they may sue you for “breach of contract.” They also collect personal data such as SIM cards, bank accounts, policy details, home addresses, and even children’s school information — data that can be sold on, leading to fraud or identity theft. A June 2026 notice from Ningxia’s financial regulator provides further detail: such agents demand 30–50% of the refund amount as a fee and impose steep penalties if you back out. They even instruct clients to fabricate claims of sales misrepresentation or forged signatures. Following such advice could violate public security laws; in severe cases, it may constitute slander or extortion. Once cancelled, coverage ends immediately. Future applications for similar policies may be rejected or cost more due to age or health issues. If you truly feel misled, first contact the insurer’s official customer service; if unresolved, call 12378. If you’re temporarily unable to pay premiums, ask the insurer about options like reduced paid-up value or policy loans. Reduced paid-up value means you stop paying premiums, though coverage decreases proportionally (nationwide, 2026).
5-43.note: In 2025, Hunan’s financial regulator reported a case: a woman followed “advice” from a “friend” to use a cancellation agent, paying a “consultation fee.” Ultimately, her policy was refunded only at its cash value. Three months later, she was diagnosed with breast cancer — and no longer had critical illness coverage. You must weigh the pros and cons: if coverage remains valuable, consider reduced paid-up value instead of cancellation. If you’re still within the cooling-off period, see Section 42 (Cooling-off Period). Your own well-being is the ultimate priority.

5-44.t: Writing a specific beneficiary on the policy lets family claim the payout: 5 years for life insurance, 2 years for other policies
5-44.cost: No cost involved. You fill this in once at purchase; any later changes to the beneficiary require written notice to the insurer.
5-44.human: If no beneficiary is listed, or if the named beneficiary passes away first, the payout is treated as part of the deceased’s estate and must first cover any debts owed by the deceased. If “Spouse: [Name]” is listed as beneficiary but the couple later divorces, the policy is effectively treated as having no beneficiary at the time of a claim. Family members must be aware of the policy’s existence: for life insurance, claims must be filed within 5 years of learning of the insured’s death; for other policies, the deadline is 2 years. In total, 100,000 people are affected by such situations, and another 100,000 face related complications.
5-44.gain: Insurance law stipulates that beneficiaries must be designated by either the insured or the policyholder, with the latter requiring the insured’s consent. In three specific scenarios, payouts are classified as part of the insured’s estate and distributed per standard inheritance rules: 1) No beneficiary is named, or the designation is ambiguous; 2) The named beneficiary dies before the insured, with no other eligible beneficiaries; 3) The beneficiary legally loses or voluntarily waives their right to benefits, again with no other eligible beneficiaries. If both the insured and beneficiary die in the same incident with no clear order of death, the beneficiary is presumed to have died first. Any payout classified as an estate must first settle all outstanding taxes and debts owed by the deceased, with remaining funds distributed to heirs. Supreme Court rulings clarify that if a beneficiary is listed only by name and familial relationship, any subsequent change to that relationship renders the designation invalid. Unnotified changes to beneficiaries hold no legal weight with insurers. The statute of limitations for filing claims is 5 years for life insurance and 2 years for other policies, both starting from the date the claimant learns or should have learned of the insured’s death. Given that typical life insurance payouts reach hundreds of thousands of yuan, this benefit is rated as “high” (national data, revised 2015, effective 2021).
5-44.note: Once the statute of limitations expires, insurers may legally deny payouts, and legal action to recover funds is highly unlikely to succeed. For this reason, family members must at minimum know which insurers you hold policies with. After events like divorce, remarriage, or the birth of a child, update the beneficiary designation accordingly. To claim payouts after a death, follow the steps outlined in Section 25, Item 9 (claiming funds from multiple policies individually). Note that using the policy payout to settle the deceased’s debts is not a viable option; see Section 29, Item 13 (debt settlement) for further details. The beneficiary category for this item falls under Tier ②, which includes your spouse and children.

5-45.t: Don’t spend money on virtual currencies like Bitcoin or Tether; even if others try to get you to invest, don’t join in: these transactions receive no legal protection, so you won’t be able to recover any losses through court
5-45.cost: There’s no direct cost. You simply avoid buying these coins and steer clear of “signal groups” or “guaranteed‑profit” crypto communities. The trade‑off is that you won’t profit when crypto prices rise.
5-45.human: China does not recognize virtual currencies as legal tender. Individual purchases of such coins can be ruled invalid by courts, meaning any losses fall on the buyer. One person paid roughly 448,000 yuan to buy Tether, but later couldn’t withdraw funds from the platform; his lawsuit was dismissed. Theft of crypto is a separate criminal matter — thieves are prosecuted for theft.
5-45.gain: In February 2026, eight Chinese authorities issued Notice No. 42 (Yinfa [2026] 42), stating that Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tether and similar virtual currencies “have no legal tender status and must not be used as currency in any market.” Converting RMB to crypto, trading one crypto for another, or using crypto for fundraising are all illegal financial activities, strictly prohibited. Foreign firms may not offer such services to Chinese residents. The notice also clarifies that any civil transaction involving virtual currencies or tokenized real‑world assets that runs counter to public order is void, with all resulting losses borne by the parties involved. This provision echoes wording from the 2021 Notice No. 237, which was also repealed. A court case illustrates this: between February 2018 and July 2019, Mr. Tang paid about 448,000 yuan to two alleged platform operators for Tether; after the platform became inaccessible he sued for repayment. The court ruled his investment contract invalid and dismissed his claim, a decision upheld on appeal (Yixing, Jiangsu, March 2025). Theft of crypto is a separate crime; for example, a hacker stole crypto worth over 4 million yuan from a victim, and the thief was sentenced to seven years in prison and fined 20,000 yuan (Zhengzhou, Henan).
5-45.note: The clause “losses borne by the investor” applies only to disputes between you and the seller or promoter; it does not entitle you to recover funds through litigation, so don’t count on a court win. If your crypto is stolen or scammed, treat it as a criminal case and report it to police. Existing holders should also guard against QR‑code theft; in Lianshui, Jiangsu, a man scanned a code during a meeting and lost roughly 57,000 Tether worth about 393,665 yuan; the People’s Court has ruled such acts should be prosecuted as theft. In 2022 the FBI warned of a similar tactic: a pop‑up window granting unlimited transfer rights to a wallet; the recommended safeguard is to avoid linking wallets to untrusted sites and to regularly audit permissions via third‑party tools. Using your own bank card to receive payments, buy crypto, or transfer funds for others can constitute a criminal offense — see Section 9, Item 5 (“part‑time work” involving personal cards). For “high‑return” investment offers, refer to Section 6 (“high yield”, “guaranteed profit” warnings). Legal ways to invest in overseas assets are outlined in Section 38 (QDII funds or Stock Connect). This information is not investment advice. 〔394000〕 〔393665.461434〕

5-46.t: If you have no employer, pay into the employee pension yourself at the minimum base and get the years in first; don’t assume you profit from the first payment — even at the minimum base it takes about 10 years of payouts to break even
5-46.cost: You pay all of it yourself, 20% of your contribution base; even at the lowest tier that is several hundred to over a thousand yuan a month. You must pay in on time for at least 15 years, and from 2030 that requirement rises year by year toward 20 years. Until you have paid in the full period and retired, the money cannot be withdrawn.
5-46.human: If you have no employer and pay in on your own, the best deal is the minimum tier with enough years paid. Most of what you receive follows the average wage in your area in the year you retire. Measured in that year’s wage levels, paying at the minimum tier for 15 years and starting to collect at 60 breaks even after about 10 years; the extra paid for higher tiers takes about 17 years to recover. It is worth paying, but it is not a gain from the first payment.
5-46.gain: How to pay in and how to collect are set out in the State Council’s 2005 decision. People with no employer who pay in themselves (formally, flexible-employment workers) pay 20% of their contribution base, of which 8% is credited to a personal account. Since 2019 you can choose your own contribution base, anywhere from 60% to 300% of the province-wide average wage of urban employees in all types of units. The pension after retirement has two parts. The first is the basic pension: the local average monthly wage for the previous year and your own average contribution wage are added together and divided by 2, and for each full year of contributions you receive 1% of that figure. The second is the personal-account pension: the balance in the account divided by the number of payout months. For retirement at 60 the number of payout months is 139, at 55 it is 170; the later you retire, the fewer the months. What follows is an example worked out from the formula, not an official figure. Assume the local average monthly wage in your retirement year is 8,000 yuan and both average wages equal that number. All amounts below are expressed in that year’s wage levels, with account interest assumed to just keep pace with wage growth. At the minimum tier of 60%, the contribution base is 4,800 yuan and the monthly payment is 960 yuan. Fifteen years of payments total about 173,000 yuan (exactly 172,800). From age 60 you collect about 1,457 yuan a month: a basic pension of 960 yuan plus a personal-account pension of about 497 yuan. That is about 17,500 yuan a year (about 17,487 exactly), and it takes about 9.9 years to break even, that is, until around age 70. At the 100% tier, 15 years of payments total about 288,000 yuan (exactly 288,000) and the monthly pension is about 2,029 yuan. The extra roughly 115,000 yuan (exactly 115,200) over the minimum tier buys only about 572 yuan more a month and takes about 16.8 years to recover. The reason is that half of the basic pension is based on the local average wage and has nothing to do with how much you paid, so those who pay less come out ahead. At the minimum tier, every additional year of contributions still breaks even in about 9.9 years, which beats moving up a tier. At the minimum tier, the basic pension makes up most of what you collect. This break-even period does not depend on how high local wages are: where wages are higher, what you pay and what you receive rise by the same proportion, so the break-even period stays the same. Money paid in the early years has a smaller face value but is paid out at retirement according to that year’s average wage. So if you look only at the face value of what you paid and what you receive, break-even comes sooner than 9.9 years. By law, you must have accumulated 15 years of contributions by retirement to collect a monthly pension; if you fall short, you can keep paying until you reach it. From January 1, 2030, this minimum number of years rises by 6 months each year until it reaches 20 years. When a person dies, the balance left in the personal account can be inherited. The state raises pensions from time to time in line with average wage growth and price increases. If the pension fund runs short, the government subsidizes it (nationwide)
5-46.note: The example is only for judging orders of magnitude. What you actually collect depends on the local average wage, the tier you pay at, the interest credited to the personal account, and the year you retire. Pension increases after retirement are not counted, so the real break-even will be somewhat earlier. After the retirement age is raised, the number of payout months is smaller, so the personal account pays more each month. When you work for an employer, the employer pays 16% and you pay 8%. With no employer, nobody pays that 16% for you, and the whole 20% comes out of your own pocket. If you die before collecting it all, the balance in the personal account can be inherited, and surviving family can also receive a funeral subsidy and a survivor’s pension. If you cannot afford even the minimum tier every month, you can first join the urban and rural residents’ pension insurance; see Section 31, item 11 (not working for an employer counts as flexible employment). For whether you can get a social-insurance subsidy, see Section 7, item 12 (recognition as a person with employment difficulties). For gaps in payments and making them up, see Section 7, item 18 (breaks in social-insurance payments). For how your pension record transfers when you move to another city, see Section 19, item 19 (transferring pension and medical-insurance records to the new place of coverage).

6-1.t: Don’t take multivitamins just to live longer or protect your heart and blood vessels
6-1.cost: About 0.5–2 yuan per day, or 200–700 yuan per year. Taking them takes almost no time — just one pill each day. Over time, though, people can become dependent, feeling they’ve missed out on something important if they skip a day.
6-1.human: 14,400 male doctors took multivitamins for 11 years. The number of serious heart or blood vessel problems and deaths among them was no different from those who didn’t take them. When nine studies involving over 50,000 people were combined, there was still no effect on overall mortality. Skipping multivitamins saves you 200–700 yuan each year. This does not apply to people who truly lack certain nutrients or pregnant women needing folic acid.
6-1.gain: The PHS II trial followed 14,641 male doctors for a median of 11.2 years. Both groups — those taking multivitamins and those who didn’t — showed the same rate of major cardiovascular events. The hazard ratio was 1.01 (meaning no real difference), with a 95% confidence interval of 0.91–1.10. Similarly, overall mortality rates were identical, with a hazard ratio of 0.94 (95% CI 0.88–1.02). In 2022, USPSTF evaluated nine randomized controlled trials involving 51,550 participants and concluded there is no link between multivitamin use and reduced mortality; they assigned it a Grade I rating, meaning evidence is insufficient to draw any firm conclusions. The idea that multivitamins are a good deal stems partly from the convenience of “one pill for all nutrients” and their low daily cost.
6-1.note: A point of debate: among these same male doctors, cancer rates were slightly lower among multivitamin users — about 8% fewer cases (95% CI 0.86–0.998, P=0.04, just barely significant). Deaths from cancer were also reduced by roughly 12% (95% CI 0.77–1.01), though this range includes 1, so it may simply be a coincidence. Any such benefit is very small and has only been observed in male doctors. It does not apply to people with proven nutrient deficiencies, pregnant women needing folic acid, or those with extremely poor diets. 〔14000〕

6-2.t: Don’t take regular fish oil just to prevent heart disease
6-2.cost: Roughly 1–3 yuan per day, or 400–1,000 yuan per year. It requires no extra time to take.
6-2.human: Two large trials enrolled 26,000 and 15,000 people with diabetes respectively. Those who took 1 gram of fish oil daily showed no difference from non-users in terms of major cardiovascular events or death rates. The fact that eating fish is healthy does not mean fish oil capsules are equally beneficial. Skipping them can save you 400–1,000 yuan each year.
6-2.gain: The VITAL trial followed 25,871 participants for 5.3 years; those taking 1 gram of fish oil daily showed no difference in major cardiovascular events or mortality compared to non-users. The hazard ratio for major events was 0.92 (95% CI 0.80–1.06), well below 1, indicating no benefit. All-cause mortality showed a similar pattern (HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.90–1.15). The ASCEND trial, involving 15,480 diabetic patients over 7.4 years, also found no difference in severe vascular events (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.87–1.08) or mortality (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.86–1.05). These results appear favorable only because many assume “eating fish is healthy” equates to “fish oil capsules are beneficial.”
6-2.note: Controversy exists: One trial did show benefits. The REDUCE-IT trial included 8,179 high-risk patients with existing cardiovascular disease or diabetes, already on statins and with elevated triglyceride levels (135–499 mg/dL). Those taking 4 grams of prescription-grade pure EPA daily saw a 25% lower risk of events (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.68–0.83). However, this was a high-dose prescription medication for a specific high-risk group, not ordinary fish oil supplements for the general population. This discussion excludes the health benefits of eating fish itself. 〔17.2〕

6-3.t: Don’t give vitamin D supplements to people who already have adequate levels
6-3.cost: It costs roughly 0.2–0.5 yuan per day, or 100–200 yuan per year. That isn’t much money, but the real cost is the false sense of protection it creates.
6-3.human: For people who already have normal vitamin D levels, taking supplements for five years does not lower their risk of cancer, cardiovascular disease, or death compared to those who don’t supplement. This does not apply to people who are actually deficient, have osteoporosis, or get little sun exposure — they should follow their doctor’s advice.
6-3.gain: The VITAL trial included 25,871 participants who took 2,000 IU of vitamin D daily for a median of 5.3 years. No difference was seen in cancer rates, cardiovascular disease, or overall mortality. The hazard ratio for aggressive cancers was 0.96 (95% CI 0.88–1.06); for major cardiovascular events it was 0.97 (95% CI 0.85–1.12); for all-cause death it was 0.99 (95% CI 0.87–1.12). The D-Health trial involved 21,315 Australians over 60 who received 60,000 IU monthly for five years; again, no significant differences appeared, with an all-cause mortality HR of 1.04 (95% CI 0.93–1.18). The death rates were 5.3% versus 5.1%. The impression that supplementation is beneficial arises because some studies only observe people without intervening, finding higher mortality among those with low vitamin D levels — this is wrongly interpreted as proof that supplements help.
6-3.note: Note: Neither trial specifically enrolled people known to be deficient in vitamin D, so these results apply only to those who already have adequate levels. Individuals with confirmed deficiency, osteoporosis, limited sun exposure, or infants should still follow medical guidance. These trials examined only overall mortality, cancer, and cardiovascular outcomes; no other effects were evaluated.

6-4.t: Don’t take antioxidant supplements to prevent cancer (beta-carotene, vitamins E and A)
6-4.cost: Approximately 0.5 to 2 yuan per day. For smokers, the real cost is a higher risk of lung cancer.
6-4.human: This isn’t just ineffective — it’s actually harmful. A combined analysis of 78 trials involving nearly 300,000 participants showed that people taking antioxidant supplements had a slightly higher overall mortality rate. Two large trials focused specifically on smokers found that beta-carotene increased the likelihood of developing lung cancer by 18% to 28% and raised mortality risk by 8% to 17%. Smokers and individuals exposed to asbestos should absolutely avoid these supplements.
6-4.gain: Cochrane reviewed 78 randomized controlled trials with 296,707 participants total. The overall risk ratio for mortality among supplement users was 1.02 (95% CI 0.98–1.05). When only higher-quality trials were considered, the risk ratio rose to 1.04 (1.01–1.07). Specifically, beta-carotene raised mortality risk to 1.05 (1.01–1.09) and vitamin E to 1.03 (1.00–1.05). The ATBC trial tracked 29,133 male smokers who took 20 mg daily; it found a 18% increase in lung cancer incidence (3%–36%) and an 8% rise in overall mortality (1%–16%). The CARET trial involved 18,314 smokers or asbestos-exposed individuals; it showed a 28% higher risk of lung cancer (RR 1.28, 1.04–1.57) and a 17% higher risk of all-cause mortality (RR 1.17, 1.03–1.33). The perception that these supplements are beneficial stems from the flawed logic that antioxidants prevent aging, which in turn prevents cancer — each step of this reasoning seems intuitive but is untrue.
6-4.note: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) rated both beta-carotene and vitamin E as “D” in 2022, meaning they advise against their use. Smokers and asbestos-exposed individuals have already suffered harm from taking them. Naturally occurring antioxidants found in fruits and vegetables are not included in this recommendation; you may continue eating those as normal.

6-5.t: Don’t expect glucosamine/chondroitin to treat knee osteoarthritis
6-5.cost: Roughly 2–5 RMB per day, or 700–1,800 RMB per year.
6-5.human: Even people with knee osteoarthritis who took a placebo for 24 weeks reported less pain in about 60% of cases. Those taking glucosamine or chondroitin saw only a 4–5% improvement over this baseline — a difference so small it could easily be due to chance. Spending 700–1,800 RMB yearly nets you little more than that same 60% placebo effect.
6-5.gain: The GAIT trial enrolled 1,583 patients with knee osteoarthritis who took the supplements for 24 weeks. Among those receiving a placebo, 60.1% also reported pain relief. Glucosamine produced just a 3.9% extra improvement (P=0.30), while chondroitin added 5.3% (P=0.17). Taking both together yielded a 6.5% gain (P=0.09) — all differences far too small to rule out random variation. For comparison, celecoxib, a genuine medication used as a control in the same trial, delivered a 10.0% improvement (P=0.008). The supplements appear “cost-effective” only because “cartilage-building ingredients” sound relevant to the condition, and because a placebo alone already helped six out of ten patients.
6-5.note: Controversy: In this same trial, among participants with severe baseline pain, those taking both supplements reported a 79.2% improvement rate versus 54.3% in the placebo group (P=0.002). However, researchers note this finding was derived post-hoc from the data and should be viewed as a tentative clue rather than a definitive conclusion. Proven strategies for managing knee osteoarthritis remain weight loss and muscle-strengthening exercises — see Section 2.

6-6.t: Don’t rely on vitamins C to prevent colds
6-6.cost: Each effervescent tablet costs roughly 1–2 RMB; annual expense ranges from 300 to 700 RMB.
6-6.human: Regularly taking vitamin C won’t significantly lower your chances of catching a cold, and taking it only after you’ve already fallen ill yields inconsistent results. For the general population, daily intake shortens the duration of a cold by about 8%, which equals roughly half a day of reduced discomfort. Whether this is worth the annual cost is up to personal judgment. Marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers stationed in cold climates are exceptions: for them, daily vitamin C intake cuts cold incidence by half.
6-6.gain: Cochrane reviewed 29 randomized controlled trials involving 11,306 participants. For ordinary people, regular vitamin C consumption does not meaningfully reduce overall cold incidence; the risk ratio here is 0.97, meaning there is virtually no difference between groups. The 95% confidence interval for this figure is 0.94–1.00. Trials where vitamin C was taken only after cold symptoms appeared showed mixed results: some indicated a benefit, others did not. For the general population, long-term daily intake does shorten cold duration by about 8% in adults (95% CI 3%–12%) and 14% in children (95% CI 7%–21%). Marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers in cold climates again form an exception: 5 trials with 598 participants showed their cold incidence dropped by roughly half, with a risk ratio of 0.48 (95% CI 0.35–0.64). The perceived value of vitamin C for cold prevention is largely driven by its low cost, pleasant sweet-and-sour taste, and the fact that this claim has been widely circulated for half a century.
6-6.note: Controversy note: The same Cochrane review confirms that regular vitamin C intake does shorten the duration of cold symptoms. For adults, this reduction is about 8% (95% CI 3%–12%); for children, it is 14% (95% CI 7%–21%). This translates to roughly half a day of reduced illness per cold episode. Marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers in cold climates are again the exception: 5 trials with 598 participants showed their cold incidence fell by about half (risk ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.35–0.64). The vast majority of people do not fall into these special groups. 〔500〕

6-7.t: Don’t get a whole-body PET-CT or tumor marker panel just because you have no symptoms
6-7.cost: A whole-body PET-CT costs roughly 7,000–10,000 RMB per scan and exposes you to ionizing radiation. Tumor marker panels cost a few hundred RMB. The real cost comes later: if a test flags an “abnormality” that turns out to be a false positive, you’ll need follow-up tests, biopsies, and possibly surgery — all of which add up financially and physically.
6-7.human: For people without symptoms, most screening results are false alarms. Over 80% of those who get a whole-body CT find at least one “abnormality,” and nearly 40% are called back for more tests — yet most of these findings are benign. In women tested for ovarian cancer markers, the death rate from ovarian cancer is actually slightly higher; some even undergo unnecessary surgery because of a false positive.
6-7.gain: The USPSTF, which evaluates preventive measures in the U.S., gave a D rating to using CA-125 and ultrasound to screen asymptomatic women for ovarian cancer — meaning it does not recommend this screening. Their basis is the PLCO trial, which showed a 0.34% death rate from ovarian cancer in the screened group versus 0.29% in the control group (RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.82–1.71). Screening offers no real benefit. The rate of unnecessary surgery due to false positives ranges from 0.2% to 3.25% across studies, with up to 15% of those patients experiencing serious complications. Another study screened 1,192 symptom-free individuals with whole-body CT; 86% had at least one “abnormality” noted, and 37% were advised to undergo further tests. Most of these findings were benign. The idea that screening is “worth it” because it enables early detection stems largely from intuition rather than solid evidence.
6-7.note: The tumor marker portion of this recommendation is supported by randomized controlled trials. In contrast, the evidence for whole-body CT and PET-CT relies mainly on observational follow-ups without proper control groups, so it falls to a B rating. Other proven screening methods — such as tests for colorectal and cervical cancer, breast cancer screening, or low-dose chest CT for high-risk individuals — are discussed in Section 1. For people already showing symptoms or diagnosed with cancer, PET-CT is a diagnostic tool, not a screening measure, and is handled separately.

6-8.t: Don’t expect fitness trackers to help you lose weight
6-8.cost: Devices cost between 200 and 2,000 RMB. Plus, you have to constantly check those numbers every day.
6-8.human: Overweight people following the same diet and exercise plans lost 3.5 kg in two years if they wore fitness trackers, while those who didn’t wear any lost 5.9 kg. To lose weight, buying such devices won’t help — actual exercise does the job.
6-8.gain: The IDEA trial involved 471 overweight or obese adults and followed them for 24 months. Everyone followed identical diet and exercise routines; the only difference was whether they wore wearable devices. The group wearing trackers lost 3.5 kg (95% CI 2.6–4.5). The other group lost 5.9 kg (95% CI 5.0–6.8), a difference of 2.4 kg (95% CI 1.0–3.7, P=0.002). It seems cost-effective only because the idea “you must measure to manage” sounds logical, and the devices are a one-time purchase.
6-8.note: This is just one trial, using devices from the early 2010s worn on the arm; we can’t conclude that all wearable devices are useless. Exercise itself remains effective, as discussed in Section 2. The bottom line: buying fitness trackers isn’t necessary if you want to lose weight.

6-9.t: Don’t pay a premium for organic food just to be “healthier”
6-9.cost: Typically 1 to 3 times the price of regular versions of the same foods.
6-9.human: There is no solid evidence that organic food is more nutritious. Only three studies have actually examined how eating organic affects human health, and none showed any difference. While organic produce does have pesticide residues at a rate 30 percentage points lower than conventional produce, finding residues does not mean they exceed safety limits. Eating more fruits and vegetables is beneficial regardless of whether they are organic or not.
6-9.gain: One systematic review combined findings from 17 human studies and 223 studies analyzing food composition. Its conclusion was that “there is insufficient evidence to show organic food is significantly more nutritious than conventional food.” Of those human studies, just three looked at actual health outcomes such as allergies and symptomatic infections; no differences were observed between organic and conventional diets. The perception that organic food offers better value stems from the common-sense chain of reasoning: “no pesticides means greater safety, and greater safety means better health.”
6-9.note: Very few studies have directly examined how organic food impacts human health. Therefore, the conclusion is “there is no evidence that organic food is superior,” rather than “it has been proven to offer no benefits.” Environmental impact, animal welfare, and taste are not addressed here. Eating more fruits and vegetables remains beneficial regardless of whether they are organic or not.

6-10.t: Don’t spend a lot of money on health supplements, tonics, or “body‑balancing” products
6-10.cost: Prices range from a few hundred to tens of thousands of yuan. Once packaged as gifts, the price often multiplies several times over.
6-10.human: Multivitamins, fish oil, and vitamin D — common ingredients in these products — have all been examined in the first six sections of this chapter. None of them show any real benefit. The statement “Health supplements are not medicines and cannot replace medical treatment” must appear on every package by regulatory rule. Many people buy these items as gifts for their parents, and that intention is admirable; the problem is simply choosing the wrong products.
6-10.gain: The real benefit is simply saving that money. The reasons are laid out in the first six sections: for the most common supplement ingredients — multivitamins, fish oil, vitamin D, antioxidants, glucosamine, and vitamin C — randomized controlled trials found no expected advantages; the corresponding numbers are listed in the “Benefit” columns of those sections. Regulatory rules only define what claims a product may make; they do not prove a product is useless. The State Administration for Market Regulation requires that at least 20 % of a health‑supplement package’s front surface carry the mandatory line: “Health supplements are not medicines and cannot replace medical treatment.” The same rules limit their purpose to “supplementing dietary nutrients, maintaining or improving overall health, or reducing disease risk factors.” These products seem worthwhile because the phrase “they don’t cure disease, they only help balance the body” is technically true; no one can prove it false. When bought as gifts, the value comes from the gesture, not from any scientific evidence.
6-10.note: The conclusion is “no evidence supporting benefit,” not “proven ineffective,” which is why the grade is C. For products whose ingredients are clearly listed, check the relevant studies described in the earlier sections. People who truly lack certain nutrients or who are undergoing medical treatment should follow their doctor’s advice. What should be avoided are the products themselves, not the goodwill behind the gift. If an elderly person is already taking them without substituting them for prescribed medicines and shows no adverse effects, there’s no need to argue; instead, make sure they receive recommended vaccines and screenings. That same amount of money can be spent on far better options: annual flu shots for seniors (see Section 1, Item 20); shingles vaccine after age 50 (Section 1, Item 21); pneumococcal vaccine for those over 65 (Section 1, Item 22). Buying a blood‑pressure monitor and ensuring they take antihypertensive meds as directed (Section 1, Item 7) also yields real benefits. Home modifications such as bathroom and stair upgrades, plus balance and leg‑strength exercises (Section 1, Item 13), are equally valuable. Age‑appropriate cancer screenings should also be arranged (Sections 1, Items 17‑19). For bedridden seniors, pressure‑ulcer prevention and long‑term care insurance are covered in Section 17, Items 7‑8. Instead of tonics, delivering fresh fruit, rice, noodles, or other favorite foods is far more practical. Two types of schemes should be avoided: pre‑payment “retirement‑investment” programs and products marketed as substitutes for prescribed medicines (see Section 17, Item 5).

6-11.t: Don’t take probiotics long-term if you have no gut problems
6-11.cost: Approximately 2–5 RMB per day, or 700–1800 RMB per year.
6-11.human: A review of 45 trials conducted on healthy adults found that probiotics do not cause lasting changes to the gut microbiome; once people stop taking them, the microbial composition returns to its original state. There was also no improvement in blood lipid levels. Separate evidence exists for cases where antibiotics cause diarrhea, but that falls outside the scope of this review.
6-11.gain: The same review concluded that there is no reliable evidence that probiotics can produce lasting alterations in gut flora or improve blood lipid profiles in healthy adults. While gut bacteria do shift temporarily while taking probiotics, these changes reverse once use stops. The practice may seem cost-effective simply because “gut health” is a broad concept that can be loosely applied, and the daily cost of a single probiotic dose is quite low.
6-11.note: The review also notes a few minor benefits in healthy individuals, such as firmer, better-textured stools and increased Lactobacillus levels in women’s vaginas. Separate evidence exists for probiotics used to treat antibiotic-induced diarrhea or for specific strains targeting particular medical conditions; those cases are not covered here. This review pertains solely to healthy adults using probiotics as a daily supplement.

6-12.t: Don’t force yourself to take cold showers just to “boost immunity”
6-12.cost: No cost at all. It requires enduring discomfort for 30 to 90 seconds each day; staying consistent in winter demands real willpower. People with cardiovascular conditions should be cautious, as cold exposure poses certain risks for them.
6-12.human: In a trial involving 3,018 participants, those who took cold showers had 29% fewer sick days. However, the total number of days taken off for illness remained identical across groups, so it doesn’t actually reduce overall illness. A 2025 systematic review analyzing 11 trials found that cold showers temporarily raised markers of inflammation while leaving immune indicators unchanged. Feel free to take cold showers if you enjoy them, but don’t treat them as a genuine health investment.
6-12.gain: A randomized controlled trial conducted in the Netherlands enrolled 3,018 participants who took hot showers followed by 30, 60, or 90 seconds of cold exposure. These individuals showed a 29% reduction in sick days (IRR 0.71). Yet the study explicitly notes “no significant difference in total sick days between groups,” meaning the overall duration of illness remained equal. No meaningful differences emerged regarding quality of life, work productivity, or anxiety levels. The 2025 review synthesized 11 RCTs totaling 3,177 participants; it revealed that cold exposure temporarily increased inflammatory markers both immediately and one hour post-shower, with no change in immune markers. Stress levels decreased only at the 12-hour mark. Authors themselves acknowledge the evidence is “limited by the small number of RCTs and modest sample sizes,” reflecting how few such trials exist and how few participants each includes. Cold showers appear cost-effective solely because they’re free and align with the intuitive belief that enduring hardship yields health benefits.
6-12.note: Controversy: The 29% drop in sick days is statistically significant and unlikely to be coincidental. Yet total illness duration didn’t decrease, suggesting participants simply continued working despite being unwell rather than actually getting sick less often. Using cold water for post-exercise recovery among athletes constitutes a separate application outside this context. Cold showers pose no inherent harm to healthy individuals; they simply shouldn’t be marketed as a health-promoting practice.

6-13.t: Don’t buy detox, colon-cleansing, enzyme, or alkaline water products
6-13.cost: Several hundred to several thousand yuan. Diets meant to “detox” by starving oneself can even lower blood sugar and cause nutritional deficiencies.
6-13.human: The detox industry is massive, yet there is very little clinical evidence to back it up, and no proper trials have been conducted on commercially available detox diets. When researchers looked into whether diet pH, alkaline water, or cancer are linked, only one study met the criteria — and it found no connection.
6-13.gain: One review concluded that “despite the booming detox industry, there is very little clinical evidence supporting these diets,” and that “no randomized controlled trials have been done on commercial detox diets.” Another systematic review examined diet pH, alkaline water, and cancer: after screening 8,278 studies, just one qualified for inclusion, and it showed no link either. The authors wrote, “It is not reasonable to promote alkaline diets and alkaline water to the public for cancer prevention or treatment.” These products seem cost-effective only because the assumptions “the body contains toxins needing removal” and “an acidic body state causes cancer” sound plausible from a physiological standpoint.
6-13.note: There is simply no evidence to support these products, which is why they receive a C rating. Removing metabolic waste is naturally the job of the liver and kidneys; as long as these organs are healthy, there is no need for any extra “detox” measures.

6-14.t: Don’t force yourself to drink water just to hit “8 glasses a day”
6-14.cost: No monetary cost. It does require some effort and time to remember to drink, and it may also lead to more nighttime bathroom trips.
6-14.human: Some people have tried to trace the origin of the “8 glasses a day” rule, but no studies actually support it. Food and other beverages already provide plenty of water, so there’s no need to drink that much. Simply drink when you’re thirsty and check your urine color. Those who work in hot environments, engage in intense exercise, have a history of kidney stones, or older adults who don’t feel thirsty as much should make a conscious effort to drink more water.
6-14.gain: One literature review specifically examined the “8×8” guideline — meaning 8 glasses per day, each containing 8 ounces of water. Its conclusion was clear: “No scientific evidence supporting the 8×8 rule was found.” The review also noted that surveys of thousands of adults showed they obtain sufficient hydration from food and other drinks, making extra water consumption unnecessary. This idea seems appealing mainly because water is free, the number 8 is easy to remember, and recommending “drink more water” sounds harmless in any context.
6-14.note: What needs to be rejected is the rigid “must drink X glasses daily” rule, not the general idea of drinking more water. When you’re thirsty, just drink enough and check your urine color. For people working in hot conditions, doing heavy exercise, with a history of kidney stones, or older adults who don’t feel thirsty as much, drinking extra water is still advisable.

6-15.t: Don’t spend money on fortune‑telling, tarot, or astrology to make decisions
6-15.cost: It costs nothing. The real challenge is giving up this easy shortcut for decision‑making and having to think for yourself from now on.
6-15.human: There’s a classic classroom experiment: students receive a “personality analysis” that is identical for everyone, yet most find it very accurate. This is exactly why fortune‑telling seems reliable. Astrologers perform only slightly better than random guesses. The price isn’t just a few dollars: in Xixian County, Henan Province, a fortune‑telling ring charged “offering fees” and “donation packages” up to 3,888 yuan; the ringleader was sentenced to 11 years in prison.
6-15.gain: In that same experiment, students rated the generic personality description they received as highly accurate — an average of about 4.26 out of 5 points. This illustrates the “Barnum effect,” which explains why fortune‑telling feels so spot‑on. A double‑blind test of astrology was also published in Nature: astrologers were asked to match a client’s horoscope to one of three personality profiles; they succeeded 40 times out of 116, whereas random guessing would have yielded 38.5 matches. Official records show a similar pattern in Henan: a fraud ring lured victims with free palm‑reading services, then demanded “offering fees” and “donation packages” up to 3,888 yuan. Over 50 victims lost more than 2 million yuan; the ringleader received an 11‑year sentence plus a 100,000‑yuan fine.
6-15.note: Both studies cited here are single‑experiment research pieces. The average score of 4.26 wasn’t stated outright in Forer’s original paper; it was calculated from the distribution shown in Table 1. This note merely points out that such predictions lack reliability; it does not comment on any personal beliefs. Spending a modest amount for entertainment is fine, but relying on these services to decide on career moves, marriage, or investments is a costly mistake. 〔58.5〕

6-16.t: Don’t buy blue-light-blocking glasses to “protect your vision,” and don’t believe claims that staring at screens for months will ruin your eyes — but severe eye pain, redness, and swelling require emergency care
6-16.cost: These glasses cost nothing; you also avoid paying the extra few hundred to a few thousand yuan for blue-light-blocking lenses.
6-16.human: Blue-light-blocking lenses provide no real benefit. Skipping them saves you money, and they make no difference to eye fatigue or visual clarity compared to regular lenses. There is no evidence they protect the retina. While screen use can cause temporary eye strain and dryness, the true threats to eye health are welding arcs, UV radiation, lasers, and acute angle-closure glaucoma.
6-16.gain: A 2023 Cochrane systematic review analyzed 17 randomized controlled trials involving 5 to 156 participants each, with follow-up periods ranging from under a day to five weeks. Due to limited data, significant differences in participant profiles, and inconsistent follow-up times, the authors did not combine results into a single overall figure. All results below compare participants wearing blue-light-blocking lenses to those wearing regular lenses. After less than a week of use, self-reported eye fatigue showed “likely no difference” between groups, though evidence certainty was low. One trial with 120 participants found a 9.76-unit difference between groups, but the 95% confidence interval spanned from −33.95 to 53.47, indicating no meaningful distinction. Critical flicker fusion frequency, an objective measure of eye fatigue, also showed “likely almost no difference” between groups, with low evidence certainty. Best-corrected visual acuity remained “probably unaffected” after wearing these glasses; the difference was 0.00 logMAR (95% CI −0.02 to 0.02), based on just one study with 156 participants, resulting in moderate evidence certainty. Whether these lenses affect daytime alertness remains unclear, based on two trials involving 42 participants and extremely low evidence certainty. The review found no evidence supporting retinal protection from blue-light-blocking lenses.
6-16.note: Screen use commonly causes eye strain and dryness, manifesting as soreness, dryness, and blurred vision after prolonged exposure. These symptoms typically resolve with rest and frequent blinking; they do not permanently damage vision. This consensus among ophthalmologists is not a conclusion drawn from the Cochrane review cited here, so it is classified as Grade C evidence. The only conditions capable of causing irreversible eye damage in a short period are intense light sources such as welding arcs, UV radiation, and lasers. Eye injury from welding arcs, known as photic keratitis, is a legally recognized occupational disease; protection requires specialized goggles and face shields, not blue-light-blocking lenses — see Section 19, Item 10 on protection against dust, noise, and chemical toxins. For individuals staying up late while using screens, the only true emergency is acute angle-closure glaucoma, which manifests as severe eye pain, redness, halos around lights, headache, nausea, and vomiting; this condition can irreversibly damage the optic nerve within days, requiring immediate emergency eye care — see Section 13, Item 6.
