Risk factors include dilated pupils in dim lighting, prolonged forward head posture, age over 50, hyperopia, and shallow anterior chamber depth. Chronic screen-induced dryness may also develop into a long-term medical condition needing professional treatment, rather than resolving after a single night’s rest. Persistent eye discomfort or declining vision warrants prompt evaluation by an ophthalmologist rather than simply switching lenses. Guidance on preventing myopia in children and teens can be found in Section 30, Items 4, 12, and 9: at least two hours of daily outdoor activity, pupil dilation tests, and avoidance of products claiming to “cure” myopia.

6-17.t: Don’t treat blood donation as a health habit: claims that it “detoxifies, lowers cholesterol, and prevents heart attacks” lack randomized trial support; frequent donation does, however, cause iron deficiency
6-17.cost: There is no monetary cost. A single donation — including registration, blood draw, and post-donation observation — takes roughly one hour. Over the following weeks, the body works to replace the lost iron.
6-17.human: Assertions that donating blood helps detoxify, lowers cholesterol, or prevents heart attacks are not reliable. People who donate regularly tend to be healthier to begin with; after accounting for this factor, the mortality benefit of donating once more per year drops from nearly 20% to just 7.5%. In studies that directly compared donors and non-donors, overall death rates were similar. On the other hand, donating too often does make people feel weak and cold — this is due to iron deficiency.
6-17.gain: The Kuopio study in Finland followed 2,862 men aged 42–60 for nearly 9 years. During the 24 months prior to the start of monitoring, 153 men donated blood; only one (0.7%) suffered an acute heart attack. Among the remaining 2,529 non-donors, 316 (12.5%) experienced the same outcome (P<0.0001 for the difference between groups). After adjusting for age and other coronary risk factors, donors showed an 88% lower risk of heart attack; the relative risk was 0.12 (95% CI 0.02–0.86, P=0.035). However, this finding came from observational data, not a controlled trial. The Nordic SCANDAT database includes 1,182,495 blood donors followed for a total of 9,526,627 person-years; 15,401 deaths occurred. When only age and gender were considered, donating once more per year correlated with an 18.6% reduction in mortality (95% CI 16.8%–20.4%). Once the fact that only healthy individuals are allowed to donate is also taken into account, the benefit shrinks to 7.5% (95% CI 5.7%–9.4%). The authors conclude that this cannot be interpreted as conclusive proof of health benefits. The FeAST randomized trial enrolled 1,277 patients with symptomatic peripheral artery disease; one group underwent regular blood removal every 6 months while the other served as a control. Overall mortality rates were 20% in the treatment group versus 23% in controls (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.67–1.08, P=0.17). When deaths and non-fatal heart attacks or strokes were combined, rates were 28% versus 32% (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.72–1.07, P=0.20). No significant differences emerged. The INTERVAL trial involved 45,263 blood donors assigned to three different donation intervals: 12, 10, or 8 weeks for men and 16, 14, or 12 weeks for women. Shorter intervals resulted in significantly more blood collected over two years (the 8‑week group donated 1.69 extra units compared to the 12‑week group, 95% CI 1.59–1.80). No differences appeared in quality of life, physical activity, or cognitive function across groups; however, shorter intervals increased side effects such as fatigue, shortness of breath, dizziness, and restless legs. Average hemoglobin and ferritin levels also fell, and more donations were postponed due to low hemoglobin levels (all P<0.0001). Iron deficiency impairs thermoregulation: 10 women with iron‑deficiency anemia, 8 with depleted iron stores but no anemia, and 12 controls were immersed in 28 °C water for 100 minutes. The anemia group’s rectal temperature was 36.0 ± 0.2 °C versus 36.2 ± 0.1 °C in controls (P=0.001); oxygen consumption was 5.28 ± 0.26 versus 5.99 ± 0.29 mL·min⁻¹·kg⁻¹ (P=0.04). Levels of thyroid hormones thyroxine and triiodothyronine were also lower (P<0.002). These findings are largely explained by the fact that donors are already a carefully screened, healthier population; the hypothesis that iron removal itself protects the heart has not been confirmed in randomized trials.
6-17.note: What should be rejected is the idea of donating blood “for one’s own health,” not blood donation per se. Donated blood benefits others and falls under category ④ (strangers) in this book’s beneficiary classification. The real personal benefit comes from institutional policies. Article 14 of the Blood Donation Law stipulates that unpaid donors, their spouses, and direct relatives may be exempt from or receive reduced fees for blood collection, storage, separation, and testing when they need blood themselves. A January 2024 notice from the Health Commission states that 28 provinces now offer direct fee waivers for unpaid donors and their relatives at local hospitals. Recipients of the “Voluntary Blood Donation Award” may also enjoy local “three‑free” benefits: free public transport, free entry to government‑run parks, and waived outpatient consultation fees at public hospitals. Follow legal donation intervals: Article 9 of the Blood Donation Law permits 200 mL per donation (maximum 400 mL) with at least 6 months between sessions; the recommended age range is 18–55 years. Do not shorten the interval merely to earn honors or meet group quotas. Women, those with lower body weight, and women with heavy menstrual flow already have limited iron reserves; frequent donors may wish to have their ferritin levels checked privately. Persistent fatigue, cold intolerance, or restless legs after donation are not signs of “vital energy loss” but may indicate iron deficiency; a blood test and ferritin measurement are advisable. If deficiency is confirmed, follow medical advice for iron supplementation and extend the donation interval. The data on cold intolerance come from a small sample of only 10 individuals; they illustrate a physiological mechanism rather than indicating how common this effect is. 〔636〕 〔148〕 〔641〕 〔180〕 〔205〕

6-18.t: Don’t rely on generic health check packages to prevent disease; instead, get only those evidence‑based screenings appropriate for your age and gender
6-18.cost: There’s no cost at all; you even save hundreds to thousands of yuan each year by avoiding these packages. The trade‑off is that you must remember which tests you need and how often to get them.
6-18.human: People who regularly undergo generic health checks have the same mortality rate as those who don’t, including deaths from cardiovascular disease and cancer. It’s enough to get only those screenings backed by evidence and suited to your age and gender. People aged 35 and older can have their blood pressure measured for free once a year; those 65 and older receive a free annual health check.
6-18.gain: An updated 2019 Cochrane systematic review included 17 randomized controlled trials. When calculating overall mortality, 11 of these trials involving 233,298 participants and 21,535 deaths were pooled; the relative risk for the screening group versus the control group was RR 1.00 (95% CI 0.97–1.03). For cardiovascular‑related deaths, nine trials with 170,227 participants and 6,237 deaths yielded RR 1.05 (95% CI 0.94–1.16). For cancer‑related deaths, eight trials with 139,290 participants and 3,663 deaths gave RR 1.01 (95% CI 0.92–1.12). In all cases no meaningful difference was found. The authors concluded that generic health checks are unlikely to provide any benefit.
6-18.note: What should be avoided is using annual check‑up packages as a disease‑prevention strategy; this does not mean you should skip all tests. The free annual blood‑pressure measurement for those 35+ and the free annual health check for those 65+ are part of the national basic public‑health program, so no personal expense is required. Tests that are medically indicated should still be done. Details on when and how often to get blood‑pressure, blood‑glucose, and hepatitis B tests are provided in sections 1.7, 1.8, and 1.14. Breast, cervical, and colorectal screening instructions appear in sections 1.17, 1.18, and 1.19. Helicobacter pylori testing and low‑dose CT are covered in sections 1.23 and 1.24. Bone‑density testing for women over 65 is described in section 1.39. For anyone with high‑risk behaviors, relevant screening is outlined in section 1.31. Most of the trials included in the Cochrane review were conducted in high‑income countries where medical care is readily available; therefore, this conclusion should be applied with caution in regions with limited health resources.

6-19.t: Don’t start taking uric‑acid‑lowering drugs just because a routine check shows high uric acid levels but you’ve never had any symptoms
6-19.cost: There’s no cost at all; you also avoid long‑term medication expenses, repeated follow‑up tests, and the unnecessary risk of taking drugs you don’t need.
6-19.human: For people whose uric acid levels are high but who’ve never experienced gout attacks or developed tophi, the American College of Rheumatology recommends not taking uric‑acid‑lowering drugs at all. In a study of 24 participants, only one gout attack was prevented after three years of treatment. These drugs also fail to protect kidney function — patients taking them still saw a similar decline in kidney performance as those taking a placebo. Treatment should be started only after a genuine gout episode occurs.
6-19.gain: The 2020 gout guidelines from the American College of Rheumatology define asymptomatic hyperuricemia as blood uric acid levels above 6.8 mg/dL in individuals with no prior gout attacks or tophi. Under certain conditions, the guidelines advise against initiating any uric‑acid‑lowering therapy; such drugs include allopurinol, febuxostat, and probenecid. The evidence supporting this recommendation is rated as “high.” A footnote clarifies that, based on attributable risk, 24 patients must be treated for three years to prevent a single gout attack. The CKD‑FIX randomized controlled trial involved 363 participants with stage 3 or 4 chronic kidney disease, no history of gout, and an elevated risk of kidney deterioration. One group received 100–300 mg of allopurinol daily while the other received a placebo; after 104 weeks, eGFR — a key measure of kidney function expressed in mL/min/1.73 m² — declined at an annual rate of –3.33 (95% CI –4.11 to –2.55) in the drug group versus –3.23 (–3.98 to –2.47) in the placebo group. The difference between groups was –0.10 (–1.18 to 0.97), with a P‑value of 0.85, indicating no meaningful difference in kidney‑function decline. Rates of serious adverse events were comparable at 46% versus 44%. The PERL trial enrolled 530 patients with type 1 diabetes and early‑to‑moderate diabetic kidney disease; after three years of allopurinol therapy followed by a two‑month washout period, uric acid levels fell from 6.1 to 3.9 mg/dL in the treatment group. Yet the resulting change in GFR between the two groups was merely 0.001 mL/min/1.73 m² (95% CI –1.9 to 1.9, P = 0.99). Moreover, urinary albumin excretion rose by 40% (range 0–80%) in the allopurinol group. The apparent “benefit” of these drugs stems largely from the intuitive belief that any elevated marker must be lowered by medication.

6-20.t: Don’t have a gallbladder removed prophylactically just because an ultrasound found gallstones but you’ve never felt pain
6-20.cost: There’s no cost at all — in fact, you avoid the expense of general anesthesia and a hospital stay. The trade-off is simply remembering a few warning signs that mean you must seek medical care right away.
6-20.human: People with gallstones but no pain have stayed symptom-free for nearly 80% of them over the past nine years. Without any intervention, only about 0.1% to 0.3% develop acute cholecystitis or pancreatitis each year. Gallbladder removal isn’t risk-free either — roughly 1.5% of patients suffer bile duct injury. That’s why European and UK medical guidelines recommend against surgery for asymptomatic individuals.
6-20.gain: In Italy, the MICOL study followed 11,229 people aged 29 to 69 using ultrasound screening. Of the 856 participants with gallstones, 580 had no symptoms and were tracked for an average of 8.7 years. Out of those 580, 453 (78.1%) remained symptom-free, while 61 (10.5%) experienced mild symptoms and 66 (11.4%) had severe symptoms. Only 189 gallbladder removals were performed during the study, and 41.3% of those were on symptomless patients. The authors concluded that watchful waiting remains the best approach for most patients. A similar U.S. study of 691 patients with gallstones showed that only 10% of the 135 symptomless participants developed symptoms over 58 months, and just 7% needed surgery. Of all 50 deaths in the group, only two were linked to bile duct problems, and both occurred in symptomatic patients. The UK’s NICE CG188 guideline explicitly states that people with incidental asymptomatic gallstones should not be treated unless symptoms appear. European hepatology guidelines estimate that 0.7% to 2.5% of asymptomatic individuals develop symptoms yearly, while acute cholecystitis, pancreatitis, obstructive jaundice, or cholangitis affect only 0.1% to 0.3% annually. After the first episode of pain, that risk rises to 1% to 3% per year, meaning most people experience pain before facing serious complications. Nationwide Swedish data on 51,041 gallbladder removals found that 1.5% resulted in bile duct injury, with 0.3% involving partial or total duct rupture. Mortality within a year was 3.9% for those with duct damage versus 1.1% for others. Even after surgery, 10% to 40% of patients continue to feel discomfort or see symptoms return. Overall, guidelines agree that surgery neither extends life nor reduces long-term costs for asymptomatic patients, since its risks outweigh those of watchful waiting. One 1983 calculation estimated that a 30-year-old man who elects prophylactic removal lives 4 days less on average, while a 50-year-old loses 18 days. To date, no randomized trials have compared prophylactic removal to watchful waiting, though intuition suggests early surgery is preferable given the inevitable future pain.
6-20.note: This topic remains controversial. China’s 2021 expert consensus on biliary surgery includes certain asymptomatic gallstone cases as surgical candidates, though the specific criteria remain unclear. Critics point out that small stones under 5 millimeters are more strongly linked to pancreatitis, and Dutch research suggests prophylactic removal may either extend or shorten life depending on local pancreatitis rates. European guidelines do make exceptions: surgery is advised for porcelain gallbladder, gallstones larger than 1 centimeter, or concurrent gallbladder polyps. It may also be considered when another major abdominal surgery is planned. Crucially, this guidance applies only to stones confined to the gallbladder — stones in the common bile duct require immediate removal regardless of symptoms. Seek emergency care if you experience persistent upper abdominal pain, fever, chills, yellowing of the eyes or skin, or dark urine. When a doctor recommends surgery, ask whether it’s based on bile duct involvement, polyps, or other abnormalities — this guideline only counters unnecessary prophylactic removal without valid medical justification. Both cited studies followed patients over 4 to 9 years to assess natural progression, not to compare treatment efficacy, and longer follow-ups would likely show higher symptom rates. 〔61.6〕 〔50.2〕 〔46.3〕 〔2016〕

6-21.t: Don’t cut calcium out to prevent kidney stones
6-21.cost: No cost at all. In fact, it’s easier — no need to constantly watch out for calcium-containing foods.
6-21.human: People who’ve had calcium oxalate stones are often advised to limit calcium intake, yet research shows the opposite is true. For men with recurrent stones, eating a normal amount of calcium while cutting back on animal protein and salt cut recurrence rates over five years to half that of those on a low‑calcium diet. UK guidelines likewise advise against restricting calcium.
6-21.gain: A five‑year randomized trial enrolled 120 men with recurrent calcium oxalate stones and high urinary calcium levels. One group consumed 30 mmol of calcium daily, plus reduced animal protein (52 g/day) and salt (50 mmol sodium chloride/day). The other group followed a low‑calcium diet (10 mmol/day). Over five years, recurrence occurred in 12/60 men in the normal‑calcium group versus 23/60 in the low‑calcium group. The unadjusted relative risk was 0.49 (95% CI 0.24–0.98; P = 0.04), meaning the normal‑calcium diet cut recurrence risk by half. Both groups saw a similar drop in urinary calcium (~170 mg/day), but oxalate excretion fell by 7.2 mg/day in the normal‑calcium group while rising 5.4 mg/day in the low‑calcium group. NICE guideline NG118 states adults should aim for 700–1,200 mg of calcium daily; children and teens need 350–1,000 mg/day. The “benefit” of not cutting calcium stems from this intuitive link between calcium intake and stone formation.
6-21.note: Caveats: This trial involved only men with recurrent calcium oxalate stones and high urinary calcium; results may not apply to all stone types. Moreover, the intervention combined normal calcium intake with reduced protein and salt, so some benefits could stem from those changes. The advice is to avoid deliberately cutting calcium from the diet — not to actively increase supplementation. Separate from dietary calcium, calcium supplements should be discussed with a physician. For hydration advice, see Section 16, Item 8: aim for 2.5–3 L of water daily after a stone episode.

6-22.t: Don’t buy crystals, bracelets, or Pixiu figurines for “good luck,” “wealth attraction,” or “health benefits”
6-22.cost: There’s no direct cost involved. The real challenge is resisting the social pressure to buy them when everyone else is wearing or talking about them.
6-22.human: There’s no verifiable evidence that wearing such items brings good luck, attracts wealth, or improves health. Their perceived effectiveness works much like fortune‑telling: vague statements are easy to interpret personally. When sellers claim medical benefits, it constitutes false advertising — in 2026, several livestream vendors were penalized for making such claims. As simple decorative items, they’re perfectly fine.
6-22.gain: Classic classroom experiments show that people receive the same generic “personality analysis” yet each believes it fits them perfectly; this is known as the Barnum effect. It explains why many feel their lives improve after wearing these items. The researchers concluded that personal acceptance alone doesn’t prove the description is accurate. Official examples: in June 2026, China’s State Administration for Market Regulation released several cases of “crackdowns on fraud” in the craft‑goods sector. One jewelry shop in Sihui, Guangdong, fabricated material details on livestreams and falsely advertised benefits such as “treating rheumatism, boosting immunity, improving sleep, and clearing blood vessels.” Such deceptive practices violate Article 9, Paragraph 1 of China’s Anti‑Unfair Competition Law.
6-22.note: The bottom line is simple: there’s no way to verify any special effects or predictive power of these items. This assessment makes no judgment about personal beliefs or cultural traditions, nor does it address their use as gifts, mementos, or heirlooms. Two points must be distinguished: sellers’ advertised benefits are subject to legal regulation and can be reported; statements like “bringing good luck” lack any research support and can’t be disproven, so you must decide for yourself whether the expense is justified. Before buying, treat the item purely as an ornament and ask yourself, “If it changed nothing, would I still pay this price?” For guidance on checking materials and certifications, or why they’re poor investments, see Sections 5, Items 33 and 34 (bracelets and watches are evaluated by cost, while gemstones require CMA certification). Information on paid fortune‑telling can be found in Section 5, Item 15.

6-23.t: Don’t expect shopping to lift your mood or boost your sense of self-worth
6-23.cost: No cost at all. The real challenge is resisting the urge to buy things when you’re feeling down.
6-23.human: People who place a higher value on money and material possessions tend to report lower levels of happiness. However, this link is quite weak, and it’s unclear whether valuing material goods causes lower happiness or vice versa. Research also shows that spending money on experiences brings more joy than buying physical items. So when you’re in a bad mood, spending on a trip or a meal with friends is far more likely to help than filling your shopping cart.
6-23.gain: One meta-analysis (combining findings from many studies) examined 259 separate samples and 753 effect sizes. The results showed that individuals who prioritized material possessions reported lower happiness levels. On the most commonly used multi-dimensional scale, the correlation coefficient was r = -0.19 (adjusted ρ = -0.24). On scales that measured only “material valuing,” the link was even weaker, with r values ranging from -0.08 to -0.11. The strength of this association varied depending on the outcome measured: it was strongest with risky health and spending behaviors and negative self-evaluations (r = -0.28 to -0.44), and weakest with life satisfaction and negative emotions (r = -0.13 to -0.15). Mediation analyses suggested this negative link may arise because unmet psychological needs drive it. Another study found that across two separate surveys, respondents consistently reported greater happiness from spending on experiences than on material goods. Subsequent lab experiments also showed that recalling a positive mood after spending on an experience led to higher happiness ratings than recalling a similar positive mood after a shopping spree. Both studies used samples from outside China.
6-23.note: Caveats: Most of the included studies asked participants at a single point in time whether they valued material goods and how happy they felt, so they cannot determine which factor comes first. The authors themselves note that further experiments and long-term follow-ups are needed to clarify this directionality. Therefore, this finding should not be interpreted as “shopping makes people unhappy”; rather, it means “relying on shopping to improve your mood is unlikely to work.” Moreover, the association is quite weak: an r value of -0.19 explains only a few percentage points of variation, and individual differences are substantial. Both studies used foreign samples, so there are no comparable data available for Chinese populations. This does not mean you shouldn’t spend on things you enjoy; rather, it warns against using shopping as a way to regulate your emotions, as doing so makes impulse buying your first reaction when you’re feeling down. Specific money-saving tips are covered in Section 5. Evidence-based ways to improve your mood when you’re feeling low are outlined in the latter part of Section 22 and in Section 29. Advice on budgeting for the goal of “keeping up with peers” is provided in Subsection 24 of this section.

6-24.t: Don’t spend extra money to move up a social tier by buying a pricier home, car, or social circle
6-24.cost: No cost at all. All you need to do is ask one extra question before increasing your budget: is this extra expense buying a real product or service, or merely securing a higher standing among those around you? The difficulty lies in resisting the urge to upgrade when everyone else does.
6-24.human: When comparing people with similar incomes, those whose neighbors earn more report lower levels of happiness. This effect appears only among neighbors with comparable education levels and frequent social interaction. Therefore, spending extra money to move into a neighborhood where everyone is wealthier actually pushes you down a social tier. Yet when incomes rise across the board, people still feel better off, so absolute standards remain relevant.
6-24.gain: The National Survey of Families and Households (NSFH) in the U.S. surveyed the same individuals twice. The authors matched this data with local average incomes calculated from a 5% sample of the 1990 census. After controlling for personal characteristics and income, they found that higher neighbor incomes correlated strongly with lower reported happiness. This effect held true under various analytical methods and remained highly significant. In fact, the drop in happiness caused by a rise in neighbor incomes matched the drop caused by a similar fall in one’s own income. Even after accounting for individual differences or regional factors, the pattern persisted. It was strongest among people who interacted closely with neighbors and absent among those with mostly external friendships. Renters and homeowners showed no difference, contradicting the idea that high housing costs reduce disposable income. Happiness declined only when comparing neighbors with similar education levels, not when they differed. The effect operated mainly through satisfaction with one’s material circumstances rather than other life domains. Finally, when both personal and neighbor incomes rose proportionally, happiness still increased.
6-24.note: Several reasons justify a B rating: the data come from repeated surveys of the same participants, but this is the sole study of its kind and originates from a foreign population; the outcome measured is self-reported happiness rather than actual financial figures. The authors applied statistical controls such as within-individual comparisons and regional adjustments, yet the study remains non-randomized. No comparable data exist for Chinese populations. The benefit magnitude is classified as moderate, consistent with earlier findings in this section (e.g., buying goods rarely boosts happiness). Savings can indeed reach tens of thousands of yuan, but there is no evidence linking this amount to a comparable rise in happiness, hence it is not classified as substantial. This does not discourage spending on larger homes, quieter neighborhoods, or shorter commutes when those features are genuinely valued; the warning applies only to decisions driven by a desire to match or exceed peers. Section 4, item 18, discusses appropriate criteria for housing choices, placing commute time high on the list. For information on using purchases to improve mood, see section 3, item 20, which advises against constantly monitoring how others live.

6-25.t: Don’t believe that “willpower is like a muscle that gets exhausted after use”
6-25.cost: No cost at all. All that needs changing is how we talk about it.
6-25.human: The popular idea is that after doing something that requires self‑control, it becomes easier to give in to temptations later on, so we should “conserve” our willpower. Yet 23 laboratories and 2,141 participants repeated the same experiment under identical conditions, and found virtually no effect. Stop using the excuse “I’ve run out of willpower today,” and don’t spend money on courses that promise to help you “build up” willpower.
6-25.gain: In a multi‑lab preregistered replication study, 23 labs with 2,141 participants followed Sripada et al.’s standardized protocol: they first performed a task demanding self‑control and then a second similar task. The pooled results showed a very small self‑exhaustion effect; its 95% confidence interval included zero (d = 0.04, 95% CI −0.07 to 0.15). Another replication, also preregistered, involving 36 labs and 3,531 participants yielded d = 0.06 — again a negligible effect. These findings call into question the model that self‑control is a finite resource. It’s important to note that this does not mean people never get tired; lack of sleep or prolonged effort can indeed reduce performance, which is addressed elsewhere in this chapter.
6-25.note: What’s being refuted is the notion that self‑control is a consumable resource, not the fact that people can feel fatigued. Adjusting one’s environment and planning actions in advance — e.g., moving undesirable items out of reach or writing down exact times, places, and steps for tasks — costs little or nothing and saves time and mental effort. This approach is far more effective than trying to “build up” willpower; it won’t improve your judgment in the afternoon, but it does eliminate unnecessary hesitation and wasted minutes.

6-26.t: Don’t expect skipping breakfast or following a 16:8 eating schedule to help you control your weight; instead, pick a meal timing you can stick to long-term
6-26.cost: It costs nothing. What you save is the mental energy you’d otherwise spend worrying about when to eat.
6-26.human: Popular belief holds that skipping breakfast leads to overeating at lunch and dinner, resulting in a higher total daily calorie intake. Research does not support this: people who skip breakfast consume over 200 fewer calories per day on average, and tend to weigh slightly less. Compared to simply reducing overall calorie intake, a 16:8 eating schedule yields no meaningful difference in weight loss over a year. That said, people who consistently skip breakfast do have a roughly 17% higher risk of cardiovascular disease, though no significant difference in overall mortality is observed.
6-26.gain: Let’s first address the claim that skipping breakfast causes people to eat more later. A meta-analysis of 13 randomized trials found that participants who ate breakfast consumed 259.79 kcal more per day on average than those who skipped it (95% CI: 78.87–440.71). Their weight was also 0.44 kg higher on average (95% CI: 0.07–0.82). However, people who skipped breakfast did not make up for the missed calories at later meals. These trials had relatively short follow-up periods: weight was tracked for an average of 7 weeks, and calorie intake for an average of 2 weeks. Next, consider 16:8 eating schedules, which restrict food intake to a specific daily window. One trial involving 116 overweight adults over 12 weeks found no significant weight difference between the group eating only between 12 PM and 8 PM and the group eating three regular meals per day: the former group weighed 0.26 kg less on average, but this difference fell well within the margin of error (−1.30 to 0.78 kg). Another trial conducted in Guangzhou with 139 obese participants over 12 months showed that combining time-restricted eating with calorie restriction led to 1.8 kg more weight loss than calorie restriction alone, though this difference was also not statistically significant (−4.0 to 0.4 kg). Finally, we look at the long-term effects of skipping breakfast. A pooled analysis of data from 2.38 million people found that those who skipped breakfast had a 17% higher risk of cardiovascular disease (OR 1.17, 95% CI: 1.09–1.26) and a 49% higher risk of cardiovascular-related death (OR 1.49, 95% CI: 1.20–1.84). However, these studies only recorded meal habits without grouping participants by eating pattern. The original long-term study with 17–23 years of follow-up reported a 19% higher risk of all-cause mortality among breakfast skippers, but this figure fell within the margin of error (95% CI: 0.99–1.42), so no meaningful difference was found.
6-26.note: This topic remains controversial. The 17% higher cardiovascular risk figure comes from observational studies that did not group participants by eating habits. Breakfast skippers also tend to smoke more, drink more alcohol, lead more sedentary lifestyles, and have lower incomes; these factors are not fully accounted for in the data, so it is unclear how much of this risk is directly attributable to skipping breakfast. The all-cause mortality figure also falls within the margin of error. The benefits of 16:8 eating schedules are also debated: a pooled analysis of 30 trials involving 1,341 participants found that when both groups consumed the same amount of calories, the time-restricted eating group lost 1.46 kg more weight on average (−2.65 to −0.26 kg), but also lost 0.41 kg more lean body mass. Most of these trials were very short in duration, and the longest, most rigorous 12-month trial found no meaningful weight difference between the two groups. Prolonged fasting may also affect gallbladder health. A cross-sectional survey of 6,547 people found that for every hour later a person ate their first meal, their risk of gallstones rose by 5% (OR 1.05, 95% CI: 1.02–1.08); those whose first meal was eaten between 9 AM and 2 PM had a 49% higher risk than those who ate earlier (OR 1.49, 95% CI: 1.24–1.77). The mechanism is that bile remains in the gallbladder for longer periods, increasing the likelihood of stone formation. However, this is a cross-sectional study, so it is possible that people with pre-existing gallbladder issues changed their eating habits. The Kaiping Cohort Study in China tracked 369 cases of digestive tract cancer over 5.6 years and found that breakfast skippers had a 2.32 times higher risk of colorectal cancer (95% CI: 1.34–4.01) and a 5.43 times higher risk of gallbladder and extrahepatic bile duct cancer (95% CI: 1.34–21.93); the wide confidence interval for the latter figure indicates very few events, so this should be viewed as a preliminary clue rather than a definitive finding. Overall, when it comes to weight control, meal timing has very little impact, so there is no need to spend mental energy on this factor. As for whether skipping breakfast long-term is beneficial, current evidence is purely correlational and does not prove causation, but the trends are generally unfavorable. To be on the safe side, eat regular meals — just don’t expect this to help you lose weight. The main causes of gastritis and gastric ulcers are Helicobacter pylori infection and long-term use of painkillers; information on testing for H. pylori and treating positive cases can be found in Section 1, Item 23. Guidance on what to do if gallstones are found during a routine checkup but cause no symptoms is provided in Section 1, Item 20. For proven ways to control weight, focus on what and how much you eat: see Section 2, Item 27 (eat at least 5 servings of fruits and vegetables daily), Section 2, Item 28 (limit ultra-processed foods), and Section 2, Item 32 (keep your BMI between 20 and 25). These recommendations do not apply to people with diabetes, those taking blood sugar-lowering medication, or pregnant individuals; skipping meals may lead to hypoglycemia in these groups, so they should follow their doctor’s instructions. Extreme fasting and induced vomiting are separate issues entirely; see Section 28, Item 1 for details on why these methods are not advisable for weight control.

6-27.t: Don’t believe claims that masturbation harms health or that abstaining improves wellbeing; what really matters is whether it interferes with sleep, work, or relationships
6-27.cost: There is no cost involved. You save money you would otherwise spend on dubious “kidney‑tonic” remedies, “abstinence” courses, and the chronic anxiety that comes from self‑blame.
6-27.human: No credible research shows that masturbation harms health. Men who ejaculate more often have about 20% fewer cases of prostate cancer, though some studies also find a slightly higher risk among those with very frequent ejaculation in youth. A tiny fraction of men experience fatigue or flu‑like symptoms lasting several days after each ejaculation; this is a rare condition called Post‑Orgasmic Illness Syndrome (POIS) and should be evaluated by a urologist or andrologist. Feelings of “addiction” to pornography usually stem from a clash between personal moral beliefs and the behavior itself.
6-27.gain: One U.S. study followed 31,925 men through 2010, asking them to report how often they ejaculated each month. Compared with men ejaculating 4–7 times per month, those ejaculating more than 21 times per month had a hazard ratio for prostate cancer of 0.81 (95% CI 0.72–0.92, a roughly 19% reduction) when data were analyzed for ages 20–29; for ages 40–49 the HR was 0.78 (0.69–0.89, about a 22% reduction). These reductions applied mainly to low‑risk forms of prostate cancer. A British case‑control study of 431 prostate‑cancer patients and 409 controls found a higher risk among men who reported frequent masturbation in their twenties, but a lower risk among those who remained active later in life. Regarding pornography, a systematic review and meta‑analysis concluded that many people who feel “addicted” are simply struggling with a mismatch between their actions and personal values, rather than being driven solely by exposure frequency. The rare POIS condition can cause post‑ejaculation discomfort, but it is not a sign of bodily harm; it warrants medical attention, not abstinence. In a Dutch cohort of 45 patients, 87% developed symptoms within 30 minutes of ejaculation, 80% reported fatigue, and 78% experienced flu‑like symptoms; French data from 37 patients show an average recovery time of 4.7 days. The exact cause remains unknown; in the Dutch study, 29 of 33 participants (88%) tested positive for semen allergy. Conversely, a Chinese study of 24 patients found no evidence of semen‑specific antibodies, though anxiety and depression scores were elevated. A 2025 review identified only 14 treatment studies, 12 of which describe single cases. Among 211 global sexual‑medicine experts, just 18% believe that more than 30% of patients improve with treatment (data from the U.S., UK, Netherlands, France, and China).
6-27.note: This topic remains controversial. Both prostate‑cancer studies merely observed associations without controlled randomization, and frequency data relied on self‑report, so the conclusion can only be that there is no evidence of harm; it does not justify encouraging frequent ejaculation. The British authors themselves note that the later‑life risk reduction might reflect pre‑existing health issues. The pornography review did not provide effect sizes, so only directional trends are reported here. The overall benefit is rated as modest because the observed reductions pertain mainly to low‑risk prostate cancer rather than mortality. POIS research involves only a few dozen participants; the condition is acknowledged as rare, yet no population‑wide prevalence figures exist. Anyone experiencing near‑constant post‑ejaculation fatigue or flu‑like symptoms should consult a urologist or andrologist and mention POIS specifically. Signs that psychological help is needed include chronic sleep loss, missed work, damaged relationships, and an inability to curb the behavior despite negative consequences. Excessive late‑night use of pornography should be avoided for the same reasons as gaming, short‑video binge‑watching, or other sleep‑disrupting habits (see Section 3, Item 9). If concerns arise about erectile problems linked to porn consumption, follow the advice in Section 1, Item 28: first evaluate cardiovascular health. Legal risks associated with sharing or selling pornographic material are outlined in Section 9, Item 4. Ultimately, the main beneficiaries are the individuals themselves.

6-28.t: Don’t spend money on “sexual orientation conversion” or “gay therapy,” and don’t send family members to such programs
6-28.cost: No cost at all. What you save is the money that would otherwise go to conversion clinics, counseling centers, and “conversion therapy” providers. The hard part is getting family members to accept that they shouldn’t go.
6-28.human: After reviewing the research, an expert panel from the American Psychological Association concluded that these conversion efforts cannot change sexual orientation and may actually cause harm. In a U.S. survey, nearly 90% of people who had undergone conversion therapy reported having suicidal thoughts. In China, a psychiatric hospital forcibly admitted a man under the label of “sexual preference disorder”; a court ruled this was a violation of his rights and ordered the hospital to pay him 5,000 yuan in compensation.
6-28.gain: The 2009 APA task force report states that attempts to change sexual orientation “are unlikely to succeed and carry some risk of harm.” It advises both parents and minors to avoid any mandatory or inpatient conversion programs. A nationally representative U.S. survey of 1,518 LGBTQ+ adults found that about 7% had undergone conversion therapy, and 80% of them were referred by religious figures. After adjusting for age and childhood trauma, people who had undergone conversion therapy had an odds ratio of 1.92 (95% CI 1.01–3.64) for lifetime suicidal thoughts — roughly 92% higher than others. Their odds ratio for planning suicide was 1.75 (1.01–3.06), and for non‑serious suicide attempts it was 1.88 (1.01–3.50). Another study of 245 young adults aged 21–25 showed that 22.0% of those who had never undergone conversion therapy had attempted suicide, compared with 48.1% whose parents tried to change their orientation and 62.8% whose parents sent them to therapists or religious counselors. WHO’s ICD‑10 explicitly states that “sexual orientation itself is not considered a disorder.” In 2017, a court in Henan Province ruled that a psychiatric hospital had violated a man’s rights by forcibly admitting him under the same label; the hospital was ordered to apologize publicly and pay 5,000 yuan in compensation.
6-28.note: This topic remains controversial. Sullins (2022) re‑analyzed the same data while excluding participants who already had suicidal thoughts prior to therapy; under those conditions, conversion therapy showed no significant link to suicidal thoughts (OR 0.44, 0.20–0.94). Sullins’ organization opposes LGBTQ+ rights, and the original authors also responded to his findings. Thus, while the extent of harm is still debated, there is no evidence contradicting the conclusion that conversion therapy cannot change sexual orientation. The “B” grade reflects that most harm data come from retrospective self‑reports. Legally, involuntary hospitalization is allowed only for individuals with severe mental disorders who pose a danger to themselves or others; counseling professionals are prohibited from providing such therapy. Intentionally admitting someone without a mental disorder to a hospital can result in liability. In 2014, a man in Chongqing sued a counseling center for using hypnosis and electric shocks to “treat” his homosexuality; a Beijing court ordered the center to apologize publicly and compensate him for economic losses, noting that homosexuality is not a mental illness and that claims of a cure were false advertising. Only a news report exists on this case; no official court document is publicly available. Anyone struggling emotionally because of this issue can seek help from a psychiatrist or clinical psychologist to alleviate their distress. Guidance on how families should respond after a child comes out is provided in Section 30, Item 15. The ultimate beneficiaries are you and your family.

6-29.t: Don’t expect that learning “proper lifting techniques” or attending lifting training will prevent back pain; what really matters is reducing the weight and frequency of lifts, plus regular exercise
6-29.cost: No cost at all. There’s no need to worry about whether you’re bending correctly while lifting, nor do you have to pay for special back‑protection classes or belts. All you need to do is break heavy loads into smaller pieces, use a cart, or get help — this only adds a few minutes to your routine. Additionally, set aside some time each week for exercise, which must be maintained over the long term.
6-29.human: Workers who’ve taken lifting‑technique courses still suffer from back pain just as often as those who haven’t. There’s no clear link between how much you bend at the waist while lifting and the likelihood of developing back pain. What does matter is lifting heavier loads and doing it more often; each extra 10 kg or 10 additional lifts per day raises the risk by roughly 10 %. People who exercise regularly experience back pain up to 40 % less often.
6-29.gain: Regarding training, a 2011 Cochrane review pooled nine randomized trials involving 20,101 workers. Seven of those trials, covering 19,317 participants, showed that workers who attended lifting training reported similar rates of back pain as those who received no training at all (OR 1.17, 95 % CI 0.68–2.02). Compared with workers who only watched a short video, the relative risk was 0.93 (0.69–1.25); again, no meaningful difference. The overall evidence quality is moderate. The authors conclude that lifting advice and training — whether or not paired with proper equipment — do little to prevent back pain or related disability. As for bending, a 2020 review of studies on lumbar flexion during lifting produced low‑quality evidence; the only longitudinal study found only a 1.5‑degree difference in maximum flexion angle between workers who later developed back pain and those who didn’t (−0.7 to 3.7), a non‑significant result. Nine of eleven studies showed no difference between groups, while seven others indicated that workers with back pain actually bent less by about 6 degrees (−11.2 to −0.9). The authors argue that there is no solid proof that excessive bending causes back pain. Finally, a meta‑analysis of eight longitudinal studies revealed that each extra 10 kg lifted per occasion raises the risk of back pain by 11 % (OR 1.11, 1.05–1.18). Likewise, each additional 10 lifts per day increases risk by 9 % (OR 1.09, 1.03–1.15). Another review of 21 randomized trials involving 30,850 participants found that combining exercise with instruction lowered the risk of back‑pain episodes by 45 % (RR 0.55, 0.41–0.74; moderate evidence). Exercise alone gave a 35 % reduction (RR 0.65, 0.50–0.86; low‑to‑very‑low evidence), while instruction alone or wearing a back belt showed no benefit (RR 1.03 and RR 1.01 respectively). The UK Health and Safety Executive’s official guidance echoes these findings: training alone cannot guarantee safe lifting; proper technique cannot replace appropriate equipment, task redesign, or load handling.
6-29.note: This topic remains controversial. Some studies suggest a link between heavy or frequent lifting and back pain, while others find none. A 2010 systematic review identified nine high‑quality studies; four showed an association and five did not. Its authors argue that heavy lifting at work is unlikely to be the sole cause of back pain, so the “less heavy lifting” recommendation is supported by correlative data but not definitive proof of causation. The research on lumbar flexion is of low quality, and most studies merely compared two groups at the same point in time. The training review’s confidence interval is very wide, and it also notes that no randomized trials have tested whether training can actually cure existing back pain. Nonetheless, the HSE still recommends certain techniques: keep loads close to the body, stand with feet firmly planted, avoid twisting the waist or pulling abruptly. When standing up, gently bend the back, hips, and knees rather than bending fully at the waist or squatting deeply. Following these steps can’t hurt, but don’t rely on them alone to prevent back pain. The overall benefit is moderate: regular exercise can produce sizable reductions, yet evidence for exercise alone is weak, and combined exercise‑instruction programs have not been shown to cut sick‑leave rates; back pain is rarely fatal. Details on how to exercise can be found in Section 2, items 16 (30–60 minutes of strength training weekly) and 11 (walking 7,000–8,000 steps daily). Ultimately, you are the one who stands to gain. 〔1.27〕 〔1.44〕

6-30.t: Don’t expect that taking extra calcium or drinking bone broth after a fracture will speed up bone healing
6-30.cost: This costs nothing — it even saves money and effort compared to buying calcium tablets, vitamin D supplements, and spending time simmering bone broth. All you need to do is get tested to see if you’re deficient, and only supplement if you are; otherwise there’s no need for extra intake.
6-30.human: No clinical trials on vitamin D supplementation after fractures have shown any improvement in bone healing. There are very few studies looking at combined calcium and vitamin D intake, so it’s unclear if this combination is beneficial at all. The amount of calcium in a large bowl of bone broth is only a fraction of the daily recommended intake. This does not apply to people who are already deficient in vitamin D or have osteoporosis.
6-30.gain: Starting with vitamin D: A 2023 systematic review included 14 studies involving 2,734 fracture patients. The authors concluded that standalone vitamin D supplementation has minimal impact on bone healing, union, or post-recovery function. The few studies that did show some benefit generally had poor methodological quality. The authors also noted that none of the randomized controlled trials they reviewed found any positive effect from vitamin D supplementation. One of these trials enrolled 100 patients with long bone fractures and low baseline vitamin D levels; half received a single dose of 100,000 IU of vitamin D within two weeks of injury, while the other half took a placebo. In both groups, 2 patients each failed to achieve bone union, resulting in a 4% overall failure rate. Another trial included 102 patients aged 18–50 with thigh or lower leg fractures, who were assigned to four different treatment groups with varying doses of vitamin D or a placebo. After 3 and 12 months, no differences in healing scores were observed across any group. A third trial involved 32 postmenopausal women with wrist fractures; those taking a high daily dose equivalent to 1,800 IU of vitamin D showed lower bone compressive strength compared to those not supplementing. Moving on to calcium: A 2014 systematic review noted that there are very few clinical studies examining the effect of vitamin D deficiency or supplementation on fracture healing, so no clear conclusions can be drawn. The two studies it identified looked at combined calcium and vitamin D intake, and found increased bone density or callus formation at fracture sites, but no evidence of faster healing. Finally, regarding bone broth: A study in Kaohsiung, Taiwan, analyzed three types of packaged bone broth noodle soups, each containing 450–550 grams of liquid. The average calcium content per serving was 14–39 milligrams, which is only 1.4%–3.9% of the recommended daily intake of 1,000 milligrams for adults. Chinese dietary guidelines recommend 800 milligrams per day for people aged 18–49 and 1,000 milligrams for those over 50, with a maximum daily intake of 2,000 milligrams. These guidelines also warn that excessive long-term calcium intake raises the risk of kidney stones. A U.S. trial involving 36,282 postmenopausal women found that those taking 1,000 milligrams of calcium plus 400 IU of vitamin D daily for an average of 7 years had a 17% higher risk of kidney stones (HR 1.17, 95% CI 1.02–1.34). Meanwhile, their risk of hip fracture dropped by 12%, though this difference was not statistically significant (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.72–1.08). The perceived cost-effectiveness of this approach stems from the common intuition that “bones are made of calcium, so eating more calcium will make them grow faster.”
6-30.note: There are a few minor hints of potential benefit worth noting. One Danish trial enrolled 30 elderly women with proximal arm fractures who had either osteoporosis or low bone mass; those taking 800 IU of vitamin D plus 1 gram of calcium daily showed higher bone density at the fracture site after 6 weeks (0.623 vs 0.570 g/cm²). However, this study only measured bone density, not actual healing progress, and the sample size was very small. A post-hoc analysis of the 102-patient trial mentioned earlier found that participants taking high-dose vitamin D had slightly better functional scores, though the authors stressed that further research is needed to confirm this finding. This also does not apply to people who are already deficient in vitamin D. Dutch follow-up data showed that 9.7% of patients who remained vitamin D deficient despite supplementation experienced delayed healing, compared to 0.3% of those who were not deficient and 1.7% of those whose levels normalized after treatment. These are observational records, however, and cannot prove a causal relationship. If testing reveals a deficiency, follow your doctor’s advice to bring levels back to normal. For people already diagnosed with osteoporosis or those prone to fractures even from minor impacts, anti-osteoporosis medications are the appropriate treatment — see Section 1, Item 40 for details. Calcium tablets cannot replace these drugs. Long-term supplementation provides no benefit for people who are not vitamin D deficient; see Section 3 for more information on vitamin D supplementation. What needs to be avoided is “excessive over-supplementation”, not reducing normal dietary calcium intake — make sure to get enough calcium from regular meals, as outlined in Section 21 on preventing kidney stones. If you suspect a fracture after an injury, see Section 13, Item 41 for guidance. The estimated benefit described here is calculated based on the annual cost of calcium and vitamin D supplements; the main beneficiaries are you, the patient.

6-31.t: Don’t expect AI chatbots to accurately diagnose medical conditions or legal issues on their own. Before seeking medical care, filing a lawsuit, or spending a lot of money, verify the sources they cite
6-31.cost: There is no monetary cost. Each verification takes just a few minutes to half an hour. Ask the AI to provide the exact legal statutes, guidelines, or research papers it relies on, then look up those sources yourself to confirm the statements. The key habit to develop is not to blindly follow its advice just because it sounds confident.
6-31.human: When you feed a full medical case into an AI, it correctly identifies the condition over 90% of the time. Yet when ordinary people ask it about their own symptoms, it performs worse than those who simply search online; it also fails to give more accurate guidance on whether emergency care is needed. Regarding legal questions, at least 58% of responses from general-purpose AIs contain fabricated content, and they often build on any incorrect premises present in the user’s query.
6-31.gain: A 2026 randomized trial published in Nature Medicine involved 1,298 UK residents; the study protocol had been registered in advance. Each participant received two prepared case descriptions and had to determine both the condition and whether emergency care or home observation was appropriate. One group used AI chatbots—specifically GPT-4o, Llama 3, and Command R+—while the control group relied on their usual methods, mostly online searches or the NHS website. When the full case details were submitted to AI, it correctly identified the relevant condition 94.9% of the time and recommended the proper level of care 56.3% of the time. In contrast, ordinary users achieved correct identification rates below 34.5% and proper care recommendations below 44.2%. The control group’s identification rate was 1.76 times higher (95% CI 1.45–2.13), and their detection of serious, potentially life-threatening conditions was 1.57 times higher (1.28–1.92). Both groups performed similarly when deciding on emergency care. Reviewing the conversations revealed two main issues: users often omitted crucial symptoms, and even when the AI named the right disease, users frequently disregarded that information. Turning to law, a 2024 U.S. study tested ChatGPT-4 and other public models against actual federal court rulings; ChatGPT-4 produced fabricated answers in 58% of cases, while Llama 2 reached 88%. Such fabrication—termed “hallucination”—occurs because models cannot distinguish their own output from factual reality. When a user’s query contains erroneous legal premises, the AI tends to accept them wholesale. A 2025 follow-up study examined specialized legal AI tools marketed to attorneys; despite claims of zero fabrication, 17%–33% of their responses still contained inaccuracies. These tools appear cost-effective only because they are instantly available, free to use, and present answers with the confident tone of seasoned professionals.
6-31.note: This item remains somewhat controversial. A 2023 study sampled 195 patient questions from U.S. forums and asked medical professionals to rate the responses without knowing their source; 78.6% judged ChatGPT’s answers superior to those given by doctors. However, that assessment focused solely on writing quality, not on whether patients ultimately reached correct conclusions. The study used 2024-era models, which may now perform even better. Yet the same research also demonstrated that an AI’s standalone test scores do not reliably predict how well ordinary users will fare when employing it. OpenAI researchers offered an explanation in an unfunded 2025 paper: training and evaluation frameworks reward “guessing an answer” rather than admitting uncertainty, so models often state things confidently even when unsure. To verify claims, ask the AI to name specific statutes, guideline titles, or research papers, then locate those exact passages on official websites; if they cannot be found, treat the statement as unsubstantiated. Avoid framing questions with your own conclusions—instead of asking “Will I definitely win this case?”, ask “What does the law say about this situation?” For sudden symptoms such as facial drooping, unilateral weakness, or crushing chest pain, do not consult AI first; call emergency services immediately (see Section 13.3 and 13.7). Individuals lacking funds for legal representation should consult Section 7.3 on obtaining legal aid. The benefit rating is modest because only intermediate metrics—such as disease identification accuracy—were measured; there are no data indicating actual reductions in mortality. The primary beneficiaries are the users themselves and their families.

7-1.t: Apply online for unemployment insurance benefits after losing a job
7-1.cost: There is no cost. You can submit the application via smartphone using any of three portals: the “12333 Mobile App”, the e-Social Security Card mini-program on WeChat or Alipay, or the National Social Insurance Public Service Platform. Having a social security card or ID card is enough; in most regions you won’t need to visit an office in person. The prerequisite is completing unemployment registration first.
7-1.human: If both your employer and you have paid into the system for at least one year, and you did not resign voluntarily, you can receive benefits after finishing unemployment registration. If contributions total between one and five years, benefits last up to 12 months; between five and ten years, up to 18 months; and over ten years, up to 24 months. During this period, yibao (basic medical insurance) premiums are paid on your behalf by unemployment insurance funds.
7-1.gain: All three conditions must be met. First, both your employer and you must have contributed to unemployment insurance for at least one year. Second, you must have lost the job through no fault of your own (legally termed “employment termination not due to personal choice”). Third, unemployment registration must be completed and you must be actively seeking work. Benefit duration depends on contribution history: up to 12 months for under five years of contributions, up to 18 months for five to ten years, and up to 24 months for over ten years. Monthly amounts are set by provincial authorities and vary by region; they are higher than the urban dibao threshold yet lower than local minimum wage levels. The national target is gradually raising these payments to 90% of minimum wage standards. While receiving benefits, you retain full coverage under employee medical insurance; the corresponding premiums are paid by unemployment insurance funds, so you pay nothing personally (this policy has been in effect nationwide since 1999).
7-1.note: Voluntary resignation does not qualify as “termination not due to personal choice”, so benefits cannot be claimed. Avoid signing any documents stating “resignation for personal reasons” — see Section 19, Item 7. Benefits begin accruing from the date of unemployment registration; any delay reduces the total payout period. Immediately register after leaving a job, using the termination certificate issued by your employer (see Section 19, Item 17). Questions regarding non-compete agreements or lack of compensation should be addressed in Section 11, Item 12. Exact benefit amounts differ widely by province; consult local regulations for precise figures. The “90% of minimum wage” benchmark originates from a 2017 guideline issued jointly by the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security and the Ministry of Finance (Document No. 71 [2017]), which states that payments should “gradually be raised to 90% of minimum wage standards”; this is a long-term goal rather than an immediate requirement.

7-2.t: Filing a complaint with the labor inspection bureau or initiating one-instance arbitration are both free options; most cases yield results within a few months
7-2.cost: There are no fees for either option. You’ll need to gather your employment contract, pay stubs, attendance records, bank transfer statements, and any relevant chat logs, then visit the local Human Resources and Social Security Bureau or arbitration commission one to three times. For arbitration, there is a one-year statutory deadline (known as the arbitration limitation period). Employees still working for the employer are exempt from this deadline; former employees must file within one year of leaving. The main challenge is the repeated trips and evidence collection, which can be discouraging.
7-2.human: Neither option costs anything. First, call 12333 or file a complaint with the labor inspection bureau; investigations must be completed within 60 working days, and if the employer fails to pay, it may be ordered to pay an additional 50%–100% as compensation. If that doesn’t work, you can initiate one-instance arbitration, which must be concluded within 45 days. However, “case closure” does not guarantee payment: if the employer has no assets or the owner has fled, you might still receive nothing even after winning.
7-2.gain: The first step is filing a complaint. Call 12333 or visit your local labor inspection bureau. By law, investigations must be finished within 60 working days, extendable by another 30 days for complex cases. If violations are confirmed, the employer can be ordered to pay wages immediately; failure to do so triggers an extra penalty of 50%–100% of the owed amount. In 2024, labor inspection agencies nationwide handled 137,000 cases, securing 8.65 billion yuan for 654,000 workers. If you have a written IOU or clear wage records, you may also apply directly to a local court for a payment order, which must be issued within 15 days of acceptance. The second step is arbitration: legally required to conclude within 45 days, extendable by 15 days. Workers can request provisional enforcement even before the full ruling, and if the owed amount does not exceed 12 times the local minimum monthly wage, the arbitration decision is final and binding. In 2024, 4.257 million arbitration cases were filed, with 4.156 million resolved, totaling 93.47 billion yuan in recovered wages. The mediation success rate stood at 79.6%, while 98.2% of cases were closed and 73.7% resulted in final rulings. Some claim the process takes “six months to a year,” referring to cases that proceed to court after arbitration: a first-instance trial takes six months (or three months under simplified procedures) plus three months for any appeal. In 2024, courts resolved 88,000 wage-recovery cases, securing 28.54 billion yuan, and 998 individuals were convicted of refusing to pay wages.
7-2.note: Both complaints and arbitration are effective tools, but it’s crucial to distinguish between “case closure” and “actual payment.” The 98.2% closure rate refers solely to procedural completion; if an employer lacks assets or absconds, workers may still receive nothing. The Supreme People’s Court only reports total enforcement amounts (23 trillion yuan in 2024) and a “high completion rate,” leaving no official data on how much of that actually reaches victims. The term “arbitration termination rate” lacks a formal definition in official reports; here it is interpreted as cases not appealed further. Wage theft meeting certain thresholds can trigger criminal prosecution: either when one worker is owed wages for three months or more, totaling 5,000–20,000 yuan, or when 10 or more workers collectively suffer losses of 30,000–100,000 yuan. In such cases, failure to pay after a court order constitutes a crime. Provincial courts and procuratorates set exact thresholds within these ranges; check your local figure before filing. Construction workers benefit from dedicated wage accounts and a requirement for general contractors to assume liability, making them more reliable targets than subcontractors. Both pathways apply only to workers with a formal employer; unlicensed workshops and shops still qualify, but private domestic work—such as hiring a nanny—does not constitute an employment relationship and must be pursued via civil litigation (see Item 22). Legal aid for migrant workers seeking wage recovery is granted regardless of financial status. Quotes from labor and civil procedure laws are drawn from republished government pages, as official legislative sites remain inaccessible; verification of the Criminal Law Amendment (VIII) was performed via command-line tools. 〔2300000000000〕

7-3.t: Legal aid is available at no cost for cases such as wage disputes, alimony claims, and workplace injury compensation
7-3.cost: No cost at all. Legal aid services are provided free of charge to all applicants.
7-3.human: Anyone seeking unpaid wages, alimony, social insurance benefits, dibao payments, or compensation after acting in defense of others can apply for free legal assistance. Simply call 12348 or visit your local legal aid center. You no longer need to obtain proof of financial hardship from your hometown — just describe your situation honestly. For defendants facing the death penalty, or those who are blind, deaf, mute, or minors, a lawyer is assigned regardless of their financial status.
7-3.gain: According to national regulations, legal aid covers six main categories of civil cases: claims for state compensation; requests for social insurance or dibao benefits; applications for pensions or relief funds; demands for alimony, child support, or spousal maintenance; wage recovery claims; and civil claims arising from acts of bravery. In criminal cases, defendants facing capital punishment or those who are blind, deaf, mute, or minors are guaranteed legal representation irrespective of their financial circumstances.
7-3.note: The Legal Aid Law took effect on 1 January 2022, introducing one key change: applicants no longer need to submit official proof of financial hardship. A straightforward statement of one’s financial situation now suffices. Legal aid can be accessed via local legal aid centers, public legal service hubs, or by calling 12348.

7-4.t: Turning to a shelter when you have nowhere else to go – they provide food, lodging, and even a ticket home
7-4.cost: There is no cost. You can go to your local civil affairs bureau or shelter on your own, or ask police or civil affairs officials to take you there. Upon arrival, you must truthfully provide your name and list any personal belongings. The hard part is simply admitting that you have no money and nowhere to stay.
7-4.human: These shelters provide meals and a place to sleep. If you fall ill, they send you to a hospital and help you contact your family. Those who cannot afford a trip home receive a free ticket. Typically, stays are limited to 10 days. Entry and departure are completely voluntary – this is not a detention center, and no cash is handed out. Tickets are issued based on your household registration or current residence, so think carefully about where you want to go before arriving.
7-4.gain: Shelters supply food and lodging that meet basic hygiene standards. Should you suffer a medical emergency while there, they arrange prompt hospital treatment. They also assist in reaching out to relatives or employers. For those unable to pay for travel back to their registered home or current residence, a free transport voucher – essentially a train or bus ticket – is provided. “Household registration” refers to your hometown, while “current residence” is wherever you currently live. Generally, stays are capped at 10 days; extensions are granted if family members are on the way, medical care is needed, or other arrangements must be made. Police and other government officials encountering homeless individuals in the course of their duties must inform them of this assistance option. Special care is given to disabled persons, minors, the elderly, and anyone with mobility issues – they are guided and escorted to shelters (nationwide, since 2003).
7-4.note: Entry and departure are entirely voluntary; this is not a detention facility. Basic food and lodging are provided, but no cash is given. Transport vouchers are issued based on household registration or current residence – be sure to decide where you wish to go before seeking help. For shelter arrangements at night or during winter, see Section 21 (when there truly is nowhere else to sleep).

7-5.t: Use free public employment services and gig platforms instead of paid agencies
7-5.cost: No cost at all. You can register at any public employment service agency at the county level or higher — such as employment service centers or human resources markets. Local gig platforms also allow free registration. If you don’t know the exact location, call 12333 for help.
7-5.human: Public agencies like employment service centers and human resources markets provide job referrals, career guidance, policy advice, and both employment and unemployment registration — all completely free of charge. In fact, the law explicitly forbids them from charging for these services. Registration and posting job listings on gig platforms is likewise free. It’s a good idea to complete your unemployment registration at the same time, since it’s required to receive unemployment benefits and qualify for assistance as someone facing employment difficulties.
7-5.gain: The law guarantees that the following services must be provided at no cost: advice on employment policies; information about current job openings and labor shortages; career guidance and job matching; processing of both employment and unemployment registration; and targeted employment support for individuals facing employment difficulties. These agencies are prohibited from engaging in any commercial activities or profiting off these services. Gig platform job postings and registrations are also offered to the public free of charge, as part of the broader public employment information system. Special support is further extended to long-term unemployed workers and low-income gig workers facing financial hardship (nationwide).
7-5.note: Unemployment registration is a prerequisite for receiving unemployment benefits and qualifying as someone facing employment difficulties — so it’s worth completing at the same time. For gig workers paid on a daily basis, always verify your earnings on the spot, and be sure to collect the employer’s contact details and a record of the work performed.

7-6.t: Apply for emergency assistance when unexpected events occur
7-6.cost: No cost at all. Simply submit an application to the local township government or subdistrict office, explaining what happened at home — such as a fire, traffic accident, sudden serious illness of a family member, or an unexpected spike in essential expenses. After review and public notice, the county-level civil affairs bureau approves the request. Prepare documents according to the local checklist; usually only one or two visits are required.
7-6.human: If an unexpected crisis strikes — like a fire, car crash, or sudden serious illness of a family member — and it temporarily overwhelms your ability to cover basic living costs, you can apply for emergency assistance from the local township government or subdistrict office. You do not need to already be a dibao recipient. Most often, a one-time payment is issued; exact amounts vary widely by region.
7-6.gain: Two categories of households qualify for this aid. The first includes families facing immediate hardship in covering basic needs such as food, shelter, and medical care due to unexpected events or sudden serious illnesses of family members. The second comprises dibao households experiencing an unexpected rise in unavoidable expenses that exceeds their financial capacity. What types of expenses qualify and how much aid is granted are determined and publicly announced by local governments at or above the county level (this nationwide policy has been in effect since 2014).
7-6.note: You do not need to already be a dibao recipient. Typically, a one-time payment is provided; exact amounts differ greatly across regions and are set by local authorities each year.

7-7.t: Apply for dibao if household income falls below the local threshold
7-7.cost: There are no fees. Household members living together must submit a written application to the local township government or subdistrict office based on their hukou registration. If handling it independently proves difficult, they may ask the villagers' committee or residents' committee to assist. The application requires verification of household income and assets. Typically, 2–3 visits are needed, bringing along ID cards, hukou registration books, and proof of income and assets. The main challenge lies in disclosing personal financial details for inspection and waiting for the public notice period to end.
7-7.human: If the per-person household income is lower than the local dibao threshold and assets meet eligibility criteria, a dibao application can be filed. As of late 2024, the average monthly dibao standard stood at 798.1 yuan per person in urban areas and 593.9 yuan in rural regions. Approved recipients receive an amount equal to the difference between the local standard and their per-person monthly income. Owning property, vehicles, or sizable savings, or having children capable of providing support, may disqualify applicants.
7-7.gain: Households whose per-person income remains below the local dibao threshold and whose assets comply with regulations qualify for dibao benefits. In late 2024, the average monthly standard was 798.1 yuan per person in cities and 593.9 yuan in rural areas. Approximately 6.25 million urban residents and 33.615 million rural residents received dibao support. Payments are issued monthly based on the difference between the local standard and per-person income. For instance, if the standard is 798.1 yuan and a household member earns 500 yuan monthly, the dibao payout per person amounts to 298.1 yuan, not the full 798.1 yuan. This threshold is determined by multiplying the previous year’s average per-person consumption expenditure by a fixed percentage, with periodic adjustments nationwide.
7-7.note: Dibao serves as a final safety net, and applications must be submitted at one’s place of hukou registration. Exceeding local asset limits or having financially capable children may result in rejection. Upon approval, additional perks apply: financial aid for basic medical insurance (see Section 9), eligibility for medical assistance programs (see Section 10), and automatic qualification for legal aid regardless of financial status (see Section 3).

7-8.t: Apply for the two disability subsidies with a disability certificate
7-8.cost: There is no cost. Simply bring your disability certificate and submit one application at your local subdistrict office or township government.
7-8.human: Disabled individuals living in dibao households can receive a living subsidy. Those with a disability rating of level 1 or 2 who require long-term care can also qualify for a care subsidy. Both subsidies can be received simultaneously. Each province sets its own subsidy amounts, which vary widely, so it’s best to ask your local subdistrict office for exact figures. All you need to do is bring your second-generation disability certificate and file one application at the subdistrict office or township government.
7-8.gain: The State Council has established these two subsidies. The first is the Living Subsidy for Disabled Persons in Need; the official wording specifies that it is intended for “disabled individuals living in dibao households, with eligible regions gradually expanding eligibility to low-income disabled persons and other disadvantaged groups.” In short, priority is given to disabled people in dibao households, though regions with sufficient funds may extend coverage further. The second subsidy is the Care Subsidy for Severely Disabled Persons; it is designated for “individuals with a disability rating of level 1 or 2 who require long-term care.” Both subsidies can be claimed at the same time.
7-8.note: Subsidy amounts are determined by provincial governments and differ significantly across regions, ranging from just a few dozen yuan to several hundred yuan per month. To apply, you must present a second-generation disability certificate. If you are unable to apply in person, a family member may submit the application on your behalf.

7-9.t: Don’t let your annual dibao and yibao payments lapse — subsidies are available for low‑income households
7-9.cost: Individuals must pay at least 400 yuan per year. This is the national standard for 2024 and 2025; local authorities may set higher amounts. Payments must be made during the designated annual enrollment window. Extremely disadvantaged individuals receive full government funding, while those receiving dibao get a fixed government subsidy.
7-9.human: Each person must contribute a minimum of 400 yuan per year; the government then adds roughly 700 yuan per person. Full funding is provided for the most vulnerable, while dibao recipients receive a set subsidy. Letting payments lapse carries a penalty: anyone who enrolls outside the window or fails to maintain continuous coverage must wait three months before receiving any benefits; each additional year without payment adds another month to that waiting period.
7-9.gain: In addition to the individual contribution, the government contributes at least 670 yuan per person in 2024, a figure that rises to at least 700 yuan in 2025 — an increase of 30 yuan over the previous year. The minimum personal contribution remains 400 yuan (based on the 2025 Notice No. 22 from the National Healthcare Security Administration, as paraphrased from provincial documents). The 2026 Government Work Report projects a further 24‑yuan rise. For dibao recipients and the most disadvantaged, any medical expenses not covered by yibao can be reimbursed at a rate of at least 70 % through additional medical assistance programs.
