11-7.human: Even code written by you personally remains the company’s intellectual property — taking it away is essentially stealing company assets. Client lists also qualify as trade secrets. In one case, a former employee who took source code and core algorithms of a security inspection system to a new employer was sentenced to 5 years in prison and fined 500,000 yuan; the new employer was fined 4 million yuan. Another individual who exploited system vulnerabilities to download over 33,000 design files was sentenced to 1 year and 10 months in prison and fined 100,000 yuan. Beyond criminal penalties, companies can also pursue separate civil compensation claims.
11-7.gain: Violating confidentiality obligations by disclosing or personally using trade secrets may result in imprisonment of up to 3 years, along with a fine or both. In more serious cases, the sentence ranges from 3 to 10 years, plus a fine. The Anti-Unfair Competition Law also deems two acts as violations: using technical means to illegally access systems and obtain trade secrets, and aiding or abetting others in breaching confidentiality. Official examples include the aforementioned cases where former employees took source code and algorithms to new employers, resulting in heavy criminal and financial penalties. Additionally, an engineer who stored App module source code on personal devices and later developed a similar product after changing jobs was prosecuted for trade secret infringement nationwide.
11-7.note: Code written by employees remains the company’s property, as stipulated in Article 13 (code developed using company resources belongs to the company). Taking such code away is equivalent to stealing company assets. Client lists are classified as business information and also qualify as trade secrets. Apart from criminal penalties, companies may also file separate civil lawsuits for compensation.

11-8.t: Do not run your own programs on others’ computers, servers, or cameras; do not use company machines for mining
11-8.cost: No expense and no time loss
11-8.human: Controlling someone else’s computer, server, or camera without permission is illegal. Operating 20 or more such devices qualifies as a serious offense, punishable by up to 3 years in prison; especially severe cases may incur 3 to 7 years. Even if it does not rise to a criminal offense, offenders can still be detained for up to 5 days and fined between 50,000 and 500,000 yuan. For tech professionals, the most damaging consequence is a lifelong ban from holding key positions in cybersecurity management and network operations after any criminal conviction.
11-8.gain: Illegally controlling computer information systems is a crime. Serious cases result in up to 3 years in prison plus a fine; especially severe cases incur 3 to 7 years. Controlling 20 or more devices is deemed “serious.” Those not meeting criminal thresholds still face confiscation of illegal gains, up to 5 days of detention, and fines ranging from 50,000 to 500,000 yuan. More serious violations bring 5 to 15 days of detention and fines from 100,000 to 1,000,000 yuan. Anyone with a prior public security penalty is barred for 5 years, while those with a criminal record are barred for life from critical cybersecurity and network operation roles. Example: Li was sentenced to 3 years in prison suspended for 5 years and fined 20,000 yuan after using software to illegally control 105 surveillance cameras; Wu and others received 2 to 4 years and 6 months in prison for implanting malware into mobile phone motherboards to harvest verification codes from over 3.3 million devices.
11-8.note: No published cases from China’s Supreme People’s Procuratorate or Supreme People’s Court address mining on company servers; this entry is written under the legal provision concerning unauthorized system control. The lifelong ban from key roles is an additional consequence under China’s Cybersecurity Law, carrying heavier weight for tech professionals than monetary fines alone.

11-9.t: Testing someone else’s systems without written permission — “good intentions” and “reporting afterward” are not excuses
11-9.cost: No cost at all. Before joining a vendor’s SRC or public beta test, obtain a document that clearly defines the permitted scope, target systems, and allowed testing windows. An SRC is a vendor-run security response center designed to receive external vulnerability reports. Once a vulnerability is confirmed, testing must stop. The real challenge is resisting the urge to “give it a quick try.”
11-9.human: Whether a crime is established depends solely on whether you had permission and how much access you obtained — not on your intentions. Possessing 500 sets of ordinary account credentials, or earning 5,000 yuan while causing 10,000 yuan in losses, is enough to warrant a sentence of up to three years. Even a single attempt to export a user list to prove a vulnerability often exceeds that 500‑credential threshold. Using credentials you already possess outside their authorized scope also constitutes unauthorized access.
11-9.gain: This law applies to computer information systems belonging to ordinary companies and individuals, excluding those used for national affairs, defense, or cutting‑edge scientific research. Unauthorized intrusion or use of any technical means to obtain stored, processed, or transmitted data may lead to imprisonment of up to three years, a fine, or both, if the circumstances are serious; for especially serious cases, the sentence ranges from three to seven years with a fine. “Serious circumstances” include obtaining ten or more authentication credentials for online financial services such as payments or securities trading, 500 or more other authentication credentials, illegally controlling 20 or more computers, or earning illicit profits exceeding 5,000 yuan or causing losses above 10,000 yuan. Five times these thresholds define “especially serious” circumstances. Prosecutorial Example No. 36 states that “using accounts or passwords beyond the granted scope to log into a computer system is itself an act of unauthorized intrusion.” In that case, three individuals used work‑related credentials to access their company’s internal system, downloaded non‑work data, and sold it for 37,000 yuan; they received sentences of 4 years, 3 years 9 months, and 4 years respectively, plus fines of 40,000 yuan each.
11-9.note: Prosecutorial Example No. 36 involves a data‑selling scheme; it is cited only for the principle that exceeding authorized scope counts as intrusion, not to suggest that well‑meaning tests incur identical penalties. Intentions and post‑test reporting cannot erase criminal liability; they may only influence sentencing or whether charges are filed. A vendor’s initial thanks and later filing of a report are not mutually exclusive — gratitude does not equal permission. At the time of writing, no publicly documented cases on permissible testing were found on the Supreme People’s Court or Supreme People’s Procuratorate websites; therefore this description relies on statutory provisions and penalty criteria. Always participate through a vendor’s official SRC or under a written contract that specifies scope, targets, and time limits. To prove a vulnerability, collect only minimal evidence and avoid bulk data extraction. Even conduct that does not meet criminal thresholds remains subject to administrative penalties, professional bans, and fines comparable to those outlined in Section 8 (running unauthorized programs on others’ machines). Guidance on post‑disclosure procedures appears in Section 10 (reporting vulnerabilities as required). 〔2016〕

11-10.t: Vulnerabilities must be reported per regulations; no details, exploit tools, or disclosure to foreign entities before patching
11-10.cost: No cost involved. Simply report the vulnerability to the product vendor or an official platform. Until the vendor releases a patch, no details or verification code should be disclosed.
11-10.human: The “Regulations on the Management of Security Vulnerabilities in Network Products” applies not only to companies but also to individuals. There are five strict rules for vulnerability disclosure; the first two state that no details about vulnerabilities affecting active systems may be released before a vendor provides a fix. Additionally, no programs or tools specifically designed to exploit those vulnerabilities may be published, and any release must include instructions on how to remediate them. One often-overlooked rule: unreported vulnerabilities must not be shared with any foreign organizations or individuals outside the vendor.
11-10.gain: These regulations govern three main groups: domestic network product vendors, network operators, and any organizations or individuals involved in discovering, collecting, or publishing vulnerability information. No entity may use vulnerabilities to compromise network security, nor may they illegally collect, sell, or distribute such information. Five additional rules apply to public disclosure: first, nothing may be released before a vendor provides a patch; second, no details about vulnerabilities in active networks or systems may be published; third, no exaggerated claims about risks or malicious exploitation attempts may be made; fourth, no tools or programs designed for malicious exploitation may be released; and fifth, any disclosure must include remediation steps. Unreported vulnerabilities must also not be shared with foreign entities. The regulations encourage reporting to four official platforms: the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology’s Cybersecurity Threat and Vulnerability Information Sharing Platform; the National Cybersecurity Information Notification Center’s Vulnerability Platform; the National Computer Network Emergency Response Technical Team/Coordination Center of China’s Vulnerability Platform; and the China Information Security Evaluation Center’s Vulnerability Database. Violators may face penalties ranging from fines of 10,000 to 100,000 RMB, suspension of services, revocation of licenses or business licenses, and even criminal liability for responsible personnel.
11-10.note: This regulation explicitly includes individuals as subjects; claiming “I’m just an amateur” does not exempt anyone from compliance. Submitting vulnerabilities found in domestic systems to foreign bug bounty platforms violates the rule prohibiting disclosure to foreign entities. This rule addresses how vulnerabilities must be handled after discovery. Whether one is legally permitted to test systems depends on other provisions, such as the requirement for written authorization before testing any system. Even legally discovered vulnerabilities may incur penalties if disclosed improperly. Unauthorized testing results in violations on both fronts. Among reporting channels, the MIIT platform and CNCERT are most commonly used. The regulations do not specifically address cases where a vendor is notified but fails to act; in practice, documentation of negotiation and reporting processes is required before official submission.

11-11.t: No selling of tools for bypassing firewalls or VPN accounts, no setting up such nodes for others
11-11.human: Any individual or entity that builds their own outbound network connections or uses international channels outside of state-provided public telecom services may be ordered by police to cease internet access, receive a warning, and face fines up to 15,000 yuan plus confiscation of any illegal earnings. Those running businesses based on such services may be charged with illegal business operations; in severe cases, imprisonment of up to five years applies. This rule specifically addresses selling or setting up such nodes. For personal use only, the maximum penalty remains limited to a warning and fine as stipulated in Article 14 of the provisional regulations.
11-11.gain: Direct international internet connectivity must be facilitated via international gateway channels supplied by state-owned telecom networks. No organization or individual may independently establish or utilize any other channels, meaning neither private outbound connections nor third-party nodes are permitted. Violators face police orders to disconnect from the internet, warnings, and possible fines up to 15,000 yuan plus confiscation of illicit profits. Commercial operators violating this rule may be prosecuted for illegal business operations; severe violations incur up to five years imprisonment plus fines ranging from one to five times the illegal earnings. Particularly egregious cases may result in imprisonment exceeding five years nationwide.
11-11.note: At the time of drafting, no publicly documented court rulings regarding firewall circumvention were found on Supreme People’s Court or Supreme People’s Procuratorate websites, and regional enforcement practices vary widely; hence this B rating was assigned. This section exclusively addresses selling or setting up such nodes. For personal usage alone, the maximum penalty remains limited to warnings and fines as outlined in Article 14 of the provisional regulations.

11-12.t: After signing a non-compete agreement, if the employer fails to pay compensation monthly, send a written notice; if payment still doesn’t come after 3 months, you may terminate the agreement. Workers who never handled any trade secrets can request that the clause be declared invalid
11-12.cost: No cost involved. Keep the original non-compete agreement and any proof that the employer didn’t make monthly payments after leaving the job.
11-12.human: A non-compete clause simply means you’re not allowed to work for a competitor for a certain period after leaving your job. This rule is there to protect you. The maximum duration is 2 years, and the employer must pay compensation every month. If the amount isn’t specified, it’s calculated as 30% of your average monthly wage over the previous 12 months, and it can’t be lower than the local minimum wage. If the employer fails to pay for 3 months due to its own reasons, you can ask to end the agreement. Starting in 2025, workers who never learned about or handled any trade secrets at their job can request that the non-compete clause be ruled invalid.
11-12.gain: Non-compete clauses only apply to senior executives, highly skilled technicians, and anyone with a duty to keep secrets. The maximum term is 2 years, and the employer must provide monthly financial compensation during that time. If the amount isn’t set, it’s 30% of your average monthly wage over the last 12 months, never lower than the local minimum wage. If the employer doesn’t pay for 3 months for reasons on its end, you can ask to cancel the clause. If the employer ends it voluntarily, it must pay an extra 3 months of compensation. From 2025, workers who never knew about or touched any trade secrets can ask to have the clause declared void. Any part of the clause that goes beyond what they actually knew about is also invalid. Official case example: A pharmaceutical firm sued its former CTO, Zheng, seeking 7.1 million yuan in damages. The court ruled that Zheng’s new employer’s products had no overlap with the original firm’s offerings, so the non-compete scope should be limited to what Zheng actually knew. The claim was dismissed in full (nationwide ruling).
11-12.note: This rule is there to protect you. On the flip side, if the agreement is valid and the employer pays as required, but you still go to work for a competitor, you’ll have to pay the agreed-upon penalty. Even after paying that, you might still be required to serve out the remaining non-compete period. Non-compete terms agreed upon while you’re still employed also count as valid, even if no extra payment is made by the employer.

11-13.t: Code written during work hours using company resources belongs to the company; personal open‑source projects should be done in your own time and on your own equipment, without mixing them
11-13.cost: No cost involved. When you start a new job, be sure to read the intellectual‑property clauses in your employment contract. The main difficulty is that personal projects and work tasks often share the same computer, so you must keep them separate.
11-13.human: Work‑related creations are defined as works made in the course of your duties. Software is explicitly listed in law as “copyright belonging to the employer.” If a program is primarily produced using company hardware, internal networks, or business data — and the company assumes responsibility for it — then the copyright rests with the employer. The same applies when the contract states this. As the creator, you retain only the right to be credited. Inventions developed using company resources also belong to the company, with patent rights following the same rule. Even if you write code “after hours,” using a company computer or business data can still make it qualify as a work created mainly with employer resources.
11-13.gain: Works produced to fulfill job duties are considered “work‑made‑for‑hire.” Under normal circumstances the author keeps copyright, while the employer has the right to use them for its own business and may not allow third parties to use them in the same way for two years. However, two exceptions exist: works such as software or engineering designs that are created mainly with employer resources and for which the employer bears responsibility, and any works expressly assigned to the employer by contract. In both cases the author retains only the right to be credited. “Employer resources” include hardware, internal networks, and business data. Inventions created while performing job duties or using those same resources are classified as “work‑made‑for‑hire inventions,” with all patent rights belonging to the employer nationwide.
11-13.note: Software is explicitly categorized as “copyright belonging to the employer,” so programmers rarely qualify for the standard rule granting them copyright while the employer retains a two‑year exclusive right to use it. Code written outside work hours can still be deemed a product of employer resources if it is produced on a company computer, accessed company networks, or uses business data. To keep personal projects truly separate, use your own machine, avoid company repositories, and ensure they do not overlap with any company work.

11-14.t: Using open-source code such as GPL in products: Open-source it per the license or switch licenses — don’t treat this as “no one cares”
11-14.cost: There is no cost involved. Before using someone else’s open-source code, check its license for any stated usage terms. The GPL family of licenses requires that any product built using it must also have its source code released, which conflicts with selling the product as closed-source software for profit. If such a conflict exists, you must switch to another license. The hard part is giving up a library you’ve already grown comfortable using.
11-14.human: Copyright infringement requires you to compensate the copyright holder based on their actual losses or the profits you earned from the infringement. If you commit infringement intentionally and under aggravating circumstances, you may be ordered to pay damages ranging from 1 to 5 times the original amount. One company hired a former employee of a competitor and developed software that was substantially similar to the competitor’s product. The company argued that since the competitor’s software used GPLv2, it was required to be open-source anyway. The Supreme People’s Court ruled that whether a developer complies with GPLv2 or not has no bearing on their copyright rights, and ordered the company to cease infringement and pay 500,000 yuan in damages.
11-14.gain: Copyright infringement demands compensation based on the rights holder’s actual losses or the infringer’s profits. If neither of these can be accurately calculated, damages are determined by how much it would cost to obtain a proper license for the same software. Intentional and aggravated infringement can also result in 1 to 5 times the standard compensation amount. If the infringement harms public interests, any illegal profits may be confiscated and fines imposed. A relevant official case is Supreme People’s Court Civil Appeal No. 51 of 2021. In this case, a defendant hired a former employee of a plaintiff and developed gateway software that was substantially similar to the plaintiff’s product. The defendant claimed the plaintiff’s software used GPLv2 and thus should have been open-source. The Supreme People’s Court reiterated that compliance with GPLv2 and copyright ownership are two separate issues, and ordered the defendant to cease infringement and pay 500,000 yuan in damages nationwide.
11-14.note: This case makes it clear that “the other party used GPL code” cannot serve as justification for copying their software. Conversely, there are already effective court rulings in China where GPL authors successfully sue commercial entities that fail to release source code. No original text of these rulings could be found on the Supreme People’s Court website, so they are not cited here. This item is graded B because compliance with open-source licenses is governed only by general contract and copyright laws, without any specific legal provisions dedicated to this area.

11-15.t: Only collect personal data strictly necessary for the app’s operation; consent from guardians is required for users under 14, and the privacy policy must be clearly written
11-15.cost: No cost involved. Before launch, cross‑check the list of permissions the app requests against the privacy policy and remove any unnecessary permissions. The main challenge is that product teams often want to retain data “just in case it might be useful later.”
11-15.human: Only gather information that is genuinely needed for business purposes, and obtain consent from a guardian for any user under 14. For violations, regulators first order corrections and issue warnings, and may also confiscate illegal earnings; the app can be ordered to suspend or terminate its services. If the violation persists, fines up to 1 million RMB can be imposed on the app, while individuals directly responsible may be fined between 10,000 and 100,000 RMB. In severe cases, fines can reach 50 million RMB or 5 % of the previous year’s revenue, and responsible personnel may face fines from 100,000 to 1 million RMB. The term “directly responsible personnel” can include the technical and product staff who actually implement the app.
11-15.gain: Personal data should be processed only for a clear, legitimate purpose that is directly related to that purpose, using methods that minimize impact on individuals’ rights. Consent from the individual is required unless another legal basis applies. For users under 14, consent from parents or guardians is mandatory. Violations lead to regulatory orders to correct the problem, warnings, and confiscation of illegal earnings; the offending app may be suspended or shut down. Persistent breaches incur fines up to 1 million RMB, while responsible managers and staff may be fined between 10,000 and 100,000 RMB. In extreme cases, fines can exceed 50 million RMB or 5 % of annual revenue, and those individuals may be barred from serving as directors, supervisors, or executives of related companies. Criminal acts involving the sale or disclosure of personal data are covered under Section 4 (National).
11-15.note: In practice, the “directly responsible personnel” label often applies to developers and product managers. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology regularly publishes lists of removed or penalized apps; however, no specific announcement was identified for this section, so it is not cited here.

11-16.t: Before launching a website or app, complete ICP registration and retain logs for at least 6 months per classification protection requirements
11-16.cost: Registration itself is free; using a cloud provider’s process takes a few weeks. Fees for classification protection assessments vary by level. Classification protection, also known as “DB”, is a set of national security management measures that classify systems based on their importance; small websites generally do not need to undergo assessments.
11-16.human: ICP registration costs nothing, and the cloud provider’s process takes a few weeks. Domestic servers without registration will be shut down. Providers that claim registration is free but charge fees face fines ranging from 100,000 to 1,000,000 yuan. You must retain logs for at least 6 months; failure to comply or causing any consequences results in fines of 10,000 to 100,000 yuan.
11-16.gain: Commercial internet information services require a license, while non-commercial ones need only registration. Operating without a license or registration is prohibited. Non-compliant sites will be ordered to make corrections by telecom authorities; refusal leads to site closure. Unlicensed operators face confiscation of illegal earnings plus fines of 3 to 5 times those earnings, or fines ranging from 100,000 to 1,000,000 yuan. Failure to display the ICP registration number on a website’s homepage incurs fines of 5,000 to 50,000 yuan. Network operators must develop security policies under classification protection rules, defend against attacks, retain logs for at least 6 months, and encrypt and back up data by category. Non-compliance leads to corrective orders and warnings; persistent violations result in fines of 10,000 to 100,000 yuan for operators and 5,000 to 50,000 yuan for responsible personnel nationwide.
11-16.note: Domestic servers cannot be accessed via domain names without ICP registration. Details on how to register, associated penalties for missing registration numbers, and how to verify a provider’s qualifications are covered in Section 26, Item 4 (domestic servers must be registered). Common pitfalls include registering as a personal non-commercial site while actually charging fees, and failing to update registration after changing domains or operators. Keeping logs for 6 months is both a legal obligation and a safeguard; they can prove your innocence in case of incidents.

11-17.t: Before offering generative AI services to the public, conduct required safety assessments and algorithm registration; mark all generated content
11-17.cost: There is no monetary cost, but you must follow procedures set by internet regulators — completing them takes some time. Small personal tools that are not made available to the public do not fall under these rules.
11-17.human: If you offer generative AI services with public influence or social mobilization potential to the general public, you must perform a safety assessment and register the algorithm per national regulations before launch. Any changes or shutdowns also require filing updates or cancellation paperwork. All generated images and videos must be clearly marked. Tools meant solely for personal use and not open to the public are exempt from these requirements. The regulation itself does not specify penalties; violations are handled under the Cybersecurity Law, Data Security Law, and Personal Information Protection Law.
11-17.gain: Providers of generative AI services that can shape public opinion or mobilize people must conduct safety assessments, register their algorithms, and handle subsequent updates or cancellations as required by law. “Public influence” or “social mobilization potential” means the ability to affect how people think or to organize them. Providers must also add identifying marks to any generated images or videos. This regulation took effect nationwide on August 15, 2023.
11-17.note: The regulation itself does not state exact penalty amounts. Violations are penalized under the Cybersecurity Law, Data Security Law, and Personal Information Protection Law, which is why this item is rated B. No civil cases involving copyright or portrait rights violations caused by AI‑generated content are cited here, as the original texts were not verified on the Supreme People’s Court website.

11-18.t: Tools that automatically skip or block ads from other apps — free and offline — may still be deemed unfair competition
11-18.cost: There is no monetary cost. The trade‑off is giving up a popular little utility. The difficulty lies in the fact that you feel you’re not making any money; you’re merely helping users click “skip” for them.
11-18.human: Creating software that automatically skips or blocks ads from other apps can lead to a finding of unfair competition, even if no fee is charged. The law applies to anyone providing services, including individuals. One browser that blocks Mango TV’s opening ads was ordered to pay 800,000 yuan in damages. Another app that lets users bypass Mango TV’s splash ads was fined 80,000 yuan for losses incurred.
11-18.gain: Statutory rules state that operators may not use technical means to interfere with or disrupt the normal operation of network products or services lawfully offered by others. “Operators” here include natural persons, legal entities, and other organizations that provide goods or services. If harm results, compensation must cover the actual loss suffered by the other party, any benefit gained by the violator, and reasonable expenses incurred to stop the infringement. Regulatory authorities may also impose fines ranging from 100,000 to 1,000,000 yuan; in serious cases the penalty can reach 5,000,000 yuan. A notable case: the built‑in feature in 720 Browser that blocks Mango TV’s opening and pause ads was initially dismissed by a lower court, but an appellate court ruled it constituted unfair competition and ordered 800,000 yuan in damages plus related costs. In 2021 the Supreme People’s Court listed this as a model case. The “Liao Jingling” app, which lets users skip Mango TV’s splash ads, was ordered to cease operation and pay 80,000 yuan in losses plus 10,000 yuan in legal costs; a 2024 appellate ruling upheld this decision. The court emphasized that the app effectively blocked ads rather than merely acting as a “skip” button for users (nationwide).
11-18.note: Both rulings cited provisions that have since been amended. As of 2025 those provisions appear in Article 13, now also covering data, algorithms, and platform rules. The appellate courts clarified that merely allowing users to click “skip” does not violate the law, whereas actual blocking does. In August 2023 the free Android ad‑skipping tool “Li Tiaotiao” received a legal notice from Tencent alleging it blocked ads in Tencent Browser and thus engaged in unfair competition; Tencent demanded removal within 48 hours. The developer, who described the tool as non‑profit and noted only occasional donations, ultimately announced an indefinite pause in updates; several similar apps followed suit. No lawsuit or judgment resulted from this incident — only media coverage. When an individual developer receives such a notice, they must either discontinue the service or bear the cost of legal defense; first‑instance proceedings typically take at least six months, with legal fees paid by the developer. No documented cases exist of a personal script used solely by its creator being penalized. For comparison, developers selling ticket‑snatching software have been fined for unfair competition; see item 3 in this section (ticket‑snatching scripts). In this case the “beneficiary” is the individual user.

11-19.t: Operating AI proxy sites to resell foreign large model APIs at low prices is illegal: a Shanghai operator was criminally detained
11-19.cost: There is no direct monetary cost, but you give up a seemingly easy side business with decent revenue potential. If you truly want to aggregate models, you must follow legal channels — obtaining operating permits and authorized model access will require both time and money.
11-19.human: AI proxy sites are platforms that resell foreign large model APIs at low prices. In Shanghai, one site operator was criminally detained for 37 days; after being released on bail, he stated he would definitely be sentenced and has already returned illicit profits. The Ministry of State Security also warned that many such sites lack proper operating licenses and illegally transmit user data overseas.
11-19.gain: The Ministry of State Security issued a risk warning in June 2026 stating that AI proxy sites act as intermediaries between users and official model providers. Numerous sites operate without proper licensing; some transmit user data abroad without obtaining required data-export clearance or undergoing mandatory security assessments, and they even help users bypass domestic network restrictions, official authorization rules, and cross-border transmission limits. A June 2026 article in China Newsweek described a specific case: in May 2026, a Shanghai proxy site operator posted a shutdown notice on a tech forum, explaining he had been detained for 37 days by police for illegally obtaining large model APIs, and is now on bail. He confirmed he would be convicted, has returned all illicit gains, and will pay fines. These sites typically register or purchase foreign model subscriptions in bulk, set up overseas servers as relays, and then resell access to domestic users at low prices.
11-19.note: This case is documented only through media reports and the operator’s own statements; there is no court verdict or official police announcement, so the exact criminal charge remains unconfirmed. Reported charges and sentences circulating online originate from legal analyses and are not cited in this book. Therefore, while operating such proxy sites is illegal, we cannot claim it is a guaranteed crime. Legitimate model aggregation requires a business license, as explained in Section 26, Item 2; offering generative AI services to the public demands registration, as noted in Section 17. Data export abroad must comply with strict legal criteria outlined in Section 26, Item 10. Users of these proxy sites also face additional risks, detailed in Section 14, Item 10. Ultimately, any potential gains from such activities are outweighed by legal and security consequences.

12-1.t: Only put in money you can afford to lose; don't touch family savings or borrow to open
12-1.cost: No money. Before you start, set a cap: you could lose every yuan of it and still pay the mortgage, support the kids, and see a doctor. Don't invest above that cap. Family money and borrowed money don't count toward the cap. The hard part is when the business looks like it's picking up and you want to pour in more.
12-1.human: Debts of a sole proprietorship come out of assets in your name. If it's unclear whether the whole family ran the business, creditors can reach family property. A company doesn't fully shield you either: when the company can't pay, what you promised as subscribed registered capital but haven't paid yet can be called in early. Size your stake by «I could lose it all and still pay the mortgage and medical bills».
12-1.gain: Losing money isn't the only risk. For sole proprietorships, if you ran the business alone, debts are paid from personal property; if the family ran it together or ownership is unclear, from family property. Debts both spouses signed count as joint marital debt; later assent by one spouse counts too. A loan in one spouse's name still counts as joint debt if the creditor shows it went into the couple's shared business. For companies: when the company can't pay a due debt, creditors may demand early payment of subscribed registered capital not yet due (nationwide).
12-1.note: «Affordable to lose» means losing it all wouldn't force you to sell the home or borrow from relatives. This round found no verifiable official statistics on survival rates or average lifespan on the National Bureau of Statistics or State Administration for Market Regulation sites, so the text gives legal consequences only, not headcount figures—grade B.

12-2.t: Don't sign personal guarantees on company loans; spouses should stay off the signature line
12-2.cost: No money. When a bank, supplier, or landlord wants a «personal joint-and-several guarantee» or a spouse's signature, pause. That page is you giving up «company debt stays with the company» (limited liability). Don't sign if you can avoid it. If you must, choose «general guarantee» only and cap how much you guarantee. The hard part is «no signature, no loan»—you have to hold the line.
12-2.human: «Joint-and-several guarantee» means if the company doesn't pay, the creditor can skip the company and come straight to you. «General guarantee» means sue or arbitrate against the company first, enforce on company assets, and only then collect any shortfall from you. If your spouse signs too, both households' assets are in play and the company's «limited» liability stops protecting you personally.
12-2.gain: Guarantee wording means «if the debtor doesn't pay, you pay». With «joint-and-several guarantee», creditors need not pursue the company first—they can demand payment from you directly. With «general guarantee», they must sue or arbitrate against the company and enforce on its assets first; only the remainder can be collected from you. Debts both spouses guaranteed count as joint marital debt; later assent counts too. A spouse's signature puts both sides' family assets on the hook (nationwide, from 2021).
12-2.note: Banks lending to small and micro enterprises almost always require shareholder personal joint-and-several guarantees. Loans are still available; know what that page costs before you sign, and keep guaranteed amounts within the «affordable to lose» cap in item 1. General rules for IOUs and guarantees: section 8, item 18.

12-3.t: Pick the right entity before opening: sole props and general partners pay to the end; only LLCs are «limited»
12-3.cost: Register on the local government services portal— a few hours once. After you form a limited liability company, monthly bookkeeping and tax filing are ongoing: your time if you do it yourself, or paid bookkeeping, with prices varying by region.
12-3.human: Sole proprietors and general partners in ordinary partnerships owe without limit—pay what you owe until it's cleared. LLC shareholders owe only up to what they subscribed at registration. But subscribed capital must be paid in within 5 years: write 1 million, you may owe up to 1 million. Mix company money with household money and «limited» can fail.
12-3.gain: Sole proprietorship debts are paid from personal or family property. General partners in an ordinary partnership bear unlimited joint and several liability—pay in full, and creditors may demand the entire debt from one partner alone. In a limited partnership, limited partners are liable only up to subscribed capital. LLC shareholders are liable only up to subscribed capital. «Limited» fails in three situations: subscribed capital must be fully paid within 5 years of formation, and if the company can't pay due debts, creditors may demand early payment; capital withdrawn after contribution must be returned; using the company as a shell to dodge debt—including a one-shareholder company that can't show separate company and personal funds—makes you personally liable for company debts (nationwide, from July 2024).
12-3.note: «Limited» requires clean separation: don't mix company and personal accounts, don't pay household bills from the company, keep complete books. Don't inflate registered capital for show—whatever you subscribe must be paid within 5 years. 1 million subscribed means up to 1 million of potential debt.

12-4.t: Don't be a nominal shareholder or hold shares for someone else
12-4.cost: No money. When someone asks to «borrow your ID for a shareholder slot» or «hold shares in your name for now», refuse.
12-4.human: If your name is on the register, you're a shareholder in law. Pay subscribed capital on time; miss the deadline and you owe make-up plus company losses. If another founder didn't really pay in, you may share liability for the gap. Someone else runs the business; the debt sits on your name.
12-4.gain: A registered shareholder is a legal shareholder. Pay subscribed capital in full by the deadline in the articles; otherwise pay the shortfall and compensate company losses. If a founder didn't contribute at formation, other founders at formation share joint liability for that gap. When the company can't pay due debts, creditors may demand early payment of capital not yet due. The operator isn't on the register; the obligation is still yours (nationwide, from July 2024).
12-4.note: A nominee agreement between nominal and actual investor is valid unless a statutory invalidity applies. The actual investor can't get their name on the register without consent from over half of the other shareholders. If the nominal holder sells or pledges shares, courts apply good-faith acquisition rules: a buyer who didn't know, paid fairly, and registered may keep the shares; the investor can only sue the nominal holder. A draft judicial interpretation was released September 2025; when finalized it replaces the current text—for now the 2020 amended version remains in force as of September 2026. Risks of being a nominal legal representative: section 8, item 28.

12-5.t: Before franchising, check MOFCOM filing, get written disclosure, and put a cooling-off period in the contract
12-5.cost: No money. On the Ministry of Commerce «Commercial Franchise Information Management System» site, check whether the brand is filed. Before signing, require written disclosure of everything they must tell you, together with the contract text. A few hours.
12-5.human: By rule the franchisor needs at least 2 company-owned stores open 1 year, and must file with commerce authorities within 15 days after signing. Before signing it must give you 12 topics in writing—fees, when deposits return, how existing stores perform, and more. No filing, no disclosure, or pay-before-you-see-contract: walk away.
12-5.gain: The franchisor must have at least 2 directly operated stores running 1 year or more. Within 15 days of the first franchise contract it must file with the commerce department; no filing: fine 10,000–50,000 yuan; late filing: 50,000–100,000 yuan plus public notice. Before signing it must deliver written disclosure on 12 items—including fee types and amounts, deposit refund conditions, franchisee count and performance, audited report summaries for the last 2 years, litigation and arbitration in the last 5 years. The contract must state that the franchisee may unilaterally terminate within a period after signing. Concealment or false disclosure lets the franchisee cancel the contract (nationwide, from May 2007).
12-5.note: No filing, no disclosure file, or pay-before-reading contract: leave. «Cooling-off» is the post-signing window for unilateral exit; the regulation only says «a certain period», so get the day count written in. On disclosed average sales, gross, or net profit, ask how the brand sourced the numbers—the rules require disclosure of sources. Schemes that skip «franchise» and only charge «store operations» or «opening training» fees: item 24.

12-6.t: Before registration, fix name, premises, scope, and registered capital; with complete papers you can get the license on the spot
12-6.cost: Registration costs nothing. Enterprise and individual-business registration fees were abolished from 1 January 2015. Do it yourself on the local government services site or at the service hall— a few hours. Seal carving, paid bookkeeping, and a registered address (address hosting) are market services, not government fees.
12-6.human: Registration is free; the registration fee has not been charged since 2015. Only five material types: application, identity or eligibility proof, premises proof, articles or partnership agreement (not for sole props), plus anything else the rules name. Complete and correct papers: license on the spot; otherwise within 3 working days. Money taken is usually agency fees.
12-6.gain: The regulation lists exactly five items. «(1) Application form». «(2) Applicant qualification documents and natural-person ID». «(3) Domicile or main business premises documents». «(4) Articles for companies, non-company enterprise legal persons, farmer specialized cooperatives (unions), or partnership agreement». «(5) Other materials required by laws, administrative regulations, and the State Council market supervision department». In plain language: one application; proof of who you are or that you're eligible; proof you may use the shop or office; articles or partnership agreement; plus anything else required. Companies also submit appointment documents and ID for the legal representative, directors, supervisors, and senior managers. Sole props don't file articles. The name is «declared by the applicant according to law». Registered capital uses «subscribed registration»—state the amount promised, no payment at the counter. Business scope is chosen from the authority's published categories. Complete and correctly formatted materials are «confirmed and registered on the spot». If not finished on the spot, «within 3 working days», with up to 3 more for complex cases. «The business license issue date is the establishment date»—that printed date is when the entity is born (nationwide, from March 2022).
12-6.note: Registration itself is free; charges are usually agency fees. Seal prices are market-set. The General Office of the State Council forbids mandating a designated seal maker—you need not accept «must use the designated shop». Registered capital doesn't buy prestige; it caps liability and must be paid within 5 years—see item 3. If scope includes licensed activities, don't open until licensed—see item 7.

12-7.t: Licensed trades: don't open until the license is issued
12-7.cost: No money. Before opening, check whether your line needs a license. Catering and selling food need a food business license. Selling only others' prepackaged food needs no license—file for record instead. Open only after the license or filing is done.
12-7.human: Opening without a license: at minimum cease operations, confiscate illegal gains, fine up to 10,000 yuan. For state-monopoly goods or securities, futures, insurance, or payment-settlement businesses without approval, serious cases can be illegal business operation—prison from up to 5 years. Renovate first, «soft open» before the license—the common misstep.
12-7.gain: Operating without authorization is handled by the department the law designates. No license where the law doesn't spell out a penalty: stop, confiscate gains, fine up to 10,000 yuan. Heavier track: monopoly or restricted goods without permission, or securities, futures, insurance, or payment settlement without approval—serious cases are illegal business operation, up to 5 years' imprisonment or short-term detention plus a fine of 1–5 times illegal gains; especially serious, above 5 years (nationwide).
12-7.note: Finance, medical, and training each have their own licensing laws; this item only checked generic enforcement and criminal articles. Milk tea and snack shops are catering—food business license required. Renovate-first, trial-before-license is a common trap. Food tiers and whether fresh meat and vegetables need a license: item 8.

12-8.t: For food, know your tier: production and catering need a license; prepackaged-only sales need filing; fresh meat and vegetables need no license
12-8.cost: The license itself is free. Premises and equipment must pass standards; site inspection plus processing take weeks. Meat sellers must keep quarantine certificates and meat quality inspection certificates for each batch.
12-8.human: Make and sell yourself—snack bar, braised goods, baking, homemade pickles—all need a license. Sell only others' prepackaged food: no license; file with the county-level or higher market supervision department. Fresh meat and vegetables need no license. Without a license, minimum fine 50,000–100,000 yuan—often above a small shop's stake.
12-8.gain: Food Safety Law: food businesses need a license first—produce, sell, or cater. «However, selling edible agricultural products and selling prepackaged food only do not require a license. Selling prepackaged food only shall be filed with the local county-level or above food safety supervision department.» Edible agricultural products are unprocessed meat, vegetables, etc. Prepackaged food is made and sold in packaging by others. «Specific rules for small food workshops and food vendors are set by provinces.» Operating without a license: confiscate illegal gains, food, tools, equipment, and raw materials. If value of goods (货值金额) is under 10,000 yuan, additionally fine 50,000–100,000 yuan; if 10,000 yuan or more, fine 10–20 times value. Pig Slaughter Regulations: pigs only at designated slaughter plants with official quarantine. «Except personal self-slaughter for consumption in rural areas, no unit or individual may slaughter pigs without designation.» «Pork sold or used in catering and centralized meals must come from designated plants with quarantine and meat quality inspection passed.» Private slaughter: shut down, confiscate pigs, tools, gains; fines same as unlicensed food operation. Animal Epidemic Prevention Law: sold or shipped animal products must carry quarantine certificates and marks; missing them: order correction, fine up to one times value of compliant goods. Judicial interpretation: food from small workshops or vendors below safety standards—buyers may claim tenfold punitive damages; courts should uphold (nationwide).
12-8.note: Thresholds for small workshops, small catering, and street vendors are provincial—no numbers here. On your provincial market supervision site search «small food workshop small catering vendor regulations». Online homemade food still needs licenses where required. Also see item 6 for entity and license, item 7 for other licensed trades, section 5 item 31 for tenfold food damages.

12-9.t: Bag it and sell it—that's prepackaged food: production date, shelf life, and ingredient list are all mandatory on the label
12-9.cost: Labels cost cents to dimes each. Every batch needs correct dates and ingredients—some time.
12-9.human: Food put in packaging before sale is prepackaged food; the package must have a label with nine required items including production date and shelf life. Bulk food still needs name, date, and seller name and address on the container. Missing required label items: if value under 10,000 yuan, fine 5,000–50,000 yuan; if 10,000 yuan or more, fine 5–10 times value.
12-9.gain: Food Safety Law: prepackaged food must have a label with name, spec, net content, production date, ingredients (配料表), producer name, address, contact, shelf life, product standard code, storage conditions, additive generic names under national standards, production license number, plus anything else law or standards require. Bulk food sold by weight needs on container or outer pack: food name, production date or batch, shelf life, operator name, address, contact. Prepackaged food without a label or with noncompliant label/instructions: confiscate gains and food. Value under 10,000 yuan: additionally fine 5,000–50,000 yuan; 10,000 yuan or more: 5–10 times value. Serious cases: stop production until license revoked. Minor label defects that don't affect safety or mislead consumers: correct first; if refused, fine up to 2,000 yuan. GB 7718-2025 Prepackaged Food Labeling General Rules published 16 March 2025, effective 16 March 2027, two-year transition—requires a dedicated area showing production date and expiry, high-contrast legible dates in year-month-day order (nationwide).
12-9.note: Two defect tiers drive fines and damages. Minor: typos, font issues—no safety impact, no misleading—correct only; if refused, fine up to 2,000 yuan; no tenfold from buyers. Missing mandatory items like production date or shelf life are not minor: fines as above; buyers may also claim tenfold on purchase price, minimum 1,000 yuan if tenfold is lower (section 5 item 31). GB 7718-2025 date and display requirements checked via announcement and official interpretation; exact format follows the standard text.

12-10.t: Ordinary food must not claim to treat disease—labels, instructions, ads, and live-stream scripts count
12-10.cost: No money. Review ad copy, product pages, and live-stream scripts. The hard part is not saying «lower the three highs» or «treat constipation».
12-10.human: Labels, instructions, and ads for ordinary food must not claim disease prevention or treatment. Except medical, drug, and device ads, no ad may claim treatment or use medical-sounding words. Penalty: 1–3 times ad spend; if spend unknown, 100,000–200,000 yuan. Serious cases can revoke the business license.
12-10.gain: Food Safety Law: «Labels and instructions for food and food additives must not contain false content and must not involve disease prevention or treatment functions. Producers and operators are responsible for label and instruction content.» «Food advertising shall be true and lawful, must not contain false content or involve disease prevention or treatment; food operators are responsible for ad truth and legality.» Packaging, instructions, and ads can't claim prevention or cure; sellers answer for what they write. False or misleading food ads are penalized under the Advertising Law: «Except medical, drug, and medical device advertising, no other advertising may involve disease treatment functions, and must not use medical terms or terms easily confused with drugs or devices.» Violations: stop the ad; advertiser must clarify and remove impact in the scope published; fine 1–3 times ad fees; if fees unknown or clearly low, 100,000–200,000 yuan; serious: 3–5 times fees or 200,000–1,000,000 yuan, and may revoke the license (nationwide).
12-10.note: «Health functions» aren't for ordinary food either—only registered health foods may claim functions from the national catalog. Buyer-side spotting of such language: section 6 item 10. Product pages, live scripts, and social posts are ads too; once posted they leave a trail.

12-11.t: Food has criminal lines: diseased or substandard meat can be a crime; toxic adulteration starts at five years regardless of sales
12-11.cost: No money. Follow item 8: keep quarantine and purchase proofs; ingredients only with traceable approval numbers on the label.
12-11.human: Earlier items fine money; this one can put you in prison. Selling diseased meat, failed-inspection meat, or goods with pesticide, veterinary drug, or heavy-metal levels «sufficient» to cause serious poisoning is enough without a victim—up to 3 years. Adding toxic or harmful non-food substances: from 5 years up, regardless of revenue.
12-11.gain: Criminal Law Article 143: food you produce or sell that doesn't meet safety standards and is «sufficient to cause serious food poisoning or other serious foodborne illness» is an offense—up to 3 years' imprisonment or short-term detention plus fine; serious health harm or other serious circumstances, 3–7 years plus fine; especially serious consequences, 7 years to life plus fine or full property confiscation. Article 144: adding toxic or harmful non-food substances to food, or selling knowing adulteration—up to 5 years plus fine; serious health harm or other serious circumstances, 5–10 years plus fine; death or especially serious circumstances, Article 141 penalties (10 years, life, or death). SPC and SPP interpretation lists «sufficient» cases including pathogen or pesticide/veterinary drug/toxin/heavy-metal levels far above limits; meat from diseased, cause-unknown, or failed-inspection animals; goods banned for disease control; special medical or infant formula with severely substandard nutrition; additive misuse at levels causing the above. «Toxic or harmful non-food substances» are legally defined—not your call. Article 144 «other serious circumstances» includes sales 100,000–200,000 yuan, sites near schools, nurseries, elder care, selling to minors or elders, unlicensed slaughter—may also be illegal business operation; «serious» from 100,000 yuan sales or 50,000 yuan illegal gains (nationwide).
12-11.note: Line vs items 8–10: this is food safety itself, not paperwork. No license, label gaps, or cure claims → fines; diseased meat, excess residues, bad additives, non-food adulteration → criminal. Cheapest defense is item 8: meat only from designated plants, batch quarantine and quality certificates, approved ingredients only. «Discount meat» and «unknown trim» are where cases cluster. Original SPC Gazette page returned 502 this round; two provincial official reprints were cross-checked word for word.

12-12.t: Once you have a license you must file returns; zero income still means on-time filing (a return that's all zeros)
12-12.cost: No money. File yourself on the e-Tax portal monthly or quarterly—minutes each time. Paid bookkeeping is separate market spend. If you hire staff, register for social insurance within 30 days of formation. The hard part is filing on months with no business.
12-12.human: After the license, file taxes on schedule. Earn nothing—you still file, with zeros throughout. Late filing: fine up to 2,000 yuan; serious, 2,000–10,000 yuan. Skip all tax types for three straight months and the system marks you abnormal—you can't issue invoices.
12-12.gain: «Taxpayers with no tax payable in the period shall still file returns as required»—zero tax due, form still due. Late filing: «ordered to correct within a time limit; may fine up to 2,000 yuan; serious, 2,000–10,000 yuan». Fail to file and underpay: back tax, daily late fee, plus fine 50%–5 times the underpaid amount. Late fee at five ten-thousandths (万分之五) per day. «Three consecutive months with no filing for any tax type: the tax collection system automatically marks abnormal status and stops invoice book and invoice use». After filing and accepting penalty, status clears automatically. Employers «within 30 days from establishment … apply to the local social insurance agency for social insurance registration» (nationwide).
12-12.note: After «multi-certificate integration» you don't separately register for tax—log into e-Tax with the unified social credit code on the license, confirm registration, declare applicable taxes. Sole props and individual-owned enterprises pay individual income tax on business income—prepay within 15 days after month or quarter end, annual reconciliation by 31 March of the next year. LLCs pay corporate income tax—prepay monthly or quarterly, annual reconciliation within five months after year-end (by 31 May). No revenue still requires filing; zero filing is still filing. Three months idle → abnormal, invoices stopped, simplified deregistration blocked—see item 23.

12-13.t: Issue invoices only for real transactions; small-scale taxpayers should use the full VAT exemption allowance
12-13.cost: No cost at all. Do not buy or sell invoices, or issue invoices for others to «走账开票» (sham bookkeeping). Invoice and file taxes based on business that actually happened.
12-13.human: If you are a small-scale taxpayer on the simplified VAT regime, and monthly sales stay under 100,000 yuan or quarterly sales under 300,000 yuan, you owe no VAT. Where the rate would have been 3%, it is reduced to 1% for the same period (real-estate sales, rentals, and land-use-right transfers excepted). The other way around, paying someone to «找人开票抵成本» (issue invoices to inflate costs) is fictitious invoicing: at minimum, up to three years’ imprisonment plus a fine of 20,000 to 200,000 yuan.
12-13.gain: Small-scale taxpayers on the simplified regime are covered by the rule that (销售额未达到起征点的，免征增值税) (sales below the threshold are exempt from VAT). That threshold runs from 1 January 2026 through 31 December 2027: 100,000 yuan per month, 300,000 yuan per quarter, or 1,000 yuan per transaction or day; below it, no VAT is due. In the same window, the 3% rate is cut to 1%, again except for real-estate sales, rentals, and land-use-right transfers. On the criminal side, issuing VAT special invoices—or other invoices usable for tax offset—without a real transaction draws up to three years’ imprisonment or criminal detention plus a fine of 20,000 to 200,000 yuan, whether you issue for others, for yourself, arrange for others to issue for you, or broker such deals. Larger tax amounts bring three to ten years; extremely large amounts, ten years or more or life imprisonment (nationwide).
12-13.note: The VAT Law took effect on 1 January 2026. The two earlier small-taxpayer relief notices (2023 No. 19 and 2023 No. 1) were repealed or stopped applying; the amounts did not change, but the legal basis did—this item follows the new texts. The Criminal Law page cited is the 1997 version; Article 205 was later adjusted by amendments—only the tiers verified here and left unchanged by those amendments are listed. What is exempt is VAT; income tax is separate. «找人开票抵成本» is fictitious invoicing, not tax planning.

12-14.t: Anyone claiming to be the tax bureau and pressing you to pay or file is a scam; handle tax matters only through the e-Tax portal or 12366
12-14.cost: No cost. For calls, texts, or friend requests about a «tax audit», «account anomaly», or «fine if you do not file», hang up and do not reply. Then call 12366 or your local tax authority’s listed landline to verify.
12-14.human: Tax authorities do not ask for bank card passwords, payment passwords, or SMS codes by phone, nor give you an account to wire tax to. Real on-site audits require an inspection notice and inspector credentials. Hang up first, then verify on 12366. If you already transferred money, call 110 or 96110 immediately to try to stop payment.
12-14.gain: The State Taxation Administration states that (税务部门不会通过微信小程序、电话、短信等方式索要银行卡密码、支付密码、账户余额及与银行卡收付款项相关的短信验证码) (tax authorities will not ask via WeChat mini-programs, phone, or SMS for bank passwords, payment passwords, balances, or SMS codes tied to card payments). It also warns that «一些不法分子冒充税务干部» (some criminals impersonate tax staff), offering «帮办纳税申报», «税收优惠代办», or «政策辅导» (filing help, preferential-tax agency, or policy coaching). To verify, use (12366 纳税缴费服务热线或主管税务机关固定电话) (the 12366 hotline or the authority’s landline). For real audits, «必须出示检查通知书和检查证» (inspectors must show a written notice and credentials). (税款只能通过电子税务局或者在办税大厅缴纳，税务部门不会提供指定账号) (tax is paid only via the e-Tax system or service hall—no designated account). Tax-service agencies have their own rules. (以税务机关和税务人员的名义敲诈纳税人、扣缴义务人的) (extorting taxpayers or withholding agents in the name of the tax bureau) is fined by severity. Impersonating state organs to defraud: 10–15 days’ detention and up to 1,000 yuan fine. If both fraud and impersonation apply, «依照处罚较重的规定定罪处罚» (the heavier charge controls) (nationwide).
12-14.note: These scams target newly registered sole proprietors and small companies: «you have not filed; pay today or be fined», then a private official account or mini-program charging hundreds of yuan for filing that is free and takes minutes on your own. Hiring a bookkeeping firm is legal, but it is not the government and cannot demand payment in the tax bureau’s name. If you paid or transferred, follow Section 8, item 2 (stop payment after fraud)—call 110 or 96110 at once. Impersonating market regulators over missed annual reports and paid «agency» is the same playbook; see Section 12, item 25 (annual reports are free).

12-15.t: Write «定金» not «订金» in contracts, state penalty amounts in figures, and treat payment terms like lending
12-15.cost: No cost. Use the two characters «定金» in the contract; the amount must not exceed 20% of the contract total. Collect payment before delivery. Before agreeing to deliver first and pay later (credit terms), check the counterparty first.
12-15.human: Only «定金» triggers the double rule: if you breach, you forfeit it; if they breach, they return double. Amounts above 20% of the contract total do not count as deposit. «订金» has no such rule in law. Credit terms are interest-free use of your money; if they fail, it is a bad debt.
12-15.gain: A deposit is formed «自实际交付时成立» (when money is actually delivered). If the paying party breaches, the deposit is forfeited. If the receiving party breaches, they return the original sum plus an equal amount (double return). The portion above 20% of the main contract amount is not treated as deposit. If agreed liquidated damages are far above or below actual loss, a court may adjust up or down on request. If both liquidated damages and a deposit clause appear, the injured party may claim only one, not both (nationwide, from 2021).
12-15.note: «订金» under the Civil Code lacks the deposit rules and is usually treated as advance payment—common practice; this section did not verify a specific ruling. Credit terms are lending your funds at zero interest; default means a bad debt. Before granting terms, search the counterparty on the National Enterprise Credit Information Publicity System for litigation history.

12-16.t: Sign a written labor contract within the first month; register for social insurance within 30 days
12-16.cost: The employer share of social insurance must be paid continuously; rates vary by locality. The contract itself costs nothing—use the local HR department’s template.
12-16.human: If someone works a full month without a written contract, from the second month you owe double wages each month until the end of the first year. Social insurance must be registered within 30 days of hire; failure draws a fine of one to three times the premiums due. There is no «员工自愿放弃社保» (employee voluntarily waives social insurance) in law.
12-16.gain: If employment reaches one month but stays under one year with no written contract, double wages are owed every month. From day one, social insurance registration is due within 30 days. Failure brings an order to correct; after the deadline, a fine of one to three times the premiums due, plus 500–3,000 yuan on the person handling registration. Late or insufficient payment adds «滞纳金» (late fees) at 0.05% per day from the due date; still unpaid after the deadline, another one-to-three-times fine on the arrears. The employer must declare and pay in full on time; only statutory force majeure such as natural disaster allows delay or reduction. No voluntary waiver (nationwide).
12-16.note: Double wages run from month two through month twelve—delay gets expensive. An employee without contract or coverage who is injured at work or later arbitrates often costs far more in back premiums, fines, and compensation than any savings.

12-17.t: Pay wages per contract and law; put raises, loans, and bonuses in writing
12-17.cost: No cost. State wages clearly in the contract. Raises, bonuses, advances, and loans all need a signed paper—no oral promises. Do not pay staff from your personal pocket on the company’s behalf. The hard part is sticking to this when acquaintances ask.
12-17.human: Wages must be paid on time and in full per contract and law. If wages are owed, the employee can ask a court for a payment order. Oral promises on raises, bonuses, or advances lose in a dispute if you cannot prove them. Money you lend an employee needs a written IOU with amount, interest, and repayment date.
12-17.gain: A labor contract must specify how wages are paid and how social insurance is handled. The employer must pay wages timely and in full per contract and state rules. Unpaid wages allow a direct application for a court payment order. An owner lending personal money to an employee is a loan contract; except where two natural persons agree otherwise, it must be written, stating amount, interest, when and how to repay. Oral bonus promises without paper leave the party without evidence at a disadvantage (nationwide).
12-17.note: This is not about refusing to help—it is about helping through rules. Favors outside the system that become habit are hard to stop without conflict. Mixing personal loans with company books leaves bad debt on you if the company fails. Statutory parts were verified; the advice is experience, hence grade C.

12-18.t: Sell first, then produce: use pre-sales and small orders to prove demand before you invest in production
12-18.cost: Tens to hundreds of yuan for a sample or a landing page, then reach dozens of real customers for prepayment or small orders. That is slower by weeks than making stock first. The hard part is not producing before anyone pays.
12-18.human: One study followed 116 new Italian firms for about a year: founders who set a hypothesis and tested it against market feedback ran better businesses, pivoted sooner when needed, and did not quit earlier. If nobody prepays or places a small order, do not trust «做出来自然有人买» (make it and buyers will appear).
12-18.gain: A randomized controlled trial tracked 116 Italian startups for about one year (participants split at random; one group got training, outcomes compared). Founders trained to decide by (先提假设、再用市场反馈严格检验) (hypothesis first, then strict market feedback tests) performed better, were more likely to pivot in time, and did not drop out more often. The authors argue this cuts spending on false-positive projects that look viable but are not (Italy, published 2020).
12-18.note: Only this one study, small sample, Italy only—grade B. Title, venue, and abstract were checked via Crossref and Semantic Scholar; effect sizes in the full paper were not verified here. Operationally: no prepay and no small order means do not believe «做出来就有人买».

12-19.t: Run the sample through a mass-production checklist before you commit to a production run
12-19.cost: A few hundred yuan for a small trial batch, plus hours to nail down yield (how many of 100 units are salable), supplier minimum order and payment terms, cash tied up in inventory, packaging and logistics, certifications and licenses, and trademark. The hard part is not skipping straight to full production.
12-19.human: One prototype versus a thousand units differs in where money sits. Yield sets true unit cost. Minimum order and payment terms set how much you advance. Inventory sets when cash returns. Products on the mandatory certification list cannot leave the factory or be sold without certification and the mark on the product.
12-19.gain: The prototype-versus-volume gap is where capital is locked. Yield is the share of a batch that is qualified for sale. Supplier minimum order and payment terms set upfront cash need. Inventory sets recovery timing. Listed mandatory certification products must pass certification and bear the mark before production and sale. Selling without certification is penalized under the certification rules. Restaurants and food sellers need a food business license (nationwide).
12-19.note: The checklist is practical method; statutory parts were checked at source. Before production, search the CNIPA trademark system for similar marks, then file yours. Trademark and artwork red lines are Section 12, items 20 and 21 (keep purchase records; use your own art or licensed art). The mandatory certification catalogue follows the latest SAMR list.

12-20.t: Keep invoices and supplier records for every purchase batch; skip goods priced far below market—if staff buy counterfeits, the owner can still be convicted
12-20.cost: No cost. For each batch keep purchase contract, invoice, payment record, supplier business license, and authorization. Rule internally: whoever buys signs; never accept prices clearly below market. The hard part is passing up cheap stock that looks profitable.
12-20.human: Selling counterfeits: illegal gains of 30,000 yuan or sales of 50,000 yuan meets the criminal threshold—up to three years. Unsold warehouse stock counts. «我不知道是假的» (I did not know) is not yours to decide alone: buying far below market without a good explanation supports knowledge. Keeping contract, invoice, payment trail, and supplier identity is the path to the no-damages defense.
12-20.gain: Knowingly selling goods bearing counterfeit registered trademarks: illegal gains ≥30,000 yuan or sales ≥50,000 yuan triggers up to three years plus fines (or fines alone). At ten times those levels, three to ten years plus fines. Unsold stock counts if value reaches three times the sales threshold. «明知» (knowing) need not be admitted—2025 SPC and SPP interpretation lists five situations where knowledge is presumed unless you prove otherwise: (1) altered, swapped, or covered marks; (2) forged or altered authorization documents, or knowing they were forged; (3) prior criminal or administrative penalty for the same goods, then selling again; (4) no reasonable grounds, buying or selling far below market; (5) after enforcement or judicial notice, moving or destroying goods or books, or false certificates. If a company commits the offense, (对单位判处罚金，并对其直接负责的主管人员和其他直接责任人员) (fine the entity and punish responsible managers and staff on the same article)—the person who approved still faces charges even if staff sourced the goods. Trademark law offers an out: selling without knowing infringement, (能证明该商品是自己合法取得并说明提供者的，不承担赔偿责任) (lawful acquisition with provider identified)—no compensation; without invoices and supplier info the defense fails (nationwide; interpretation effective 26 April 2025).
12-20.note: Cosmetics, liquor, baby goods, electronics, and apparel see many cases—large price spreads on the same SKU. «渠道货», «尾单», «海外免税» do not replace paperwork. Beyond criminal liability, administrative fines: infringing goods and tools confiscated; illegal turnover above 50,000 yuan can draw a fine up to five times turnover. If stock is bad, stop selling, seal it, contact brand or market regulators—do not keep selling or destroy goods and books; destruction fits presumption (5). Artwork rules: Section 12, item 21. One scam: free pens or small goods «consignment», later a buyer and evidence, then infringement claims—free goods lack contract, payment, and real provider; all three conditions for lawful acquisition fail. Do not list door-to-door free stock with only a WeChat contact. Real consignment needs a written agreement, ID and business license copies, and who owns goods and bears infringement risk.

12-21.t: Art on products, packaging, tags, and ads must be yours or licensed—recoloring or adding icons is not «different enough»
12-21.cost: Licensed stock art from tens of yuan per image; original design, hundreds to thousands. Keep license proof and purchase record for every image used on goods. The hard part is not grabbing random web images.
12-21.human: Changing colors, background, or slapping on your logo on someone else’s work is still unlicensed use. Reproducing others’ art for profit—illegal gains ≥30,000 yuan, turnover ≥50,000 yuan, or ≥500 copies—can be copyright infringement, up to three years. On trademarks, «容易导致混淆的» (likely to cause confusion) is infringement by itself.
12-21.gain: Copyright law treats (未经著作权人许可，以改编、翻译、注释等方式使用作品) (adaptation, translation, annotation without permission) like copying—recolor, new background, or added icons still count. Criminal thresholds for reproducing and selling art without permission: illegal gains ≥30,000 yuan, illegal business amount ≥50,000 yuan, or ≥500 copies (sheets)—copyright infringement, up to three years plus fines (or fines alone); ten times those levels, three to ten years. Selling others’ infringing copies: illegal gains ≥50,000 yuan or sales ≥100,000 yuan—crime of selling infringing copies, up to five years. Trademarks: same goods with a similar mark, or similar goods with same or similar marks, «容易导致混淆的» is listed infringement; «近似» is explicit—small edits still infringe (nationwide; interpretation effective 26 April 2025).
12-21.note: Three common slips: (1) web cartoon or celebrity images on apparel, mugs, cases; (2) fonts—commercial fonts usually need separate license, preview ≠ commercial use; (3) client designs with unlicensed assets—the seller still liable. Easiest path: commercial stock with saved license pages, or a design contract stating asset source, scope, and designer liability. Beyond criminal exposure, civil damages and admin fines—public interest harm can mean confiscation and fines of one to five times illegal turnover. Pre-production trademark check: Section 12, item 19. If others use your art, same rules apply. Posting others’ comics or shows online for ads or membership fees: Section 9, item 24.

12-22.t: Work within posted procedures; before off-book favors, decide who bears liability
12-22.cost: No cost. Follow rules, medical orders, and process at work. Do not decide outside your authority for others. Before helping, ask who is responsible if something goes wrong. The hard part is refusing on-the-spot «通融一下» (just bend the rules).
12-22.human: Nurses, for example: regulations require immediate physician notice when a patient is critically ill, and raising non-compliant orders with the prescriber. Other jobs: know where procedures draw the «must report» line. The law does not require standing by: voluntary emergency aid that injures the person helped does not create compensation liability.
12-22.gain: Nurse regulations set duty boundaries: critical illness → notify physician at once; emergencies allow necessary rescue before physician arrival; illegal or non-standard orders → raise with prescriber, report to department head if needed. Civil Code: voluntary emergency assistance that harms the rescued party—«不承担民事责任» (no civil liability) (nationwide).
12-22.note: Inside your role, follow procedure; emergency rescue is legally protected. Otherwise separate authority from responsibility—do not replace institutional decisions with personal favors. Nurse Regulations 2020 revision (State Council Order 726) changed registration only; Article 17 unchanged. Physician Law clauses on clinical standards were not opened from official text this round, so not quoted.

12-23.t: When you are losing, exit by the book: simplified deregistration if you qualify, bankruptcy if insolvent—do not walk away
12-23.cost: Simplified deregistration you can do yourself: post on the National Enterprise Credit Information Publicity System for 20 days. If debts remain, liquidate—collect receivables, pay creditors. Bankruptcy needs a court filing and months. The hard part is facing losses instead of stalling.
12-23.human: No debts, no unpaid wages, tax, or social insurance: all investors sign a commitment, 20-day public notice with no objection → simplified deregistration. Sole proprietors skip the notice; no objection within 10 days → deregister. Cannot pay debts → apply for bankruptcy. Ignore filings for two years and become unreachable at the registered address → license revoked; responsible legal representative barred from that role for three years.
12-23.gain: No debts owed or owed to you, or all settled; no unpaid wages, social insurance, or tax; all investors’ written commitment—then 20-day notice with no objection allows simplified deregistration. Sole proprietors: no notice; no objection within 10 days → direct deregistration. Company cannot pay due debts and liabilities exceed assets («资不抵债»)—may apply to court for reorganization, composition, or bankruptcy liquidation. Dissolved but not liquidated with insolvency—the liquidator must apply for bankruptcy liquidation. Neglect: late annual report → abnormal operation listing. Two consecutive years no report, still on the list unchanged, unreachable at registered address → business license revoked. Person responsible as legal representative of a revoked entity: barred from legal representative and director, supervisor, or senior manager roles for three years from revocation.
