The China Earthquake Administration itself stipulates that “taking shelter” is only advisable “in buildings that meet seismic safety standards,” and also emphasizes that decisions must be “tailored to local conditions and individual circumstances” — meaning you must consider both the building’s structural integrity and your own physical ability to move. In Armenia, entire buildings collapsed, leaving no safe spot to hide, so evacuation was the only viable option. The U.S. Federal Emergency Management Agency advises residents to “drop to the ground, protect the head and neck, hold on tight, and avoid running outside” — where injuries are primarily caused by falling debris and falls during tremors. Research from the Northridge earthquake further shows that reaching for objects or gripping seemingly stable items can actually increase injury risk. Ultimately, the key question isn’t “should I run or stay?” but rather “is this building likely to collapse, and can I reach open ground within seconds?” For buildings constructed after 2001 that require navigating stairs or hallways to exit, staying put is the safest choice. For single-story homes, older brick buildings, and makeshift houses without seismic protection, the exit is just a few steps away — so leave immediately. It’s worth noting that the Armenian study only compared injured and uninjured survivors, excluded fatalities, and didn’t account for differences in building height; since those able to escape were more likely to live on lower floors, these figures should be interpreted with some caution. Under no circumstances should you jump from heights, use elevators, or attempt to run down stairs during tremors. Once outside, stay far away from tall structures, overpasses, utility poles, glass facades, and billboards.

13-31.t: When encountering bears, wild boars, or packs of wild dogs, don’t run — instead, turn sideways and back away slowly
13-31.cost: No cost involved. When heading into the mountains, bring a hiking pole, hike in a group, and make noise so animals know you’re coming. The hardest part is staying put instead of running.
13-31.human: Never run — bears can sprint uphill or downhill just as fast as racehorses. Also, don’t climb trees; both black bears and brown bears are excellent climbers. Stand your ground and keep speaking to the bear in a low, calm voice. Once it stops moving, turn sideways and back away slowly. If a brown bear attacks, lie down and play dead: place your hands behind your neck and spread your legs apart. For black bear attacks, do not play dead — run toward a vehicle or building; if escape is impossible, fight back using whatever is at hand. In case of dog bites, follow the steps outlined in item 13.
13-31.gain: The original guidelines issued by the U.S. National Park Service on bear encounters contain six key points: “Do not run — bears can sprint uphill or downhill just as fast as racehorses.” “Stay calm; most bears have no interest in attacking and simply want to be left alone.” “Keep speaking to the bear in a low, steady voice.” “When the bear stops moving, turn sideways and back away slowly so you can keep watching it without tripping.” “Make yourself appear as large as possible.” “Do not climb trees — both grizzly bears and black bears are capable climbers.” In the event of a brown bear attack, “lie down and play dead, placing hands behind the neck and legs apart.” For black bear attacks, “do not play dead; run toward a vehicle or building, and if escape is impossible, fight back using any available object.” Dog bites should be treated according to item 13.
13-31.note: The Grade B rating applies solely to bear encounters. The advice regarding wild boars and packs of wild dogs — namely, “don’t run, back away slowly, and seek higher ground or obstacles for protection” — is based on anecdotal experience and is rated Grade C; no official recommendations from China’s forestry authorities or local agencies were identified for these scenarios. Never try to lure animals with food, approach them for photos, or bring dogs into mountainous areas inhabited by wild boars. In China, the primary bear species are black bears and brown bears; the decision to play dead or not depends on which species is involved.

13-32.t: If caught in a thunderstorm outdoors, get into a hard-topped vehicle or building; avoid ridges, lone trees, water surfaces, and metal objects
13-32.cost: No monetary cost. The downside is that your trip gets interrupted for at least half an hour. The real challenge is actually turning back when the thunder is still far away.
13-32.human: There is no safe spot outdoors during a thunderstorm. You must get into a hard-topped vehicle or building; convertibles and motorcycles do not qualify. Tents, gazebos, areas under trees, or rocky outcrops also do not count as shelter. Stay away from open areas, mountain ridges and peaks, isolated tall trees, water surfaces, and metal railings or poles. If a group cannot all fit together, spread out rather than huddling close. Begin retreating the moment you hear thunder; it is only safe to leave 30 minutes after the final clap of thunder.
13-32.gain: There is no safe spot outdoors during a thunderstorm. It is only safe to leave 30 minutes after the final clap of thunder.
13-32.note: Tents, gazebos, areas under trees, and rocky outcrops do not qualify as shelters. Hard-topped cars do count, but convertibles and motorcycles do not. Start retreating the instant you hear thunder; do not wait until rain begins to fall.

13-33.t: Gradually increase your sleeping altitude when heading to high elevations; if symptoms worsen, descend immediately — don’t tough it out
13-33.cost: It requires an extra day or two for acclimatization. Preventive medications are prescription-only, so you must consult a doctor before traveling. The main challenge is fitting these days into an otherwise tight itinerary.
13-33.human: This guideline focuses on sleeping altitude, not daytime elevation. Sleeping above 2,450 meters already poses a risk of altitude sickness. Once above 3,000 meters, you should only raise your nighttime altitude by 500 meters per night, allowing an additional day of acclimatization for every 1,000-meter increase. Symptoms such as headache, nausea, unsteady gait, altered mental state, or shortness of breath even at rest indicate the need to descend. Descending takes priority over oxygen therapy or medication.
13-33.gain: Sleeping above 2,450 meters increases the risk of altitude sickness. Without prompt descent, high-altitude cerebral edema and pulmonary edema — fluid buildup in the brain and lungs — can be fatal.
13-33.note: The rule specifically refers to sleeping altitude, not daytime elevation. Headache, nausea, unsteadiness, confusion, or breathlessness at rest are clear signs to descend. Descending should always come before oxygen use or medication; continuing upward while on oxygen is unsafe.

13-34.t: To remove a tick, use fine-point tweezers to pull it straight out along the skin — don’t apply oil, don’t use heat
13-34.human: Use fine-point tweezers to grasp the tick’s head right against the skin, then pull steadily outward. Never apply oil, use heat, or yank sideways — doing so can force infectious fluids into the skin and often leaves the tick’s mouthparts embedded. After removal, write down the date. If you develop fever, rash, or fatigue in the following weeks, be sure to mention the tick bite to your doctor.
13-34.gain: Applying oil, using heat, or pulling sideways can provoke the tick to release infectious fluids into the skin. Those actions also raise the risk of leaving its mouthparts stuck inside. In China, tick-borne severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome led to 6,602 reported cases and 306 deaths in 2024 — the highest totals on record. From 2010 through 2024, the average fatality rate stood at 4.79%, rising with age; for those over 85 it reached 9.15%.
13-34.note: Be sure to note the date of removal. Should fever, rash, or fatigue appear in the weeks that follow, inform your doctor about the tick bite — otherwise it may be misdiagnosed as a common cold.

13-35.t: Always boil any water taken from the wild before drinking it; one minute of boiling is sufficient — there’s no need to extend the time just because you’re at high altitude
13-35.cost: You’ll need to carry extra weight in the form of a stove and fuel.
13-35.human: Any microbes capable of causing illness through water are killed within seconds at boiling temperature. Boiling for an additional minute simply provides a safety margin for any possible oversight; it isn’t necessary to prolong the process at higher elevations. If boiling isn’t feasible, use a filter or chemical purification tablets instead — each method has its own limitations regarding which pathogens they can eliminate. Even crystal-clear streams and meltwater can harbor parasites.
13-35.gain: All microbes that can cause disease via water are inactivated within seconds at boiling temperature. The belief that water fails to reach a safe temperature at high altitudes is a common misconception.
13-35.note: The same page also notes that boiling isn’t strictly mandatory: maintaining water at 60°C for 30 minutes achieves the same effect, and boiling simply offers a visible endpoint without needing a thermometer. Filters and chemical tablets each have their own gaps in pathogen coverage, so boiling remains preferable when possible. Just because water appears clear doesn’t mean it’s free of parasites — appearance alone is no reliable indicator.

13-36.t: If a stranger demands money in a remote area, hand over cash, avoid any confrontation, note their features, and call police after escaping
13-36.cost: The cash you have on you. The real challenge is keeping your temper in check.
13-36.human: Give him the money, do not fight back, and do not argue. By demanding a few hundred yuan, he is committing robbery — a crime punishable by at least three years up to ten years in prison. If he enters a residence, uses a weapon, or causes serious injury or death, the sentence rises to ten years or more, even life imprisonment or death. If you chase after him and strike him after he has taken the money, that is no longer considered self‑defence. Immediately after escaping, write down his appearance, accent, vehicle license plate, and the direction he fled, then call 110.
13-36.gain: Your life is far more valuable than a few hundred yuan. The offender is committing a serious crime for such a small amount. Article 263 of the Criminal Law states that anyone who robs public or private property by violence, coercion, or other means faces three to ten years in prison plus a fine; aggravating circumstances raise the penalty to ten years or more, even death. Article 20 limits self‑defence to stopping an ongoing unlawful attack; once the robber has taken the money and walked away, any retaliation is no longer justified. After escaping, record his description, speech patterns, vehicle details, and escape route, then call 110.
13-36.note: The “C” rating reflects the lack of direct literature supporting the principle that “handing over money avoids danger”; the legal text merely outlines the offender’s risks and your boundaries. Never follow an attacker to a secluded spot to “get money,” never reveal your phone password, and never get into his vehicle. This advice is not an invitation to fight or to refrain from calling police; it applies only when you are physically threatened in a remote setting and must first pay to ensure your safety. In contrast, if someone online threatens to release private photos or videos, you must never pay — see Section 8, Item 32 for those cases.

13-37.t: If you stumble upon a group fight, walk away immediately — don’t try to break it up, don’t stand around watching, and don’t pick up any weapons on the ground. If you want to call the police, retreat to a safe distance and dial 110
13-37.cost: No money is required. The hard part is resisting the urge to step in and the temptation to watch from the sidelines. After calling, you might be asked to give a statement later; at most, this takes half a day.
13-37.human: If you intervene, your actions shift from “trying to calm things down” to “taking part in a fight.” Participating in a group brawl can land you in prison for up to three years; if many people are involved, it happens on a road, or weapons are used, the sentence rises to three to ten years. Watching isn’t worth it either — the more onlookers there are, the messier the scene gets, and you’re more likely to get hurt. The right move is to walk away. If you do want to call the police, step back to a safe spot and dial 110, clearly stating the location, how many people are involved, whether anyone is carrying knives or sticks, and if anyone has collapsed.
13-37.gain: Article 292 of the Criminal Law states: “Those who lead or actively take part in group brawls shall be sentenced to up to three years in prison, criminal detention, or surveillance.” If the brawls happen repeatedly, involve many people, have a big social impact, occur in public spaces or on busy roads, or involve weapons, the punishment rises to three to ten years. If such fights cause serious injury or death, perpetrators are charged under laws on intentional injury or homicide. The Public Security Administration Punishment Law also sets penalties: assaulting others brings a detention of five to ten days plus fines of 500 to 1,000 yuan. Group fights handled as hooliganism can lead to up to fifteen days in jail and fines up to 2,000 yuan. Guideline 5 of the “Opinions on Properly Applying Self‑Defence” says unlawful attacks include those aimed at you, at the public, or at others. Guideline 9 adds that if one side starts the fight with excessive force, or continues attacking even after the other side tries to avoid conflict, the responding party is usually considered acting in self‑defence.
13-37.note: This grade is B because part of the consequences are backed by clear legal text, but the advice “walk away and call the police instead of intervening” isn’t directly stated in any official rule — it’s inferred from those statutes and from how group fights are judged. Saying “I was just trying to mediate” isn’t a shield; what matters is whether you actually took part and whom you hit. If an attacker is already down or has fled, chasing them to hit them no longer counts as self‑defence. Legally, you may intervene if you see someone being unilaterally beaten; self‑defence protects not only you but also others. Yet stepping in bare‑handed usually just adds another casualty. Calling for help, recording from afar, and calling police are far more effective. The safest choice here is “don’t intervene, don’t watch.” The benefit of calling 110 mainly helps the victim on the ground; overall, this entry offers one of the lowest net benefits in the book, so you must weigh whether the time investment is worth it. You should know a few key facts first. There is already a legal duty to testify: Article 62 of the Criminal Procedure Law says anyone aware of a case must testify; not calling police doesn’t erase that duty. In cases involving serious injury or death, police can still identify witnesses from surveillance footage, so standing around watching actually makes you more likely to be recorded. Authorities “must keep the identity of anonymous callers confidential” (Article 111). Simply stating the location, number of people, and whether weapons are present is enough — you needn’t stay on the scene. Only if a court summons you to testify without a valid reason and you refuse can you face up to ten days in detention (Article 193); ordinary bystanders rarely reach that point. Not calling police isn’t illegal: Article 110 of the Criminal Procedure Law mentions a “right and duty” without any penalty, and no criminal law punishes ordinary citizens for not reporting what they see, so walking away is perfectly legal. Two actions after walking away would cross the line: helping hide someone or giving false testimony to protect them (Article 310 of the Criminal Law, up to three years; serious cases bring three to ten years); and deliberately giving false testimony when called as a witness (Article 305, up to three years; serious cases up to seven years). Staying silent or telling the truth is fine; fabricating stories is not. If you yourself get caught in a fight, see Section 8, Item 10; if a stranger demands money, see Item 36 of this section; for costs after helping an injured person, see Item 39.

13-38.t: If you may have been exposed to HIV, get PEP within 72 hours — the sooner, the better
13-38.cost: A full 28‑day course of PEP can cost thousands of yuan; in most regions it must be paid out‑of‑pocket. You’ll need to rush to a hospital that same night. The hardest part is admitting you might be infected and leaving right away.
13-38.human: If you suspect you’ve been exposed to HIV, 72 hours is the hard deadline — ideally you should start PEP within 2 hours. The medication must be taken for 28 consecutive days. After 72 hours this option is no longer available, so don’t wait until the next day to decide.
13-38.gain: The Beijing Municipal Government’s HIV‑prevention outreach defines this as “post‑exposure prophylaxis,” abbreviated PEP. It recommends starting preventive medication “as soon as possible, ideally within 2 hours and no later than 24 hours, but not after 72 hours,” and continuing for 28 days. Beyond 72 hours PEP is not advised. This strict timeline means that acting immediately versus waiting a night can produce completely different outcomes.
13-38.note: Where to obtain PEP: any designated HIV‑treatment clinic affiliated with the local Chinese CDC, usually under the Infectious Diseases or STD/HIV department. Many cities now offer 24‑hour clinics; in Chongqing, for example, 29 such clinics operate across 26 districts, 14 of which are open around the clock. Call the local CDC beforehand to find a clinic with PEP on hand — don’t waste time in the emergency room. Situations considered “exposures” include unprotected sex, a broken condom, needle sticks, or blood contact with mucous membranes; only a doctor can decide whether PEP is appropriate. The full 28‑day regimen must be completed; missing doses markedly reduces its effectiveness. Follow‑up testing is required at 4–6 weeks and at 3 months as directed by your physician. This is a remedial measure, not a substitute for regular prevention; for everyday safeguards and testing, see items 30 and 31 in Chapter 1 (consistent condom use and testing after high‑risk encounters).

13-39.t: After saving someone and getting injured or incurring expenses, first seek compensation from the perpetrator and yibao; then apply for recognition as a person acting in the public interest
13-39.cost: There is no direct expense. However, submitting the application requires paperwork, waiting for approval, and multiple visits — this can take weeks or even months.
13-39.human: If you get hurt while saving someone, you’re not simply out of luck. Those injured while acting in the public interest should receive treatment first, with costs covered afterward. Medical bills are the responsibility of the perpetrator; if the perpetrator flees or cannot pay, basic medical insurance steps in. Even without a perpetrator, the person you saved is legally obligated to provide reasonable compensation — this is a legal requirement, not a matter of personal generosity. At the same time, you should apply for official recognition as a person acting in the public interest so that any injuries can be treated under workers’ compensation rules.
13-39.gain: Article 183 of the Civil Code states: “Anyone who suffers harm while protecting another person’s civil rights is entitled to compensation from the perpetrator; if no perpetrator exists, has fled, or cannot pay, the beneficiary must provide reasonable compensation.” State Council Document No. 39 of 2012 further clarifies how to handle medical care for such individuals. Healthcare facilities must establish a fast-track system based on the principle “treat first, bill later.” Specifically, medical expenses incurred during emergency treatment are the responsibility of the perpetrator or liable party; otherwise, they are covered by basic medical insurance. In cases of death, individuals meeting criteria for martyr status are recognized as such by law; those qualifying as work-related injuries receive a one-time death benefit plus an additional special allowance equal to 40 months of their salary. Injured individuals meeting workers’ compensation criteria receive benefits under the relevant regulations; others have their disability level assessed by civil affairs bureaus to determine appropriate support. Employment-wise, such individuals are prioritized for job assistance programs and placed in public-sector roles when possible. Housing-wise, they are given priority access to subsidized housing or rental assistance.
13-39.note: This grade is assigned because national documents clearly define which benefits apply; however, exact amounts of bonuses and detailed application procedures vary by province under local regulations, and these specifics were not verified across all regions in this round. Applications are typically submitted to local police departments or dedicated civil affairs bureaus responsible for recognizing acts of public service. Successful recognition depends on solid evidence: police reports, surveillance footage, witness contact details, and medical records gathered promptly at the scene. Legal aid for such cases is also available free of charge. National standards for death benefits and disability compensation calculations are explained in Sections 15 and 16 of Chapter 19; instructions for obtaining legal aid can be found in Section 3 of Chapter 7.

13-40.t: Knives, rebar, glass piercing the body – apply pressure around the foreign object to stop bleeding; do not pull it out
13-40.cost: No cost involved. The hard part is resisting the instinct to “pull it out” and instead staying with the injured person until help arrives.
13-40.human: Pulling out the object can cause severe bleeding and makes it harder for doctors to assess the extent of the injury. The correct approach is to call 120, then use your hand or a dressing to apply firm pressure around the object to control bleeding and keep it stable so it doesn’t move. If internal organs are visible through an abdominal wound, do not push them back in; simply cover them with a clean, moist dressing. For chest wounds where air bubbles are escaping, do not seal them with plastic wrap – doing so can cause the lung to collapse.
13-40.gain: The 2025 International First Aid Guidelines from the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies state: “First aiders should apply pressure around any foreign object (such as a knife) that has penetrated the body and keep it stable; do not remove it.” “Never pull any object out of abdominal or chest wounds – doing so can cause severe bleeding and makes it harder to assess the injury.” “Foreign objects embedded in the body should be kept stable; if they move with the pulse, simply hold them gently in place.” “First aiders must not push protruding organs back into the body.” For open chest wounds with active bleeding, “it is acceptable to leave them uncovered, as sealing them may trap air in the chest cavity and cause partial or total lung collapse (pneumothorax).” All penetrating abdominal or chest injuries require immediate emergency care.
13-40.note: This grade is assigned because these actions are widely accepted in official guidelines; however, no randomized trials exist, and it would be unethical to randomly assign patients to “remove” versus “not remove” such objects. The sole exception is when a foreign object blocks the airway and prevents breathing. In such cases, go directly to the emergency triage desk at the hospital and state “penetrating injury.” This falls under the highest priority category – do not wait in line at the registration desk (see Section 24, Item 8). If a penetrating injury occurs, call 120; the ambulance will alert the hospital in advance. For techniques on controlling severe bleeding and applying tourniquets, see Section 12.

13-41.t: If a fracture is suspected, don’t move the injured area — keep it supported and apply cold for up to 20 minutes; never try to realign it yourself
13-41.cost: No cost involved. Use a stiff board, rolled‑up magazines, or clothing as a splint. Wrap cold items in a cloth before applying them.
13-41.human: Treat any limb injury as a possible fracture first; being able to stand or move does not rule it out. Keep the injured part still, supported by hand or by a stiff board in its original position, and apply cold for no more than 20 minutes at a time. Do not try to realign it yourself; if bone has pierced the skin, stop the bleeding first and do not push the bone back. An X-ray can miss a fracture. If the film looks normal but the doctor still suspects a fracture or a ligament injury, follow the doctor’s advice to come back for a repeat exam or an MRI.
13-41.gain: The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies released its 2025 International First Aid Guidelines, which state that “any injury to a limb should be treated as a possible fracture” and “the only reliable way to confirm a fracture is an X‑ray; when in doubt, treat it as a fracture.” The purpose of immobilisation is “to minimise movement and pain.” Cold application “should be limited to 20 minutes at a time to reduce pain; longer exposure can damage the skin.” “For long bones such as the femur, bleeding from the bone itself can be life‑threatening.” Call emergency services if there is significant pain or swelling, signs of shock, a suspected femoral fracture, or obvious deformity of the limb. Only under two specific conditions may a fractured bone be manually realigned on site: first, when help is far away (or resources are limited) and the part of the limb below the angle appears cold and pale, or when the rescuer cannot safely immobilise it for transport; second, only if the rescuer is properly trained. For open fractures, the priority is stopping bleeding and preventing infection. But a first X-ray that shows nothing does not mean there is no fracture. The guideline on hip fracture from the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) says: if the X-ray is normal but a hip fracture is still suspected, “do an MRI”; if that cannot be done within 24 hours, consider a CT. Its fracture guideline says: for a suspected wrist scaphoid fracture, “after careful physical examination, consider an MRI first”. The scaphoid is a small bone in the wrist. A Cochrane review states: “initial X-rays cannot exclude a fracture”. In the studies it included, among people whose X-rays were normal but whose doctors still suspected a scaphoid fracture, the median share with a real fracture was 20%. The American College of Radiology has an appropriateness standard for knee trauma. It says: when the X-ray shows no fracture but an occult fracture or internal joint injury is still suspected, MRI as the next step is “usually appropriate”. It also says MRI is highly accurate for occult fractures and for meniscal and ligament injuries.
13-41.note: This grade B rating reflects that these practices are widely accepted. There is only one older study supporting the use of traction immobilisation for femoral fractures before hospital care; its reliability is low, yet it shows modest benefits such as reduced blood loss within 24 hours, shorter hospital stays, and no meaningful difference in mortality or complications. No evidence exists regarding whether early realignment yields any advantage over simple immobilisation. Three common misconceptions should be corrected: being able to walk does not rule out a fracture; cold alone — not alternating hot and cold — is appropriate; and sprains do not “work themselves out” with movement; rest is essential. Do not smoke until the bone has healed; see Section 2, item 1 (quit smoking). Don’t expect heavy calcium supplements or bone broth to make the bone heal faster; see Section 6, item 30 (calcium after a fracture). For elderly patients with suspected fractures after a fall, refer to item 2 for handling precautions. Swelling of one leg after casting or bed rest may indicate a clot; see item 11 for details. Information on disability assessment and eligibility for a disability certificate after treatment can be found in section 24, items 9 and 10.

13-42.t: After sexual assault, go to a safe place and call 110; do not shower, wash clothes, or tidy the room before a medical exam, and visit a hospital within 72 hours
13-42.cost: Calling the police costs nothing. Emergency contraceptives are over-the-counter medicines available at any pharmacy. Post-exposure prophylaxis treatment costs over a thousand yuan per course; whether it is needed must be decided by a doctor — see item 38 in this section regarding obtaining PEP within 72 hours. The real challenge is that it is extremely hard to speak up at the moment, and many victims simply want to take a shower right away.
13-42.human: Physical traces on the body, on clothing, and in the room are the most crucial evidence for identifying the perpetrator. Therefore, avoid showering, washing clothes, or cleaning the area before a medical exam, and call 110 as soon as possible. Emergency contraceptives are readily available at pharmacies and work best when taken early. Within 72 hours, visit a hospital so a doctor can determine if PEP is necessary.
13-42.gain: Prosecutors from the Beijing People’s Procuratorate state: “Whether minors or adults, anyone who experiences sexual assault should call 110 immediately.” Prompt reporting and medical care “allow investigators to examine the scene, collect physical evidence, and preserve proof in a timely manner.” A sexual assault prevention guide published by the Guizhou Provincial Civil Affairs Bureau and reprinted by People’s Daily advises: “If sexual assault occurs, preserving evidence is the top priority.” It recommends keeping “body fluids, hair, skin cells, and communication records” and warns that “after an assault, one must not shower, wash clothes, tidy the room, or throw anything away.” In cases involving acquaintances, preserving call logs and messages is essential; any threats or attempts at bribery by the perpetrator must also be documented. The Xicheng District Procuratorate in Beijing adds: “Try not to shower before undergoing a physical examination.” WHO notes that emergency contraception may be used “when a woman has been sexually assaulted without effective contraceptive protection,” recommending its use within five days for maximum effectiveness. Emergency contraceptive pills containing levonorgestrel have a pregnancy rate of 1.2% to 2.1% among users; in China, such pills are sold over the counter. According to the Wuhan Health Commission, “the sooner these pills are taken after unprotected intercourse — ideally within 72 hours — the better they prevent pregnancy.” PEP for HIV should be taken within two hours if possible, and no later than 72 hours.
13-42.note: This grade is assigned because these recommendations stem from official law‑enforcement experience and medical guidance; there are no statistics showing exactly how much they raise conviction rates. The main beneficiaries are the victim herself and her family. The 72‑hour window for emergency contraception reflects China’s product labeling; WHO states that it remains effective up to five days, though earlier use is preferable. These pills have no effect if pregnancy has already occurred. When reporting to police, provide a truthful account without exaggeration or concealment. Any attempts by the perpetrator to settle privately, pay compensation, or threaten you must be documented and never deleted. You may decide to wait before calling police, but be aware that evidence deteriorates over time. Regardless of whether you call police, seek medical care within the stipulated timeframe. Recordings related to this topic are discussed in item 41 of section 8. If the perpetrator later uses photos or police reports to blackmail you, this also constitutes a crime — see item 32 of section 8. If a friend experiences sexual assault, accompany her to report it and to the hospital; do not suggest she shower or rest first.

13-43.t: When a baby under 1 year is choking and cannot cry out, alternate 5 back blows (face-down) and 5 chest thrusts — never press the belly
13-43.cost: No cost. Watch a demonstration once or take a short infant first-aid class — a few minutes to half a day. The hard part is staying calm enough to turn the baby face-down on your forearm.
13-43.human: If the child can still cough or cry audibly, let them cough while you watch closely. If they cannot cry, their face turns blue, call 120, lay the baby face-down on your forearm, and give 5 back blows with the heel of your hand between the shoulder blades. If that fails, roll them over and give 5 quick thrusts on the center of the chest. Keep alternating — never push on the belly. If the baby becomes unresponsive, switch to CPR.
13-43.gain: The American Heart Association and American Academy of Pediatrics issued 2025 pediatric basic life support guidance. It states that choking (for example, an object blocking the airway) “is a leading cause of death in infants and children.” Liquids are what infants most often aspirate. Mild obstruction: still coughing or making sounds — let the child cough while you monitor for worsening. Severe obstruction: weak cough or none, cannot cry, cyanosis — call emergency services first, then “repeat cycles of 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts until the object is expelled or the infant becomes unresponsive.” Abdominal thrusts are not recommended for infants because they can injure internal organs. Chest thrusts are now taught with the heel of one hand because it achieves greater depth than the old two-finger method. When the infant is unresponsive, start CPR with compressions first; do not check a pulse. Remove only visible objects before giving breaths. The guideline explicitly says “do not perform blind finger sweeps.” The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies 2025 international first-aid guidance uses the same sequence: up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades, then turn the infant and give up to 5 chest thrusts, then call emergency services if needed. Its chest-thrust technique uses a two-thumb encircling grip. The Fujian Provincial Red Cross emergency-care training center describes “5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts” for infants under 1 year: hold the infant prone on the forearm with the head lower than the trunk for back blows.
13-43.note: Rated B because support comes mainly from case reports, with no “how many fewer deaths if you follow this” figure. Benefit is rated large by judgment: a fully blocked airway can stop an infant’s heart within minutes. The main beneficiaries are your own children. For children 1 year and older and adults, use abdominal thrusts; see item 26 in this section (choking: back blows plus abdominal thrusts). Chest-thrust hand position differs across sources: the U.S. guideline and newer Chinese Red Cross training use one-hand heel; IFRC uses two thumbs; older courses used two fingers. The 2025 U.S. guideline dropped two-finger compressions because depth was inadequate. Any of these beats doing nothing. Even after the object is expelled, seek medical care — fragments may remain in the lungs. Keep coins and small toys out of reach. If the baby is unresponsive, see item 44 in this section (infant CPR).

13-44.t: If a baby under 1 is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call 120 on speakerphone and perform infant CPR: 30 compressions, then 2 breaths
13-44.cost: No cost. Infant CPR takes one hands-on class, half a day to a full day. The hard parts are sealing your mouth over the infant’s mouth and nose for breaths and pressing firmly enough.
13-44.human: No response to foot stimulation and no normal breathing — call 120 on speakerphone and do not stop. Encircle the chest with both hands and compress with two thumbs; if you cannot encircle, use the heel of one hand, about 4 cm (1.5 inches) deep, about 2 compressions per second. After every 30 compressions, give 2 breaths covering mouth and nose. Most infant cardiac arrests start with breathing failure; CPR that includes breaths improves survival.
13-44.gain: The American Heart Association and American Academy of Pediatrics 2025 pediatric basic life support guideline states that respiratory problems remain the main cause of cardiac arrest in infants and children. Among infants with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, only 6.6% survive to hospital discharge. For an unresponsive infant or child with abnormal breathing and no signs of life, “CPR should be started immediately” without checking a pulse. Compression depth is at least one-third of the anteroposterior chest diameter; for infants, “about 1.5 inches (4 cm).” Rate 100 to 120 per minute. One rescuer: 30 compressions then 2 breaths. Two rescuers: 15 compressions then 2 breaths. Use one-hand heel or two-thumb encircling compressions; if encircling is not possible, use heel of one hand. Two-finger compression has been removed because depth was inadequate. The guideline also states that for out-of-hospital pediatric cardiac arrest, adding ventilations to compressions improves survival. A U.S. registry of 3,900 children under 18 with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest found 59.4% were infants. Bystander CPR was associated with an adjusted hospital discharge survival of 13.2% versus 9.5% without CPR; adjusted OR 1.57 (about 57% higher odds of survival), 95% CI 1.25–1.96. Among infants, CPR with breaths was linked to higher survival and better neurological recovery; compression-only outcomes were similar to no CPR. IFRC 2025 guidance: check responsiveness by picking up the infant or flicking the foot. If alone, call emergency services on speakerphone. If no phone allows simultaneous calling, perform 1 minute of CPR before calling. A popular-science article from the Capital Institute of Pediatrics, republished by the Beijing Municipal Health Commission, states: “If only 1 person is present, perform 2 minutes of CPR before calling 120.” Compression depth “4 cm for infants.” Mouth-to-mouth-nose for breaths under 1 year.
13-44.note: Rated B because survival figures come from registry studies with recording bias, pooled across all children; infant-only discharge numbers were not given in the summary. Benefit is rated large from the pooled figures: discharge survival 9.5% to 13.2%, a relative increase of about 40%. Main beneficiaries are your own children. Three differences from item 1 in this section (hard chest compressions for adults): infants need breaths — compression-only works poorly; use two thumbs or one heel at about 4 cm, not stacked adult hands; if you cannot call while compressing, start CPR before calling. How long to compress before calling varies: Capital Institute of Pediatrics and the U.S. single-rescuer flow say 2 minutes; IFRC says 1 minute. Speakerphone removes the trade-off. The European Resuscitation Council teaches 5 breaths first then compressions; the U.S. guideline compressions first — both beat doing nothing. Older Chinese courses taught two-finger compression; the 2025 U.S. guideline removed it. For choking, look in the mouth before breaths and remove only visible objects; see item 43 (infant choking).

14-1.t: Turn on two-factor authentication for email, payment, and social accounts; prefer phone pop-up confirmation, with SMS codes second
14-1.cost: No cost. Set it once per account; two or three minutes each.
14-1.human: Two-factor authentication means that besides your password, you confirm once more that it is really you when you log in. With a pop-up on your phone that you tap to confirm, more than nine out of ten phishing account takeovers are blocked. Old methods like answering “where did you last log in?” or “what is your backup email?” only block around one in ten phishing takeovers.
14-1.gain: Google counted 350,000 real account takeover attempts (also called account hijacking). One class uses device-based verification, such as a pop-up on your phone for you to confirm, or plugging in a security key. That class blocked “more than 94% of phishing-related hijacking attempts and 100% of automated hijacking attempts.” Phishing means tricking you into entering your password on a fake site; automated means machines trying leaked passwords in bulk. Another class uses knowledge-based verification, such as where you last logged in or what your backup email is. That class “blocked as little as 10% of phishing hijacking and 73% of automated hijacking”
14-1.note: The same study also found that this verification sometimes locks out the real user. 52% of genuine users did not get in on the first try, but 97% eventually did. Turn it on for email first, because most other accounts can recover passwords through email. Keep verification codes to yourself; what reading a code aloud for someone else can cost you is in Section 8, item 45 (reading verification codes).

14-2.t: Give your email its own password; do not reuse it on any website
14-2.cost: No cost. A password manager can store it so you do not have to memorize it. The hard part is breaking the habit of one password everywhere.
14-2.human: Passwords stolen from other sites get tried on your email directly. Once someone is in your email, every account that can reset its password through that email is lost too. So the email password stands alone; do not use it anywhere else.
14-2.gain: Trying leaked account-and-password pairs from elsewhere against your logins is called credential stuffing; it is the easiest attack, and your email gets tried this way too. Once someone is in your email, every account that uses it for password recovery goes with it. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency recommends a different strong password for every account, at least 16 characters, stored in a password manager
14-2.note: If you cannot memorize them, use your browser’s built-in password manager. It remembers each site’s password for you, which is far stronger than reusing one password everywhere. Do not store passwords in WeChat favorites or notes.

14-3.t: Set a screen lock on your phone and a PIN on your SIM card
14-3.cost: No cost. Set the screen lock and the SIM PIN once each.
14-3.human: The SIM card is the small card in your phone; SMS verification codes arrive through it. If you lose the phone, whoever finds it can pull out the card, put it in another phone, collect verification codes, and reset your accounts one by one. A PIN on the card means that when the card moves to another phone, you must enter that code at startup first, and that path is cut off.
14-3.gain: After a phone is lost, the fastest move for whoever finds it is to put the SIM in another phone and collect your SMS verification codes. With those codes they can reset your accounts one by one. With a SIM PIN, another phone asks for the code at startup, so they cannot use the card to receive codes. In October 2020 the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (工信部) reported a real case. After a user’s phone was stolen, they did not suspend the line in time. Wrongdoers used “mobile number plus verification code” to log into a government service app and obtained the user’s ID number and other data. They then changed the mobile service password and tricked customer service into unsuspending the already-suspended card. Finally they exploited a “forgot password” flaw on a lending platform, reset the payment password, and stole loan funds. MIIT used the case to remind users to set a SIM PIN promptly and to suspend the line immediately when a phone is lost. For the screen-lock half, the US Federal Communications Commission advises setting a strong password on the phone to limit others’ use; when the phone is lost or stolen, that helps stop unauthorized charges and misuse of personal data
14-3.note: Set the PIN under “SIM card lock” in phone settings. Factory default codes are usually 1234 or 0000. Three wrong entries in a row require the carrier’s PUK code to unlock, so write the PIN on paper after you set it. Rated C because both sources are official reminders plus one case, with no study quantifying how much money a PIN saves. What to do first when a phone is lost is in item 4 (if your phone is lost, follow this order).

14-4.t: If your phone is lost, do this in order: suspend the SIM, remote-lock the phone, change passwords, report to police, freeze bank cards
14-4.cost: No cost. The full sequence takes about ten minutes.
14-4.human: Order matters more than speed. Step one, suspend the SIM, and the verification-code lifeline is cut. Then remote-lock the phone, change email and payment passwords from a computer, report to police for a receipt, and freeze bank cards as needed. Without your phone, you can still call the carrier from someone else’s phone to suspend the line.
14-4.gain: Order matters more than speed. First, suspend the SIM so others cannot receive your verification codes. Second, remote-lock the phone and wipe its contents. Third, from a computer, change email and payment passwords. Fourth, report to police and get a receipt. Last, freeze bank cards as needed. The US Federal Communications Commission also says that even if you think you only misplaced the phone, remote-lock it; if it was stolen, report to police at once with model and IMEI (the phone’s identity number), and tell the carrier immediately
14-4.note: Save the customer service numbers for the three major carriers in advance: China Mobile 10086, China Unicom 10010, China Telecom 10000. Also note which city you registered the number in; customer service will ask. You can suspend the line from another person’s phone the same way.

14-5.t: If your card is fraudulently charged, suspend or freeze it and report to police first, then demand compensation from the bank: proving “you made the charge” is the bank’s job
14-5.cost: No cost. As soon as something on the card looks wrong, suspend or freeze it immediately. Keep police reports, suspension records, and transaction notices from the bank. If the physical card is still with you, make a small balance inquiry or deposit nearby to leave a record that the real card was in your hands when it happened. The hard part is not arguing with customer service first; suspend first.
14-5.human: If someone fraudulently uses your card, you do not have to prove “that was not me.” The bank must prove the charge was made by you or with your authorization; if it cannot, it must compensate you. That assumes you suspend or freeze as soon as you find out. If you delay suspension, you bear the extra losses that pile up afterward.
14-5.gain: Supreme People’s Court rules split “who must prove what.” If you say it was counterfeit-card fraud or online fraud, you go first with evidence. Counterfeit-card fraud means someone copied your card and used the copy. Usable proof includes effective legal documents, where the physical card was during the transaction, where the transaction occurred, account statements, transaction alerts, police reports, suspension records, and so on. Conversely, if the issuing bank or a non-bank payment institution (third-party payment) says the cardholder made the charge or authorized it, they must produce the evidence. After you notify the bank, if it does not verify promptly or does not provide or preserve transaction records and surveillance video, and evidence is lost because of that, the bank bears the consequence of lacking proof. Once liability is established: debit card (savings card) holders may demand that the bank return stolen deposits with interest and compensate losses; credit card holders may demand return of unauthorized overdraft principal, interest, and penalties, and compensation for losses, and courts will not support the bank demanding repayment of that overdraft from you. You may also demand that the bank promptly remove related negative credit records (nationwide, effective 25 May 2021)
14-5.note: Two situations leave you liable. First, if you did not keep your card, password, or verification codes safe and you were at fault (the original text: failure to fulfill the duty of safekeeping), you bear loss in proportion to fault. So do not tell others your password or forward verification codes (see item 1, prefer phone pop-up for two-factor authentication). Second, if you do not suspend in time and losses grow, you bear the extra part. So the first step is always suspend or freeze, not argue with customer service. Third-party payment institutions follow the same rules. If their marketing promises “pay first, investigate later” in concrete terms, you can hold them to that advance payment. Money you were tricked into transferring yourself follows a different path; see Section 8, item 2 (if you discover fraud, call 110 or 96110 immediately to request a payment stop).

14-6.t: Every so often, check logged-in devices and authorized apps on your accounts; remove what you no longer use
14-6.cost: No cost. A few minutes each time. The hard part is that nothing reminds you; you have to remember to look.
14-6.human: “Logged-in devices” means the phones and computers that can still use your account right now. If an unfamiliar device appears on the list, or software you stopped using still connects to your account, change the password first, then sign out everywhere. For email, also check whether any auto-forwarding was set without your knowledge.
14-6.gain: The logged-in-devices list records which phones and computers can still use the account. The authorized-apps list records third-party apps you allowed to sign in with the account. Unfamiliar devices and long-unused third-party apps are the easiest traces to spot. The UK National Cyber Security Centre lists “logins or login attempts from unfamiliar places or at unusual times” as signs of account compromise. It also says criminals often add a forwarding rule in email so every message to you is copied to them, which they use to reset your passwords. Its recommended order is: remove unknown forwarding rules, change the password, then sign out all devices and apps. After sign-out, anyone else needs the new password to use the account. The US Federal Trade Commission likewise advises signing out all devices after regaining an account and deleting forwarding rules you did not set
14-6.note: WeChat, Alipay, email, Apple ID, and Android accounts all have this screen. If you see an unfamiliar device, change the password first, then choose sign out everywhere; that is the order the UK NCSC gives. Rated C because both sources are official how-to guides, with no study on how much periodic checks reduce losses.

14-7.t: Do not tap “accept all” just to use an app: for non-essential data, refusing must not cost you the service
14-7.cost: No cost. The hard part is not tapping “accept all.”
14-7.human: When an app asks for your information, if it is not required to provide the service, the app cannot deny you access because you refuse. It may only collect what it actually needs. A map app needing your location is required; a flashlight app needing your contacts is not.
14-7.gain: The law states two rules. First, you may not refuse products or services on the grounds that the person does not consent or withdraws consent, except where processing that information is necessary to provide the service. Second, collection must be limited to the minimum needed for the purpose; only what is usable may be collected
14-7.note: The test is whether the information is necessary to provide this service. Location is necessary for a map; contacts are not for a flashlight. After installing an app, open app permissions in phone settings and turn off what is not necessary. When you truly need a permission, choose allow only this once.

14-8.t: You have the right to view, copy, correct, and delete your personal information; if refused, you can sue
14-8.cost: No cost. You only need to complain or sue if the other party stalls. A real lawsuit starts at several months, and you pay your own lawyer fees, so complaining first is usually better value. The hard part is following up when they drag their feet.
14-8.human: You may require a company to let you view, copy, correct, and delete your information. When service stops, retention periods end, or you withdraw consent, the company should delete on its own. If it refuses you, it must state the reason; if it still will not act, you can sue in court. Closing an account and deleting personal information are two steps; after closing the account you must request deletion separately.
14-8.gain: In several situations the company must delete proactively: service stopped, agreed retention period ended, you withdrew consent, the original collection purpose was achieved, and so on. If it did not delete, you may demand deletion. If it refuses your exercise of these rights, it must state the reason. You may sue directly in court
14-8.note: Closing an account and deleting personal information are separate; after closing, request deletion separately. Before changing phones or selling an old phone, sign out of all accounts and unlink them on the old device, then factory reset. The law gives you a post-hoc deletion right; it cannot claw back what already leaked.

14-9.t: Facial recognition is not mandatory: if other methods can do the same job, they cannot make face scan the only option; if you refuse, they must offer alternatives
14-9.cost: No cost. When asked to scan your face, ask “is there another way to verify?” If they say no, demand one. The hard part is asking out loud on the spot.
14-9.human: As long as another method can achieve the same purpose, they cannot require face scan alone. If you refuse face verification, they must offer card swipe, password, ID document, or similar alternatives, and they may not force you with “then we cannot serve you.” No one may install face recognition equipment inside hotel guest rooms, public baths, changing rooms, or restrooms.
14-9.gain: The Administrative Measures for the Safe Application of Facial Recognition Technology (人脸识别技术应用安全管理办法) state: “Where the same purpose can be achieved or equivalent business requirements met, and other non-facial-recognition methods exist, facial recognition must not be the sole verification method. Where an individual does not agree to identity verification via facial information, other reasonable and convenient methods shall be provided.” The measures also state: “No organization or individual may, under the pretext of handling business or improving service quality, mislead, defraud, or coerce an individual into accepting facial recognition to verify identity.” If processing relies on consent, there must be “separate consent given voluntarily and explicitly with full knowledge”: asked separately for this matter, and you agree separately. You may withdraw consent, and the processor must provide a convenient way to withdraw. Processing facial information of minors under 14 requires consent from a parent or other guardian. Face recognition devices in public places must be “necessary for maintaining public security” and carry prominent notices. Inside private spaces in public venues such as hotel guest rooms, public baths, public changing rooms, and public restrooms, no organization or individual may install them. Facial information shall be stored on the device and must not be transmitted over the internet, except as otherwise provided by laws or administrative regulations, or with separate consent (nationwide, effective 1 June 2025)
14-9.note: Common cases are residential gate access, rental platforms, gyms, and hotels asking you to enroll your face. When they say “the system only supports face scan,” quote the measures verbatim: “Where the same purpose can be achieved or equivalent business requirements met, and other non-facial-recognition methods exist, facial recognition must not be the sole verification method.” Then demand card, password, or ID alternatives. If they still refuse, report to the local cyberspace authority (网信部门). Where national rules require face verification for identity, such as some financial and government scenarios, follow those rules. Unlike a password, a face cannot be changed after leak, so treat it more carefully than a password. Entities storing facial information on 100,000 or more people must file with provincial-level or higher cyberspace authorities within 30 working days; that filing is also a question to ask about whether they are legitimate. Rights to access, correct, and delete personal information are in item 8. Someone using your face to take out their own loan is a different matter; see Section 8, item 45 (helping with a face scan).

14-10.t: Do not hand code, keys, or private material to unknown “AI proxy gateways,” especially when letting AI run commands automatically
14-10.cost: Official direct access is usually pricier than proxy gateways, and topping up is less convenient. The pull is that proxies are cheap and one endpoint can call several model vendors
14-10.human: A proxy sits between you and the model vendor; it can see and alter what you send and what comes back. Researchers measured 400-plus proxies: 9 injected malicious code into replies, 17 tampered with cloud service keys the researchers had planted on purpose. Where AI runs commands automatically, one altered command can be enough for someone else to control the computer.
14-10.gain: In June 2026 the Ministry of State Security issued a risk alert. Some proxies retain user submissions on servers; some intercept privately and resell data to other model vendors for training. Some hide backdoors that implant malicious code on user devices, steal account keys and cloud credentials, or even install remote-control software. The alert recommends official direct connections or properly licensed platforms, and not using platforms of unknown origin without operating credentials or security safeguards. Desensitize personal privacy and project material before use, manage keys, and rotate them on a schedule. On abnormal billing, unexplained account bans, or odd data, stop use immediately, rotate keys, run antivirus, and preserve evidence. Researchers from UC Santa Barbara and others measured in 2026. They bought 28 paid proxies from Taobao (淘宝), Xianyu (闲鱼), and overseas shops, and collected 400 free proxies from public communities. One paid and eight free injected malicious code into returned tool calls. Tool calls are commands AI has your computer run, such as installing a package. Two timed their attacks; the paper’s example is targeting only fully automated sessions. Seventeen touched Amazon Web Services keys the researchers had planted on purpose. One moved funds from a researcher’s Ethereum wallet; the wallet held very little, under $50. The demonstrated tampering was subtle: swap requests for the near-identical reqeusts in an install command, hard to spot at a glance (nationwide)
14-10.note: Rated B because there is only one study, and it is a preprint (published before formal peer review). Most measured proxies were free; only 28 were paid, so you cannot infer what share of all proxies are malicious. Some media wrote the theft as $500,000; the paper says under $50. Benefit magnitude is set at medium by consequence: loss from stolen keys and code varies widely, and the study has no amount to apply mechanically. If you already used an unknown proxy, revoke and regenerate keys at the model vendor, and rotate cloud and repository keys together. When traffic goes through a proxy, do not let AI run commands fully automatically; review commands before allowing them. Operators running proxy gateways face criminal liability; see Section 11, item 19 (AI proxy gateways). The beneficiary is you.

15-1.t: When renting, the deposit amount, refund timing, and grounds for deduction must be written into the contract
15-1.cost: No monetary cost. Spend an extra ten minutes when signing the contract. The hard part is raising it in front of the landlord.
15-1.human: How much the deposit is, when it is returned, and when it may be deducted must go into the contract before you sign. Deduction grounds not written in the contract cannot be used to withhold your deposit when you move out.
15-1.gain: Administrative regulations state clearly: “Where the lessor collects a deposit, the amount, time of return, and circumstances in which the deposit may be deducted shall be stipulated in the housing lease contract. Except as provided in the contract, the lessor shall not deduct the deposit without proper cause.” Three things must appear in the contract: how much is collected, when it is returned, and when deduction is allowed. Grounds not in the contract cannot be used to take your money.
15-1.note: On move-out day, take photos and video together with the landlord. Record water, electricity, and gas meter readings, and photograph walls and floors. If the deposit is withheld without cause, complain first to the housing lease administration (房屋租赁管理部门). For smaller amounts, use small-claims litigation; see Section 8.

15-2.t: If water or power is cut, locks are changed, or someone threatens you at the door to force you out — call the police and preserve evidence: regulations forbid using these methods to pressure you to vacate
15-2.cost: No monetary cost. One call to the police; you can do it on the spot.
15-2.human: A landlord cannot use cutting utilities, changing locks, or door-to-door threats to force you to terminate the lease or move out; regulations forbid it. If it happens, call the police first. The police response record is evidence if you later seek compensation for losses. Do not confront the other party yourself.
15-2.gain: Administrative regulations state clearly: “The lessor shall not use violence, threats, or other illegal means to compel the lessee to terminate the housing lease contract or vacate the leased housing.” Vacating means being made to move out. In such cases call the police first and keep evidence. Do not confront them yourself.
15-2.note: Calling the police is to obtain a response record; later it serves as evidence when you claim losses. Also notify the housing lease administration (房屋租赁管理部门).

15-3.t: Agents must not collect or pay rent and deposits on your behalf — pay the landlord directly
15-3.cost: No monetary cost. A few minutes to verify the payee before payment. The hard part is resisting the agent’s push to pay it to the agency.
15-3.human: By rule, rent and deposits must not pass through an agent for collection or payment; pay the landlord directly. Every extra hop through an agent is one more chance it absconds with the money. If it runs, you lose the rent and the landlord can still push you out. Before paying, check that the payee matches the name on the real property ownership certificate (不动产权属证书).
15-3.gain: Administrative regulations list “collecting or paying housing rent and deposits on behalf of others” as prohibited conduct for real estate brokerage firms; an agent cannot collect rent and deposits for the landlord. Each pass through an agent adds a chance of absconding with funds.
15-3.note: Before paying, check that the payee matches the name on the ownership certificate. If not, clarify and keep written authorization. An agent may only charge a brokerage fee for matchmaking.

15-4.t: Before signing a long-term rental apartment lease, check its regulated escrow account — do not pay a full year upfront for a small discount
15-4.cost: No monetary cost. One check takes about ten minutes.
15-4.human: Paying a full year upfront only buys a small discount. Once the company fails, your deposit and the remaining months of rent are gone together. It is worse with a rent loan: if the apartment company disappears, you still repay the loan month by month. Before signing, check whether it publicly lists a regulated housing-rent fund account.
15-4.gain: Administrative regulations require housing rental enterprises that operate by subleasing to “establish a regulated housing-rent fund account and disclose it to the public.” Subleasing means the firm leases from the landlord in bulk and re-rents to you. The small discount from paying a year upfront does not offset the risk of losing deposit and remaining rent when the firm runs. Signing a rent loan at the same time raises the risk further.
15-4.note: At signing, see whether a loan is bundled in. If an installment app pays the full year to the apartment and you repay monthly, you must keep repaying after the apartment disappears. Do not sign that kind of contract.

15-5.t: If the home is sold during the lease, the lease stays valid — you do not have to move
15-5.human: If the home is sold during the lease term, your lease remains valid. The new owner must let you stay through the original contract until it ends. You do not move out and do not renegotiate rent, provided you are already living there lawfully and you keep the contract, transfer records, and move-in timing.
15-5.gain: The Civil Code has a rule called “sale does not break lease” (买卖不破租赁). The statute reads: a change of ownership of the leased thing during the lease term does not affect the lease contract’s validity. If the owner changes during the term, the signed lease still holds; the new owner must honor the original contract through expiry.
15-5.note: This assumes you already occupy the unit lawfully — the statute calls that lawful possession and use. Keep the contract, transfer records, and evidence of when you moved in.

15-6.t: Before signing a lease, verify the ownership certificate and mortgage status; route all payments by transfer with a purpose note
15-6.cost: No monetary cost. Bring your ID to the real estate registration authority (不动产登记机构) once; the check takes about half an hour. The hard part is asking the landlord to produce the ownership certificate in person.
15-6.human: Before signing, ask the landlord for ID and the ownership certificate. Then go to the registration authority with your ID — you can check even before a contract is signed — for whether the home is mortgaged or sealed. If it was mortgaged or sealed before lease, and it is auctioned to a new owner, you cannot demand to keep living there. Pay everything by transfer with a purpose note so you have a record.
15-6.gain: Before signing, the landlord must show you identity proof and the real property ownership certificate. Without that certificate, other proof of lawful authority to lease must be provided. The landlord must also cooperate when you query and verify information on the unit — an administrative duty on lessors. Before any contract, you can go with your ID to the registration authority in the city or county where the property sits and check several items: basic facts about the home, whether there are co-owners, whether mortgage or habitation-right registration exists, and whether it is sealed. After a contract is signed, you can check registration results with the lease. This step matters because “sale does not break lease” has two exceptions. If the home was mortgaged to a bank before lease and later auctioned to repay debt, you cannot require the new owner to let you stay on the original contract. The same if it was sealed by a court before lease. When the court auctions, if the lease blocks an earlier mortgage, the court may remove the lease before sale. Conversely, if it was leased to you first and you moved in, and the landlord mortgaged later, the mortgage does not break your lease. If sealing, title dispute, or similar makes the unit unusable, you may terminate the contract. If a third party asserts rights and you cannot use the home, you may pay less rent or none. Routing all money by transfer with a note such as “rent for [address], [month]” is author experience: in a dispute it shows you paid and what you paid for.
15-6.note: Among what you can check before signing, owner identity is not included — so match the name on the certificate to the landlord’s ID in person. At signing the landlord should appear in person; if not, get a written power of attorney. If a sublessor rents to you, you need the original landlord’s written consent. Rights to terminate or pay reduced rent, if the landlord refuses, require a court suit. Ordinary first-instance procedure starts at 6 months; lawyer fees are usually yours. Transfer purpose notes are not directly required by regulation; that part is author experience.

15-7.t: If an agent collects payment on a resale, funds must go through the agency’s dedicated client transaction settlement account at a bank
15-7.cost: No monetary cost. The hard part is insisting on the dedicated account; you may need a few rounds with the agent.
15-7.human: Purchase price runs from hundreds of thousands to millions — the largest single payment in this book. If an agent collects, rules require the bank’s dedicated account, not WeChat to an individual broker. Also, two agencies on one deal may charge only one commission; loan processing and transfer registration need separate contracts and fees stated upfront.
15-7.gain: The rules state clearly: where a real estate brokerage is entrusted to collect or pay transaction funds, transfer must go through its dedicated client transaction settlement account opened at a bank. Purchase money enters a supervised dedicated account, not the agency’s own account or a broker’s private account.
15-7.note: Purchase price is hundreds of thousands to millions — the largest single payment in this book; do not WeChat an individual broker. Two common overcharges: two agencies jointly brokering one deal may take only one commission; loan processing and transfer registration are separate services — separate contracts and upfront fee disclosure. Route all payments by transfer with purpose notes; see item 6 (verify ownership certificate and mortgage before signing).

15-8.t: Do not rent subdivided units: the minimum rental unit is the originally designed room; kitchens, bathrooms, and balconies must not be lived in
15-8.cost: No monetary cost. The trade-off is that on the same budget you live farther out or in a smaller place.
15-8.human: By rule, the smallest unit you may rent is the room as originally designed. Kitchens, bathrooms, balconies, and basement storage must not be rented for people to live in. After an illegal subdivision is caught, you may have to move. During the lease the landlord also cannot raise rent unilaterally on a whim.
15-8.gain: The rules state clearly that the minimum rental unit is the originally designed room; one room must not be partitioned into several units rented separately. Per-person living area must meet the local minimum. Kitchens, bathrooms, balconies, and basement storage must not be rented for residence. During the lease the lessor may not unilaterally raise rent at will.
15-8.note: When an illegal subdivision is enforced, tenants move; deposit and rent already paid are often not recovered. Safety is worse too: partition walls often block escape routes, and many people on one circuit strain the wiring. When viewing, check three things: whether walls were added later, whether the room has a window, and whether the meter can handle that many people.

15-9.t: Urban household registration (城镇户口) holders who want to live in the countryside should only rent rural housing — do not buy homestead land (宅基地) or houses on it
15-9.cost: No monetary cost. The trade-off is that the house is not yours; one lease term is at most 20 years, then you negotiate again with the landlord.
15-9.human: Urban registrants may not go to villages to buy homestead land, farmers’ houses, or “small-property-rights housing” (小产权房); national documents forbid it. “A written contract is enough,” even from villagers, does not make the money buy ownership. To live in the countryside long term, sign a lease — at most 20 years per term — and renew when it ends.
15-9.gain: A General Office of the State Council document states clearly: “Urban residents must not go to rural areas to purchase homestead land, farmers’ housing, or ‘small-property-rights housing.’” The same document provides that after a farmer sells or leases housing, a new homestead application will not be approved. A 2019 document from the central rural work office and the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs repeats: “Urban residents are strictly forbidden to purchase homestead land in rural areas.” That document also gives the lawful path: urban residents may rent rural housing to live or operate a business; the lease term must not exceed twenty years, and the parties may agree anew when it expires.
15-9.note: Homestead land is village land allocated to registered villagers to build homes; only locals may receive it. When renting rural housing, sign a written contract with the farming household lessor stating term, rent, whether you may renovate or rebuild, and how renovation costs are settled at expiry. Leases over 20 years are invalid — do not sign “50 years” or “70 years,” and do not pay many years’ rent upfront. The documents also forbid using homestead land for villa compounds or private clubs in the countryside; do not pay villagers for “co-build” schemes.

16-1.t: Take your medication as prescribed through the full course; do not stop because you feel better
16-1.cost: No cost; it saves money on treating complications later. Daily pills take only a few minutes; the hard part is not missing a single day.
16-1.human: People who take medication exactly as their doctor says have roughly half the chance of dying in the same period as people who take it on and off. Treat that figure with caution. Even people who stick to placebo pills die less often, which shows part of the benefit comes from “people who can keep taking meds tend to take better care of their health overall.” Stopping medication still does clear harm, especially blood pressure drugs, anticoagulants, and anti-rejection drugs.
16-1.gain: Pooled from 21 studies and 46,847 people (meta-analysis): compared with intermittent use, full adherence was associated with about 44% lower odds of dying in the same period. Raw odds ratio 0.56, 95% CI 0.50–0.63 (confidence interval). For treatments with proven efficacy only, about 45% lower (0.55, 0.49–0.62)
16-1.note: Controversial. This is one of the numbers in this book that needs the most discounting. In the same meta-analysis, people who fully adhered to placebo also had lower mortality (0.56, 0.43–0.74). That suggests a large share of the benefit comes from “people who can keep taking meds tend to take better care of their health overall.” The author calls this mixed-in factor the healthy adherer effect. Harm from stopping medication is nonetheless clear, especially for blood pressure drugs, anticoagulants, and anti-rejection drugs

16-2.t: First complete outpatient chronic special-disease certification (门诊慢特病认定), then cross-region filing (异地就医备案)—hypertension, diabetes, outpatient chemo/radiotherapy, dialysis, and anti-rejection therapy can then be settled directly across regions
16-2.cost: No cost. Before travel, complete cross-region medical care filing once on the basic medical insurance (医保) app on your phone.
16-2.human: For hypertension, diabetes, outpatient chemo/radiotherapy for malignant tumors, uremia dialysis, and anti-rejection therapy after organ transplant, outpatient care in another region can go straight through yibao (医保) without paying upfront and claiming back in your home insurance region. You must first get outpatient chronic special-disease certification where you are insured, then complete cross-region filing. Both steps are required for it to work.
16-2.gain: National Healthcare Security Administration (国家医保局) policy documents state this step has largely been reached. The wording is: “Cross-region direct settlement of outpatient expenses for five chronic special-disease categories—hypertension, diabetes, outpatient chemo/radiotherapy for malignant tumors, uremia dialysis, and post-transplant anti-rejection therapy—is now largely accessible at county level.” “Accessible at county level” (县域可及) means it can be handled at the county tier. The documents also add five more disease categories on top of these five
16-2.note: Both steps are required: first outpatient chronic special-disease certification in your home insurance region, then cross-region filing. How far the five newly added categories have rolled out varies by locality; follow what your local healthcare security authority publishes

16-3.t: Follow the follow-up intervals your doctor sets, and record each measurement in the same notebook
16-3.cost: Each test costs from a few dozen to a few hundred CNY. A hospital visit plus waiting for results takes some time. The hard part is going again and again on schedule without putting it off.
16-3.human: Chronic disease is about change over time, not one reading. Measuring blood pressure at home alone does not lower it by much. Bring readings to your doctor and let treatment be adjusted from them, and pressure falls more. When you change hospitals, test results marked for mutual recognition should not be repeated.
16-3.gain: Chronic conditions require seeing how values shift over time; a single point is not enough. For hypertension, one meta-analysis pooled individual data from 15 randomized trials and 7,138 people. Compared with usual care, home self-measurement at 12 months meant mean change in office systolic blood pressure −3.2 mmHg (95% CI −4.9 to −1.6). Self-measurement alone without other support showed no clear effect: −1.0 mmHg (−3.3 to 1.2, difference may be chance). The most supported package lowered by 6.1 mmHg (3.2 to 9.0). Supported care means a doctor, pharmacist, or patient adjusting meds from readings, plus health education and lifestyle guidance. The author’s conclusion: measuring alone does not reliably lower pressure; pairing readings with dose adjustment does. These endpoints are blood pressure, not death. When changing hospitals, a joint measure from the National Health Commission «国家卫健委» and three other agencies states: if the patient’s existing test results meet mutual-recognition rules and satisfy clinical need, the hospital and clinician must not repeat tests. Recognized reports carry an “HR” mark, e.g. (全国HR) (national HR)
16-3.note: B only because direct evidence is for hypertension alone and stops at blood pressure, not mortality. No study was found on health outcomes from “keeping readings in one notebook” itself. Each time record at least four items: date, value, drug name, and dose. Photos of lab slips on your phone are fine, but keep everything in one place. Mutual recognition has exceptions: changed condition, rapidly changing results, before surgery or transfusion, and emergency rescue—hospitals may repeat tests. Copying and keeping medical records and imaging: see Section 24, item 5 (keep your own copy of records, reports, and imaging)

16-4.t: Do not stop standard treatment to try folk remedies or health supplements
16-4.cost: No cost; you also save what you would spend on supplements. No extra time. The hard part is holding firm when others keep pushing you to try something.
